Verify you can reach it:\n\n```bash theme={null}\ncurl -sI https://storage.googleapis.com\n```\n\nIf this fails, your network may be blocking the connection. Common causes:\n\n* Corporate firewalls or proxies blocking Google Cloud Storage\n* Regional network restrictions: try a VPN or alternative network\n* TLS/SSL issues: update your system's CA certificates, or check if `HTTPS_PROXY` is configured\n\nIf you're behind a corporate proxy, set `HTTPS_PROXY` and `HTTP_PROXY` to your proxy's address before installing. Ask your IT team for the proxy URL if you don't know it, or check your browser's proxy settings.\n\nThis example sets both proxy variables, then runs the installer through your proxy:\n\n```bash theme={null}\nexport HTTP_PROXY=http://proxy.example.com:8080\nexport HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy.example.com:8080\ncurl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash\n```\n\n### Verify your PATH\n\nIf installation succeeded but you get a `command not found` or `not recognized` error when running `claude`, the install directory isn't in your PATH. Your shell searches for programs in directories listed in PATH, and the installer places `claude` at `~/.local/bin/claude` on macOS/Linux or `%USERPROFILE%\\.local\\bin\\claude.exe` on Windows.\n\nCheck if the install directory is in your PATH by listing your PATH entries and filtering for `local/bin`:\n\n<Tabs>\n  <Tab title=\"macOS/Linux\">\n    ```bash theme={null}\n    echo $PATH | tr ':' '\\n' | grep local/bin\n    ```\n\n    If there's no output, the directory is missing. Add it to your shell configuration:\n\n    ```bash theme={null}\n    # Zsh (macOS default)\n    echo 'export PATH=\"$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH\"' >> ~/.zshrc\n    source ~/.zshrc\n\n    # Bash (Linux default)\n    echo 'export PATH=\"$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH\"' >> ~/.bashrc\n    source ~/.bashrc\n    ```\n\n    Alternatively, close and reopen your terminal.\n\n    Verify the fix worked:\n\n    ```bash theme={null}\n    claude --version\n    ```\n  </Tab>\n\n  <Tab title=\"Windows PowerShell\">\n    ```powershell theme={null}\n    $env:PATH -split ';' | Select-String 'local\\\\bin'\n    ```\n\n    If there's no output, add the install directory to your User PATH:\n\n    ```powershell theme={null}\n    $currentPath = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('PATH', 'User')\n    [Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('PATH', \"$currentPath;$env:USERPROFILE\\.local\\bin\", 'User')\n    ```\n\n    Restart your terminal for the change to take effect.\n\n    Verify the fix worked:\n\n    ```powershell theme={null}\n    claude --version\n    ```\n  </Tab>\n\n  <Tab title=\"Windows CMD\">\n    ```batch theme={null}\n    echo %PATH% | findstr /i \"local\\bin\"\n    ```\n\n    If there's no output, open System Settings, go to Environment Variables, and add `%USERPROFILE%\\.local\\bin` to your User PATH variable. Restart your terminal.\n\n    Verify the fix worked:\n\n    ```batch theme={null}\n    claude --version\n    ```\n  </Tab>\n</Tabs>\n\n### Check for conflicting installations\n\nMultiple Claude Code installations can cause version mismatches or unexpected behavior. Check what's installed:\n\n<Tabs>\n  <Tab title=\"macOS/Linux\">\n    List all `claude` binaries found in your PATH:\n\n    ```bash theme={null}\n    which -a claude\n    ```\n\n    Check whether the native installer and npm versions are present:\n\n    ```bash theme={null}\n    ls -la ~/.local/bin/claude\n    ```\n\n    ```bash theme={null}\n    ls -la ~/.claude/local/\n    ```\n\n    ```bash theme={null}\n    npm -g ls @anthropic-ai/claude-code 2>/dev/null\n    ```\n  </Tab>\n\n  <Tab title=\"Windows PowerShell\">\n    ```powershell theme={null}\n    where.exe claude\n    Test-Path \"$env:LOCALAPPDATA\\Claude Code\\claude.exe\"\n    ```\n  </Tab>\n</Tabs>\n\nIf you find multiple installations, keep only one. The native install at `~/.local/bin/claude` is recommended. Remove any extra installations:\n\nUninstall an npm global install:\n\n```bash theme={null}\nnpm uninstall -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code\n```\n\nRemove a Homebrew install on macOS (use `claude-code@latest` if you installed that cask):\n\n```bash theme={null}\nbrew uninstall --cask claude-code\n```\n\n### Check directory permissions\n\nThe installer needs write access to `~/.local/bin/` and `~/.claude/`. If installation fails with permission errors, check whether these directories are writable:\n\n```bash theme={null}\ntest -w ~/.local/bin && echo \"writable\" || echo \"not writable\"\ntest -w ~/.claude && echo \"writable\" || echo \"not writable\"\n```\n\nIf either directory isn't writable, create the install directory and set your user as the owner:\n\n```bash theme={null}\nsudo mkdir -p ~/.local/bin\nsudo chown -R $(whoami) ~/.local\n```\n\n### Verify the binary works\n\nIf `claude` is installed but crashes or hangs on startup, run these checks to narrow down the cause.\n\nConfirm the binary exists and is executable:\n\n```bash theme={null}\nls -la $(which claude)\n```\n\nOn Linux, check for missing shared libraries. If `ldd` shows missing libraries, you may need to install system packages. On Alpine Linux and other musl-based distributions, see [Alpine Linux setup](/en/setup#alpine-linux-and-musl-based-distributions).\n\n```bash theme={null}\nldd $(which claude) | grep \"not found\"\n```\n\nRun a quick sanity check that the binary can execute:\n\n```bash theme={null}\nclaude --version\n```\n\n## Common installation issues\n\nThese are the most frequently encountered installation problems and their solutions.\n\n### Install script returns HTML instead of a shell script\n\nWhen running the install command, you may see one of these errors:\n\n```text theme={null}\nbash: line 1: syntax error near unexpected token `<'\nbash: line 1: `<!DOCTYPE html>'\n```\n\nOn PowerShell, the same problem appears as:\n\n```text theme={null}\nInvoke-Expression: Missing argument in parameter list.\n```\n\nThis means the install URL returned an HTML page instead of the install script. If the HTML page says \"App unavailable in region,\" Claude Code is not available in your country. See [supported countries](https://www.anthropic.com/supported-countries).\n\nOtherwise, this can happen due to network issues, regional routing, or a temporary service disruption.\n\n**Solutions:**\n\n1. **Use an alternative install method**:\n\n   On macOS or Linux, install via Homebrew:\n\n   ```bash theme={null}\n   brew install --cask claude-code\n   ```\n\n   On Windows, install via WinGet:\n\n   ```powershell theme={null}\n   winget install Anthropic.ClaudeCode\n   ```\n\n2. **Retry after a few minutes**: the issue is often temporary. Wait and try the original command again.\n\n### `command not found: claude` after installation\n\nThe install finished but `claude` doesn't work. The exact error varies by platform:\n\n| Platform    | Error message                                                          |\n| :---------- | :--------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| macOS       | `zsh: command not found: claude`                                       |\n| Linux       | `bash: claude: command not found`                                      |\n| Windows CMD | `'claude' is not recognized as an internal or external command`        |\n| PowerShell  | `claude : The term 'claude' is not recognized as the name of a cmdlet` |\n\nThis means the install directory isn't in your shell's search path. See [Verify your PATH](#verify-your-path) for the fix on each platform.\n\n### `curl: (56) Failure writing output to destination`\n\nThe `curl ... | bash` command downloads the script and passes it directly to Bash for execution using a pipe (`|`). This error means the connection broke before the script finished downloading. Common causes include network interruptions, the download being blocked mid-stream, or system resource limits.\n\n**Solutions:**\n\n1. **Check network stability**: Claude Code binaries are hosted on Google Cloud Storage. Test that you can reach it:\n   ```bash theme={null}\n   curl -fsSL https://storage.googleapis.com -o /dev/null\n   ```\n   If the command completes silently, your connection is fine and the issue is likely intermittent. Retry the install command. If you see an error, your network may be blocking the download.\n\n2. **Try an alternative install method**:\n\n   On macOS or Linux:\n\n   ```bash theme={null}\n   brew install --cask claude-code\n   ```\n\n   On Windows:\n\n   ```powershell theme={null}\n   winget install Anthropic.ClaudeCode\n   ```\n\n### TLS or SSL connection errors\n\nErrors like `curl: (35) TLS connect error`, `schannel: next InitializeSecurityContext failed`, or PowerShell's `Could not establish trust relationship for the SSL/TLS secure channel` indicate TLS handshake failures.\n\n**Solutions:**\n\n1. **Update your system CA certificates**:\n\n   On Ubuntu/Debian:\n\n   ```bash theme={null}\n   sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install ca-certificates\n   ```\n\n   On macOS via Homebrew:\n\n   ```bash theme={null}\n   brew install ca-certificates\n   ```\n\n2. **On Windows, enable TLS 1.2** in PowerShell before running the installer:\n   ```powershell theme={null}\n   [Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol = [Net.SecurityProtocolType]::Tls12\n   irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex\n   ```\n\n3. **Check for proxy or firewall interference**: corporate proxies that perform TLS inspection can cause these errors, including `unable to get local issuer certificate`. Set `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` to your corporate CA certificate bundle:\n   ```bash theme={null}\n   export NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/path/to/corporate-ca.pem\n   ```\n   Ask your IT team for the certificate file if you don't have it. You can also try on a direct connection to confirm the proxy is the cause.\n\n4. **On Windows, bypass certificate revocation checks** if you see `CRYPT_E_NO_REVOCATION_CHECK (0x80092012)` or `CRYPT_E_REVOCATION_OFFLINE (0x80092013)`. These mean curl reached the server but your network blocks the certificate revocation lookup, which is common behind corporate firewalls. Add `--ssl-revoke-best-effort` to the install command:\n   ```bat theme={null}\n   curl --ssl-revoke-best-effort -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.cmd -o install.cmd && install.cmd && del install.cmd\n   ```\n   Alternatively, install with `winget install Anthropic.ClaudeCode`, which avoids curl entirely.\n\n### `Failed to fetch version from storage.googleapis.com`\n\nThe installer couldn't reach the download server. This typically means `storage.googleapis.com` is blocked on your network.\n\n**Solutions:**\n\n1. **Test connectivity directly**:\n   ```bash theme={null}\n   curl -sI https://storage.googleapis.com\n   ```\n\n2. **If behind a proxy**, set `HTTPS_PROXY` so the installer can route through it. See [proxy configuration](/en/network-config#proxy-configuration) for details.\n   ```bash theme={null}\n   export HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy.example.com:8080\n   curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash\n   ```\n\n3. **If on a restricted network**, try a different network or VPN, or use an alternative install method:\n\n   On macOS or Linux:\n\n   ```bash theme={null}\n   brew install --cask claude-code\n   ```\n\n   On Windows:\n\n   ```powershell theme={null}\n   winget install Anthropic.ClaudeCode\n   ```\n\n### Windows: wrong install command\n\nIf you see `'irm' is not recognized`, `The token '&&' is not valid`, or `'bash' is not recognized as the name of a cmdlet`, you copied the install command for a different shell or operating system.\n\n* **`irm` not recognized**: you're in CMD, not PowerShell. You have two options:\n\n  Open PowerShell by searching for \"PowerShell\" in the Start menu, then run the original install command:\n\n  ```powershell theme={null}\n  irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex\n  ```\n\n  Or stay in CMD and use the CMD installer instead:\n\n  ```batch theme={null}\n  curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.cmd -o install.cmd && install.cmd && del install.cmd\n  ```\n\n* **`&&` not valid**: you're in PowerShell but ran the CMD installer command. Use the PowerShell installer:\n  ```powershell theme={null}\n  irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex\n  ```\n\n* **`bash` not recognized**: you ran the macOS/Linux installer on Windows. Use the PowerShell installer instead:\n  ```powershell theme={null}\n  irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex\n  ```\n\n### Install killed on low-memory Linux servers\n\nIf you see `Killed` during installation on a VPS or cloud instance:\n\n```text theme={null}\nSetting up Claude Code...\nInstalling Claude Code native build latest...\nbash: line 142: 34803 Killed    \"$binary_path\" install ${TARGET:+\"$TARGET\"}\n```\n\nThe Linux OOM killer terminated the process because the system ran out of memory. Claude Code requires at least 4 GB of available RAM.\n\n**Solutions:**\n\n1. **Add swap space** if your server has limited RAM. Swap uses disk space as overflow memory, letting the install complete even with low physical RAM.\n\n   Create a 2 GB swap file and enable it:\n\n   ```bash theme={null}\n   sudo fallocate -l 2G /swapfile\n   sudo chmod 600 /swapfile\n   sudo mkswap /swapfile\n   sudo swapon /swapfile\n   ```\n\n   Then retry the installation:\n\n   ```bash theme={null}\n   curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash\n   ```\n\n2. **Close other processes** to free memory before installing.\n\n3. **Use a larger instance** if possible. Claude Code requires at least 4 GB of RAM.\n\n### Install hangs in Docker\n\nWhen installing Claude Code in a Docker container, installing as root into `/` can cause hangs.\n\n**Solutions:**\n\n1. **Set a working directory** before running the installer. When run from `/`, the installer scans the entire filesystem, which causes excessive memory usage. Setting `WORKDIR` limits the scan to a small directory:\n   ```dockerfile theme={null}\n   WORKDIR /tmp\n   RUN curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash\n   ```\n\n2. **Increase Docker memory limits** if using Docker Desktop:\n   ```bash theme={null}\n   docker build --memory=4g .\n   ```\n\n### Windows: Claude Desktop overrides `claude` CLI command\n\nIf you installed an older version of Claude Desktop, it may register a `Claude.exe` in the `WindowsApps` directory that takes PATH priority over Claude Code CLI. Running `claude` opens the Desktop app instead of the CLI.\n\nUpdate Claude Desktop to the latest version to fix this issue.\n\n### Windows: Claude Code on Windows requires git-bash\n\nClaude Code on native Windows needs [Git for Windows](https://git-scm.com/downloads/win), which includes Git Bash.\n\n**If Git is not installed**, download and install it from [git-scm.com/downloads/win](https://git-scm.com/downloads/win). During setup, select \"Add to PATH.\" Restart your terminal after installing.\n\n**If Git is already installed** but Claude Code still can't find it, set the path in your [settings.json file](/en/settings):\n\n```json theme={null}\n{\n  \"env\": {\n    \"CLAUDE_CODE_GIT_BASH_PATH\": \"C:\\\\Program Files\\\\Git\\\\bin\\\\bash.exe\"\n  }\n}\n```\n\nIf your Git is installed somewhere else, find the path by running `where.exe git` in PowerShell and use the `bin\\bash.exe` path from that directory.\n\n### Windows: Claude Code does not support 32-bit Windows\n\nWindows includes two PowerShell entries in the Start menu: `Windows PowerShell` and `Windows PowerShell (x86)`. The x86 entry runs as a 32-bit process and triggers this error even on a 64-bit machine. To check which case you're in, run this in the same window that produced the error:\n\n```powershell theme={null}\n[Environment]::Is64BitOperatingSystem\n```\n\nIf this prints `True`, your operating system is fine. Close the window, open `Windows PowerShell` without the x86 suffix, and run the install command again.\n\nIf this prints `False`, you are on a 32-bit edition of Windows. Claude Code requires a 64-bit operating system. See the [system requirements](/en/setup#system-requirements).\n\n### Linux: wrong binary variant installed (musl/glibc mismatch)\n\nIf you see errors about missing shared libraries like `libstdc++.so.6` or `libgcc_s.so.1` after installation, the installer may have downloaded the wrong binary variant for your system.\n\n```text theme={null}\nError loading shared library libstdc++.so.6: No such file or directory\n```\n\nThis can happen on glibc-based systems that have musl cross-compilation packages installed, causing the installer to misdetect the system as musl.\n\n**Solutions:**\n\n1. **Check which libc your system uses**:\n   ```bash theme={null}\n   ldd /bin/ls | head -1\n   ```\n   If it shows `linux-vdso.so` or references to `/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/`, you're on glibc. If it shows `musl`, you're on musl.\n\n2. **If you're on glibc but got the musl binary**, remove the installation and reinstall. You can also manually download the correct binary from the GCS bucket at `https://storage.googleapis.com/claude-code-dist-86c565f3-f756-42ad-8dfa-d59b1c096819/claude-code-releases/{VERSION}/manifest.json`. File a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues) with the output of `ldd /bin/ls` and `ls /lib/libc.musl*`.\n\n3. **If you're actually on musl** (Alpine Linux), install the required packages:\n   ```bash theme={null}\n   apk add libgcc libstdc++ ripgrep\n   ```\n\n### `Illegal instruction` on Linux\n\nIf the installer prints `Illegal instruction` instead of the OOM `Killed` message, the downloaded binary doesn't match your CPU architecture. This commonly happens on ARM servers that receive an x86 binary, or on older CPUs that lack required instruction sets.\n\n```text theme={null}\nbash: line 142: 2238232 Illegal instruction    \"$binary_path\" install ${TARGET:+\"$TARGET\"}\n```\n\n**Solutions:**\n\n1. **Verify your architecture**:\n   ```bash theme={null}\n   uname -m\n   ```\n   `x86_64` means 64-bit Intel/AMD, `aarch64` means ARM64. If the binary doesn't match, [file a GitHub issue](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues) with the output.\n\n2. **Try an alternative install method** while the architecture issue is resolved:\n   ```bash theme={null}\n   brew install --cask claude-code\n   ```\n\n### `dyld: cannot load` on macOS\n\nIf you see `dyld: cannot load`, `dyld: Symbol not found`, or `Abort trap: 6` during installation, the binary is incompatible with your macOS version or hardware.\n\n```text theme={null}\ndyld: cannot load 'claude-2.1.42-darwin-x64' (load command 0x80000034 is unknown)\nAbort trap: 6\n```\n\nA `Symbol not found` error that references `libicucore` also indicates your macOS version is older than the binary supports:\n\n```text theme={null}\ndyld: Symbol not found: _ubrk_clone\n  Referenced from: claude-darwin-x64 (which was built for Mac OS X 13.0)\n  Expected in: /usr/lib/libicucore.A.dylib\n```\n\n**Solutions:**\n\n1. **Check your macOS version**: Claude Code requires macOS 13.0 or later. Open the Apple menu and select About This Mac to check your version.\n\n2. **Update macOS** if you're on an older version. The binary uses load commands that older macOS versions don't support.\n\n3. **Try Homebrew** as an alternative install method:\n   ```bash theme={null}\n   brew install --cask claude-code\n   ```\n\n### Windows installation issues: errors in WSL\n\nYou might encounter the following issues in WSL:\n\n**OS/platform detection issues**: if you receive an error during installation, WSL may be using Windows `npm`. Try:\n\n* Run `npm config set os linux` before installation\n* Install with `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code --force --no-os-check`. Do not use `sudo`.\n\n**Node not found errors**: if you see `exec: node: not found` when running `claude`, your WSL environment may be using a Windows installation of Node.js. You can confirm this with `which npm` and `which node`, which should point to Linux paths starting with `/usr/` rather than `/mnt/c/`. To fix this, try installing Node via your Linux distribution's package manager or via [`nvm`](https://github.com/nvm-sh/nvm).\n\n**nvm version conflicts**: if you have nvm installed in both WSL and Windows, you may experience version conflicts when switching Node versions in WSL. This happens because WSL imports the Windows PATH by default, causing Windows nvm/npm to take priority over the WSL installation.\n\nYou can identify this issue by:\n\n* Running `which npm` and `which node` - if they point to Windows paths (starting with `/mnt/c/`), Windows versions are being used\n* Experiencing broken functionality after switching Node versions with nvm in WSL\n\nTo resolve this issue, fix your Linux PATH to ensure the Linux node/npm versions take priority:\n\n**Primary solution: Ensure nvm is properly loaded in your shell**\n\nThe most common cause is that nvm isn't loaded in non-interactive shells. Add the following to your shell configuration file (`~/.bashrc`, `~/.zshrc`, etc.):\n\n```bash theme={null}\n# Load nvm if it exists\nexport NVM_DIR=\"$HOME/.nvm\"\n[ -s \"$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh\" ] && \\. \"$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh\"\n[ -s \"$NVM_DIR/bash_completion\" ] && \\. \"$NVM_DIR/bash_completion\"\n```\n\nOr run directly in your current session:\n\n```bash theme={null}\nsource ~/.nvm/nvm.sh\n```\n\n**Alternative: Adjust PATH order**\n\nIf nvm is properly loaded but Windows paths still take priority, you can explicitly prepend your Linux paths to PATH in your shell configuration:\n\n```bash theme={null}\nexport PATH=\"$HOME/.nvm/versions/node/$(node -v)/bin:$PATH\"\n```\n\n<Warning>\n  Avoid disabling Windows PATH importing via `appendWindowsPath = false` as this breaks the ability to call Windows executables from WSL. Similarly, avoid uninstalling Node.js from Windows if you use it for Windows development.\n</Warning>\n\n### WSL2 sandbox setup\n\n[Sandboxing](/en/sandboxing) is supported on WSL2 but requires installing additional packages. If you see an error about missing `bubblewrap` or `socat` when running `/sandbox`, install the dependencies:\n\n<Tabs>\n  <Tab title=\"Ubuntu/Debian\">\n    ```bash theme={null}\n    sudo apt-get install bubblewrap socat\n    ```\n  </Tab>\n\n  <Tab title=\"Fedora\">\n    ```bash theme={null}\n    sudo dnf install bubblewrap socat\n    ```\n  </Tab>\n</Tabs>\n\nWSL1 does not support sandboxing. If you see \"Sandboxing requires WSL2\", you need to upgrade to WSL2 or run Claude Code without sandboxing.\n\nSandboxed commands cannot launch Windows binaries such as `cmd.exe`, `powershell.exe`, or executables under `/mnt/c/`. WSL hands these off to the Windows host over a Unix socket, which the sandbox blocks. If a command needs to invoke a Windows binary, add it to [`excludedCommands`](/en/settings#sandbox-settings) so it runs outside the sandbox.\n\n### Permission errors during installation\n\nIf the native installer fails with permission errors, the target directory may not be writable. See [Check directory permissions](#check-directory-permissions).\n\nIf you previously installed with npm and are hitting npm-specific permission errors, switch to the native installer:\n\n```bash theme={null}\ncurl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash\n```\n\n## Permissions and authentication\n\nThese sections address login failures, token issues, and permission prompt behavior.\n\n### Repeated permission prompts\n\nIf you find yourself repeatedly approving the same commands, you can allow specific tools\nto run without approval using the `/permissions` command. See [Permissions docs](/en/permissions#manage-permissions).\n\n### Authentication issues\n\nIf you're experiencing authentication problems:\n\n1. Run `/logout` to sign out completely\n2. Close Claude Code\n3. Restart with `claude` and complete the authentication process again\n\nIf the browser doesn't open automatically during login, press `c` to copy the OAuth URL to your clipboard, then paste it into your browser manually.\n\n### OAuth error: Invalid code\n\nIf you see `OAuth error: Invalid code. Please make sure the full code was copied`, the login code expired or was truncated during copy-paste.\n\n**Solutions:**\n\n* Press Enter to retry and complete the login quickly after the browser opens\n* Type `c` to copy the full URL if the browser doesn't open automatically\n* If using a remote/SSH session, the browser may open on the wrong machine. Copy the URL displayed in the terminal and open it in your local browser instead.\n\n### 403 Forbidden after login\n\nIf you see `API Error: 403 {\"error\":{\"type\":\"forbidden\",\"message\":\"Request not allowed\"}}` after logging in:\n\n* **Claude Pro/Max users**: verify your subscription is active at [claude.ai/settings](https://claude.ai/settings)\n* **Console users**: confirm your account has the \"Claude Code\" or \"Developer\" role assigned by your admin\n* **Behind a proxy**: corporate proxies can interfere with API requests. See [network configuration](/en/network-config) for proxy setup.\n\n### Model not found or not accessible\n\nIf you see `There's an issue with the selected model (...). It may not exist or you may not have access to it`, the API rejected the configured model name.\n\nCommon causes:\n\n* A typo in the model name passed to `--model`\n* A stale or deprecated model ID saved in your settings\n* An API key without access to that model on your current usage tier\n\nCheck where the model is set, in [priority order](/en/model-config#setting-your-model):\n\n* The `--model` flag\n* The `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` environment variable\n* The `model` field in `.claude/settings.local.json`\n* The `model` field in your project's `.claude/settings.json`\n* The `model` field in `~/.claude/settings.json`\n\nTo clear a stale value, remove the `model` field from your settings or unset `ANTHROPIC_MODEL`, and Claude Code will fall back to the default model for your account.\n\nTo browse models available to your account, start `claude` interactively and run `/model` to open the picker. For Vertex AI deployments, see [the Vertex AI troubleshooting section](/en/google-vertex-ai#troubleshooting).\n\n### This organization has been disabled with an active subscription\n\nIf you see `API Error: 400 ... \"This organization has been disabled\"` despite having an active Claude subscription, an `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` environment variable is overriding your subscription. This commonly happens when an old API key from a previous employer or project is still set in your shell profile.\n\nWhen `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is present and you have approved it, Claude Code uses that key instead of your subscription's OAuth credentials. In non-interactive mode (`-p`), the key is always used when present. See [authentication precedence](/en/authentication#authentication-precedence) for the full resolution order.\n\nTo use your subscription instead, unset the environment variable and remove it from your shell profile:\n\n```bash theme={null}\nunset ANTHROPIC_API_KEY\nclaude\n```\n\nCheck `~/.zshrc`, `~/.bashrc`, or `~/.profile` for `export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...` lines and remove them to make the change permanent. Run `/status` inside Claude Code to confirm which authentication method is active.\n\n### OAuth login fails in WSL2\n\nBrowser-based login in WSL2 may fail if WSL can't open your Windows browser. Set the `BROWSER` environment variable:\n\n```bash theme={null}\nexport BROWSER=\"/mnt/c/Program Files/Google/Chrome/Application/chrome.exe\"\nclaude\n```\n\nOr copy the URL manually: when the login prompt appears, press `c` to copy the OAuth URL, then paste it into your Windows browser.\n\n### Not logged in or token expired\n\nIf Claude Code prompts you to log in again after a session, your OAuth token may have expired.\n\nRun `/login` to re-authenticate. If this happens frequently, check that your system clock is accurate, as token validation depends on correct timestamps.\n\nOn macOS, login can also fail when the Keychain is locked or its password is out of sync with your account password, which prevents Claude Code from saving credentials. Run `claude doctor` to check Keychain access. To unlock the Keychain manually, run `security unlock-keychain ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db`. If unlocking doesn't help, open Keychain Access, select the `login` keychain, and choose Edit > Change Password for Keychain \"login\" to resync it with your account password.\n\n## Configuration file locations\n\nClaude Code stores configuration in several locations:\n\n| File                          | Purpose                                                                                                |\n| :---------------------------- | :----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| `~/.claude/settings.json`     | User settings (permissions, hooks, model overrides)                                                    |\n| `.claude/settings.json`       | Project settings (checked into source control)                                                         |\n| `.claude/settings.local.json` | Local project settings (not committed)                                                                 |\n| `~/.claude.json`              | Global state (theme, OAuth, MCP servers)                                                               |\n| `.mcp.json`                   | Project MCP servers (checked into source control)                                                      |\n| `managed-mcp.json`            | [Managed MCP servers](/en/mcp#managed-mcp-configuration)                                               |\n| Managed settings              | [Managed settings](/en/settings#settings-files) (server-managed, MDM/OS-level policies, or file-based) |\n\nOn Windows, `~` refers to your user home directory, such as `C:\\Users\\YourName`.\n\nFor details on configuring these files, see [Settings](/en/settings) and [MCP](/en/mcp).\n\n### Resetting configuration\n\nTo reset Claude Code to default settings, you can remove the configuration files:\n\n```bash theme={null}\n# Reset all user settings and state\nrm ~/.claude.json\nrm -rf ~/.claude/\n\n# Reset project-specific settings\nrm -rf .claude/\nrm .mcp.json\n```\n\n<Warning>\n  This will remove all your settings, MCP server configurations, and session history.\n</Warning>\n\n## Performance and stability\n\nThese sections cover issues related to resource usage, responsiveness, and search behavior.\n\n### High CPU or memory usage\n\nClaude Code is designed to work with most development environments, but may consume significant resources when processing large codebases. If you're experiencing performance issues:\n\n1. Use `/compact` regularly to reduce context size\n2. Close and restart Claude Code between major tasks\n3. Consider adding large build directories to your `.gitignore` file\n\n### Auto-compaction stops with a thrashing error\n\nIf you see `Autocompact is thrashing: the context refilled to the limit...`, automatic compaction succeeded but a file or tool output immediately refilled the context window several times in a row. Claude Code stops retrying to avoid wasting API calls on a loop that isn't making progress.\n\nTo recover:\n\n1. Ask Claude to read the oversized file in smaller chunks, such as a specific line range or function, instead of the whole file\n2. Run `/compact` with a focus that drops the large output, for example `/compact keep only the plan and the diff`\n3. Move the large-file work to a [subagent](/en/sub-agents) so it runs in a separate context window\n4. Run `/clear` if the earlier conversation is no longer needed\n\n### Command hangs or freezes\n\nIf Claude Code seems unresponsive:\n\n1. Press Ctrl+C to attempt to cancel the current operation\n2. If unresponsive, you may need to close the terminal and restart\n\n### Search and discovery issues\n\nIf Search tool, `@file` mentions, custom agents, and custom skills aren't working, install system `ripgrep`:\n\n```bash theme={null}\n# macOS (Homebrew)  \nbrew install ripgrep\n\n# Windows (winget)\nwinget install BurntSushi.ripgrep.MSVC\n\n# Ubuntu/Debian\nsudo apt install ripgrep\n\n# Alpine Linux\napk add ripgrep\n\n# Arch Linux\npacman -S ripgrep\n```\n\nThen set `USE_BUILTIN_RIPGREP=0` in your [environment](/en/env-vars).\n\n### Slow or incomplete search results on WSL\n\nDisk read performance penalties when [working across file systems on WSL](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/filesystems) may result in fewer-than-expected matches when using Claude Code on WSL. Header regex: /^##\\s+Artifact\\s+\\d+:\\s+(.+)$/m — extract artifact name.\n  2. Metadata: Parse **Label:** lines using a helper similar to P1's\n  parseMetadataLine. Labels to parse: Document Type, Source Photo, Original\n  Filename, Orientation, Customer-Facing, Source Screen, Document Set, Data\n  Format. All nullable.\n  3. ### Fields Extracted: Parse the 5-column table (# | Field Label | Value |\n  Type | Extraction Quality). Same row-parsing technique as P1's\n  parseFieldTable, mapping to ArtifactFieldEntry.\n  4. ### Tabular Data: May contain multiple **Table:** blocks within one\n  section. For each block, parse:\n    - **Table:** → tableName\n    - **Columns:** → columns (number)\n    - **Rows:** or **Data Rows:** → rows (number)\n    - **Column Alignment Confidence:** → columnAlignmentConfidence\n    - The markdown table after the metadata: first row with pipe separators is\n  headers, separator row (dashes), then data rows. The last column in each data\n  row is the row-level Extraction Quality flag.\n  5. ### Matrix/Grid Structure (P3 only): Convert to TabularDataSection:\n    - **Extraction Confidence:** → columnAlignmentConfidence\n    - **Matrix Dimensions:** → parse {rows} x {columns} for rows and columns\n    - Parse the matrix table. First column cells are bold row headers (strip **\n  markers). Remaining columns are data cells. Each data cell may contain inline\n  quality flags like [CLEAR] at the end.\n    - Strip inline quality flags from cell values. Aggregate to row-level: the\n  worst quality flag among all cells in a row becomes the row's\n  extractionQuality. Severity order: UNREADABLE > UNCERTAIN > PARTIAL > CLEAR.\n  Default CLEAR if no flag found.\n    - tableName: use the artifact name from the parent entry.\n    - Add observation: \"Original extraction included per-cell quality flags —\n  see source extraction for detail.\"\n  6. ### Supplementary Notes (P3 only): Parse bullet items. Merge into the\n  observations array.\n  7. ### Business Rules Visible: Parse bullet items → businessRules array.\n  8. ### Observations: Parse bullet items → observations array.\n\n  Tests\n\n  Test file: src/lib/pipeline/artifact-output-parser.test.ts\n\n  Test 1: \"parses P2 artifact with metadata and fields\" — Standard P2 output\n  with all metadata lines and a ### Fields Extracted table with 3 rows.      // video timestamp in seconds\n  description: string;    // Gemini-generated description of what's on screen\n  imagePath: string;\n}\n\n/**\n * Strategy A: VTT↔Otter text match.\n * Parse both VTT and Otter segments, fuzzy-match text segments (>60% word overlap),\n * calculate offset per match, return median.\n */\nexport function calculateWordOverlap(textA: string, textB: string): number {\n  const wordsA = new Set(textA.toLowerCase().split(/\\s+/).filter(w => w.length > 3));\n  const wordsB = new Set(textB.toLowerCase().split(/\\s+/).filter(w => w.length > 3));\n  if (wordsA.size === 0 || wordsB.size === 0) return 0;\n  const intersection = [...wordsA].filter(w => wordsB.has(w)).length;\n  const minSize = Math.min(wordsA.size, wordsB.size);\n  return intersection / minSize;\n}\n\nexport function strategyA(\n  vttSegments: TranscriptSegment[],\n  otterSegments: TranscriptSegment[],\n): OffsetResult | null {\n  const matches: number[] = [];\n\n  for (const vtt of vttSegments) {\n    for (const otter of otterSegments) {\n      const overlap = calculateWordOverlap(vtt.text, otter.text);\n      if (overlap >= 0.6) {\n        // offset = otterTime - videoTime\n        matches.push(otter.startTime - vtt.startTime);\n      }\n    }\n  }\n\n  if (matches.length < 3) return null;\n\n  matches.sort((a, b) => a - b);\n  const median = matches[Math.floor(matches.length / 2)];\n  const variance = matches.reduce((sum, m) => sum + Math.abs(m - median), 0) / matches.length;\n\n  return {\n    offsetSeconds: median,\n    confidence: variance < 5 ? 'high' : variance < 15 ? 'medium' : 'low',\n    strategy: 'vtt_text_match',\n    matchCount: matches.length,\n    varianceSeconds: variance,\n  };\n}\n\n/**\n * Strategy B: Gemini visual↔Otter keyword match.\n * Pick scene-change frames, get Gemini descriptions, search Otter for keywords,\n * calculate offset from matches.\n *\n * frameDescriptions: pre-classified frames with Gemini descriptions (from frame-classifier).\n * otterSegments: parsed Otter transcript.\n */\nexport function strategyB(\n  frameDescriptions: FrameDescription[],\n  otterSegments: TranscriptSegment[],\n): OffsetResult | null {\n  // Pick up to 5 well-spaced frames\n  const picked = pickSpacedFrames(frameDescriptions, 5);\n  if (picked.length === 0) return null;\n\n  const matches: number[] = [];\n\n  for (const frame of picked) {\n    // Extract keywords from Gemini description (nouns, app-specific terms)\n    const keywords = extractKeywords(frame.description);\n    if (keywords.length === 0) continue;\n\n    // Find best matching Otter segment\n    let bestScore = 0;\n    let bestOtterTime = 0;\n    for (const otter of otterSegments) {\n      const score = keywords.filter(kw =>\n        otter.text.toLowerCase().includes(kw.toLowerCase())\n      ).length / keywords.length;\n      if (score > bestScore) {\n        bestScore = score;\n        bestOtterTime = otter.startTime;\n      }\n    }\n\n    if (bestScore >= 0.3) {\n      matches.push(bestOtterTime - frame.timestamp);\n    }\n  }\n\n  if (matches.length < 2) return null;\n\n  matches.sort((a, b) => a - b);\n  const median = matches[Math.floor(matches.length / 2)];\n  const variance = matches.reduce((sum, m) => sum + Math.abs(m - median), 0) / matches.length;\n\n  return {\n    offsetSeconds: median,\n    confidence: variance < 10 ? 'high' : variance < 30 ? 'medium' : 'low',\n    strategy: 'gemini_visual_match',\n    matchCount: matches.length,\n    varianceSeconds: variance,\n  };\n}\n\n/**\n * Strategy C: Manual entry fallback.\n */\nexport function strategyManual(offsetSeconds: number): OffsetResult {\n  return {\n    offsetSeconds,\n    confidence: 'high',\n    strategy: 'manual',\n    matchCount: 0,\n    varianceSeconds: 0,\n  };\n}\n\nexport function pickSpacedFrames(frames: FrameDescription[], count: number): FrameDescription[] {\n  if (frames.length <= count) return frames;\n  const step = frames.length / count;\n  const picked: FrameDescription[] = [];\n  for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {\n    picked.push(frames[Math.floor(i * step)]);\n  }\n  return picked;\n}\n\nexport function extractKeywords(description: string): string[] {\n  // Extract meaningful words (4+ chars, not common stop words)\n  const stopWords = new Set([\n    'this', 'that', 'with', 'from', 'have', 'been', 'were', 'they',\n    'will', 'would', 'could', 'should', 'there', 'their', 'about',\n    'which', 'when', 'what', 'some', 'other', 'than', 'then', 'also',\n    'just', 'more', 'very', 'into', 'over', 'such', 'after', 'before',\n    'between', 'each', 'being', 'does', 'doing', 'during', 'having',\n    'image', 'shows', 'showing', 'screen', 'appears', 'displayed',\n    'visible', 'window', 'application',\n  ]);\n  return description\n    .split(/[\\s,;:.!?()]+/)\n    .filter(w => w.length >= 4 && !stopWords.has(w.toLowerCase()))\n    .map(w => w.toLowerCase());\n}\n\n/**\n * Main entry point. Tries strategies in order: A → B → null (caller should prompt for manual).\n */\nexport async function calculateOffset(\n  vttSegments: TranscriptSegment[] | null,\n  otterSegments: TranscriptSegment[],\n  frameDescriptions: FrameDescription[],\n): Promise<OffsetResult | null> {\n  // Strategy A: VTT↔Otter text match (fastest, most accurate when VTT available)\n  if (vttSegments && vttSegments.length > 0) {\n    const resultA = strategyA(vttSegments, otterSegments);\n    if (resultA && resultA.confidence !== 'low') {\n      return resultA;\n    }\n  }\n\n  // Strategy B: Gemini visual↔Otter keyword match\n  if (frameDescriptions.length > 0 && otterSegments.length > 0) {\n    const resultB = strategyB(frameDescriptions, otterSegments);\n    if (resultB) {\n      return resultB;\n    }\n  }\n\n  // No automated strategy produced confident result\n  return null;\n}\n```\n\n#### Tests: `src/lib/pipeline/offset-calculator.test.ts`\n\nTest cases:\n1. **calculateWordOverlap** — 100% overlap returns 1.0, 0% returns 0, partial returns correct ratio, ignores short words (<4 chars)\n2. **strategyA** — returns high-confidence result when 5+ VTT/Otter segments match with >60% overlap, returns null with fewer than 3 matches, calculates correct median offset, variance reflects spread\n3. **strategyB** — returns result when keywords match Otter segments, returns null when no keywords match, picks spaced frames correctly\n4. **pickSpacedFrames** — returns all frames if count >= frames.length, picks evenly spaced frames otherwise\n5. **extractKeywords** — filters stop words, filters short words, lowercases\n6. **calculateOffset** — tries strategy A first when VTT available, falls back to B when A returns null, falls back to B when A returns low confidence, returns null when both fail, skips A when no VTT segments\n7. **strategyManual** — returns correct result with high confidence and manual strategy\n\nUse mock TranscriptSegment data — do NOT read real files in unit tests.       // video timestamp in seconds\n  isScreen: boolean;\n  description: string;     // Gemini description — reused for offset calculation\n  filterReason?: string;   // 'face' | 'transition' | 'blank' | 'other' if not a screen\n}\n\n/**\n * Classify a batch of frames using Gemini.\n * Batches 4-6 frames at a time to reduce API calls.\n * Returns classification + description for each frame.\n */\nexport async function classifyFrames(\n  frames: { imagePath: string; timestamp: number }[],\n  batchSize: number = 4,\n): Promise<ClassifiedFrame[]> {\n  const results: ClassifiedFrame[] = [];\n\n  for (let i = 0; i < frames.length; i += batchSize) {\n    const batch = frames.slice(i, i + batchSize);\n    const batchResults = await classifyBatch(batch);\n    results.push(...batchResults);\n  }\n\n  return results;\n}\n\nexport async function classifyBatch(\n  frames: { imagePath: string; timestamp: number }[],\n): Promise<ClassifiedFrame[]> {\n  const fileParts = await Promise.all(\n    frames.map(async (frame) => {\n      const data = await readFile(frame.imagePath);\n      const mediaType = detectMediaType(frame.imagePath);\n      return { type: 'file' as const, data, mediaType };\n    }),\n  );\n\n  const prompt = `You are classifying ${frames.length} video frames. For EACH frame (numbered 1 to ${frames.length}), determine:\n\n1. Is this a software application screen? (Yes/No)\n2. Brief description of what's shown (10-20 words)\n3. If not a software screen, why? (face/transition/blank/other)\n\nA \"software application screen\" means a desktop or web application UI with forms, fields, menus, buttons, or data grids. Zoom meeting participant video, webcam feeds, desktop backgrounds, and loading screens are NOT software screens.\n\nReply in this exact format, one line per frame:\nFRAME 1: [YES|NO] | [description] | [reason if NO]\nFRAME 2: [YES|NO] | [description] | [reason if NO]\n...`;\n\n  const { text } = await generateText({\n    model: google('gemini-2.5-flash'),\n    messages: [\n      {\n        role: 'user',\n        content: [\n          ...fileParts,\n          { type: 'text', text: prompt },\n        ],\n      },\n    ],\n  });\n\n  return parseClassificationResponse(text, frames);\n}\n\nexport function parseClassificationResponse(\n  response: string,\n  frames: { imagePath: string; timestamp: number }[],\n): ClassifiedFrame[] {\n  const lines = response.split('\\n').filter(l => l.trim().startsWith('FRAME'));\n  const results: ClassifiedFrame[] = [];\n\n  for (let i = 0; i < frames.length; i++) {\n    const line = lines[i];\n    if (!line) {\n      // Default to keeping unclassified frames as screens (conservative)\n      results.push({\n        imagePath: frames[i].imagePath,\n        timestamp: frames[i].timestamp,\n        isScreen: true,\n        description: 'Classification unavailable',\n      });\n      continue;\n    }\n\n    const parts = line.split('|').map(p => p.trim());\n    const isScreen = parts[0]?.toUpperCase().includes('YES') ?? false;\n    const description = parts[1] || 'No description';\n    const filterReason = !isScreen ? (parts[2] || 'other') : undefined;\n\n    results.push({\n      imagePath: frames[i].imagePath,\n      timestamp: frames[i].timestamp,\n      isScreen,\n      description,\n      filterReason,\n    });\n  }\n\n  return results;\n}\n```\n\n#### Tests: `src/lib/pipeline/frame-classifier.test.ts`\n\nTest cases:\n1. **parseClassificationResponse** — parses YES responses correctly, parses NO responses with filter reason, handles missing lines (defaults to isScreen=true), handles empty response\n2. **classifyFrames** — batches correctly (10 frames with batchSize=4 → 3 batches), passes frames to classifyBatch\n3. Mock the Gemini call in classifyBatch — vi.mock `@ai-sdk/google` and `ai` as done in existing tests\n\n---\n\n### File 3: `src/lib/pipeline/frame-dedup.ts`\n\n```typescript\nimport sharp from 'sharp';\nimport type { ClassifiedFrame } from './frame-classifier';\n\nexport interface FrameGroup {\n  frames: ClassifiedFrame[];\n  representative: ClassifiedFrame;  // first frame in group\n}\n\nexport interface DedupResult {\n  selectedFrames: ClassifiedFrame[];\n  groups: FrameGroup[];\n  droppedCount: number;\n}\n\n// NOTE: This dedup compares CONSECUTIVE frames only. Non-consecutive appearances of the\n// same screen (e.g., Screen A at 5:00, Screen B at 20:00, Screen A at 45:00) will NOT be\n// grouped — both go through P1 extraction. A1 assembly merges them later via title-bar\n// grouping, so correctness is preserved, but extra Gemini calls are spent.\n// TODO: Future improvement — cross-group similarity comparison to catch non-consecutive duplicates.\n\n/**\n * Generate a small thumbnail for pixel comparison.\n */\nexport async function generateThumbnail(imagePath: string): Promise<Buffer> {\n  return sharp(imagePath)\n    .resize(64, 64, { fit: 'fill' })\n    .grayscale()\n    .raw()\n    .toBuffer();\n}\n\n/**\n * Calculate normalized pixel difference between two thumbnails.\n * Returns 0.0 (identical) to 1.0 (completely different).\n */\nexport function pixelDifference(thumbA: Buffer, thumbB: Buffer): number {\n  if (thumbA.length !== thumbB.length) return 1.0;\n  let totalDiff = 0;\n  for (let i = 0; i < thumbA.length; i++) {\n    totalDiff += Math.abs(thumbA[i] - thumbB[i]);\n  }\n  return totalDiff / (thumbA.length * 255);\n}\n\n/**\n * Group consecutive similar screen frames.\n * Similarity threshold: frames with <15% pixel difference are grouped.\n */\nexport async function groupConsecutiveFrames(\n  frames: ClassifiedFrame[],\n  similarityThreshold: number = 0.15,\n): Promise<FrameGroup[]> {\n  if (frames.length === 0) return [];\n\n  const thumbnails = await Promise.all(\n    frames.map(f => generateThumbnail(f.imagePath)),\n  );\n\n  const groups: FrameGroup[] = [];\n  let currentGroup: ClassifiedFrame[] = [frames[0]];\n\n  for (let i = 1; i < frames.length; i++) {\n    const diff = pixelDifference(thumbnails[i - 1], thumbnails[i]);\n    if (diff < similarityThreshold) {\n      currentGroup.push(frames[i]);\n    } else {\n      groups.push({\n        frames: currentGroup,\n        representative: currentGroup[0],\n      });\n      currentGroup = [frames[i]];\n    }\n  }\n\n  // Push final group\n  groups.push({\n    frames: currentGroup,\n    representative: currentGroup[0],\n  });\n\n  return groups;\n}\n\n/**\n * Select 2-3 most visually diverse frames from a group.\n * For groups of 1-3, keep all. For larger groups, pick first, last, and most different from first.\n */\nexport async function selectDiverseFrames(\n  group: FrameGroup,\n  maxSelect: number = 3,\n): Promise<ClassifiedFrame[]> {\n  const { frames } = group;\n  if (frames.length <= maxSelect) return [...frames];\n\n  // Always keep first and last\n  const selected: ClassifiedFrame[] = [frames[0]];\n\n  if (maxSelect >= 3 && frames.length > 2) {\n    // Find the frame most different from the first\n    const firstThumb = await generateThumbnail(frames[0].imagePath);\n    let maxDiff = 0;\n    let mostDifferentIdx = 1;\n\n    for (let i = 1; i < frames.length - 1; i++) {\n      const thumb = await generateThumbnail(frames[i].imagePath);\n      const diff = pixelDifference(firstThumb, thumb);\n      if (diff > maxDiff) {\n        maxDiff = diff;\n        mostDifferentIdx = i;\n      }\n    }\n\n    selected.push(frames[mostDifferentIdx]);\n  }\n\n  selected.push(frames[frames.length - 1]);\n\n  // Deduplicate in case mostDifferent is the last frame\n  const uniquePaths = new Set<string>();\n  return selected.filter(f => {\n    if (uniquePaths.has(f.imagePath)) return false;\n    uniquePaths.add(f.imagePath);\n    return true;\n  });\n}\n\n/**\n * Main entry point. Groups consecutive similar frames, selects 2-3 per group.\n */\nexport async function deduplicateFrames(\n  screenFrames: ClassifiedFrame[],\n  options?: { similarityThreshold?: number; maxPerGroup?: number },\n): Promise<DedupResult> {\n  const threshold = options?.similarityThreshold ?? 0.15;\n  const maxPerGroup = options?.maxPerGroup ?? 3;\n\n  const groups = await groupConsecutiveFrames(screenFrames, threshold);\n\n  const selectedFrames: ClassifiedFrame[] = [];\n  let droppedCount = 0;\n\n  for (const group of groups) {\n    const selected = await selectDiverseFrames(group, maxPerGroup);\n    selectedFrames.push(...selected);\n    droppedCount += group.frames.length - selected.length;\n  }\n\n  return { selectedFrames, groups, droppedCount };\n}\n```\n\n#### Tests: `src/lib/pipeline/frame-dedup.test.ts`\n\nTest cases:\n1. **pixelDifference** — identical buffers return 0, completely different buffers return ~1.0, different length buffers return 1.0\n2. **groupConsecutiveFrames** — groups similar consecutive frames together, separates dissimilar frames into different groups, single frame returns one group, empty input returns empty array. Mock `sharp` via `vi.mock('sharp')` to return controlled thumbnail buffers.\n3. **selectDiverseFrames** — keeps all frames for groups of 1-3, selects 3 diverse frames for larger groups, deduplicates if most-different is the last frame\n4. **deduplicateFrames** — full integration: 10 frames with 3 groups → selects 6-9 frames, tracks droppedCount correctly\n5. videoTime + offsetSeconds\n// This module uses per-chunk offsets to index into a day-level Otter file.\n// The default case is ONE Otter transcript covering MULTIPLE video chunks.\n// Each chunk has its own offset; this module applies the chunk's offset to\n// find the correct section of the day-level Otter transcript for each frame.\n\nimport type { TranscriptSegment } from './transcript';\n\nexport interface FrameTranscriptContext {\n  imagePath: string;\n  videoTimestamp: number;    // original video timestamp\n  alignedOtterTime: number;  // videoTimestamp + offsetSeconds\n  transcriptSnippet: string; // Otter text ±60s around aligned time\n  speakers: string[];\n}\n\nexport interface ArtifactTranscriptContext {\n  artifactFilename: string;\n  transcriptSnippet: string;\n  matchedKeywords: string[];\n  speakers: string[];\n}\n\n/**\n * Get transcript context for a single frame.\n * Applies per-chunk offset to convert video timestamp to Otter time,\n * then finds Otter segments within ±windowSeconds of that aligned time.\n *\n * otterSegments: the DAY-LEVEL Otter transcript (one Otter covers all chunks).\n * offsetSeconds: THIS CHUNK's offset (otterTime = videoTime + offsetSeconds).\n */\nexport function getFrameContext(\n  videoTimestamp: number,\n  imagePath: string,\n  otterSegments: TranscriptSegment[],\n  offsetSeconds: number,\n  windowSeconds: number = 60,\n): FrameTranscriptContext {\n  const alignedOtterTime = videoTimestamp + offsetSeconds;\n  const windowStart = alignedOtterTime - windowSeconds;\n  const windowEnd = alignedOtterTime + windowSeconds;\n\n  const matchedSegments = otterSegments.filter(\n    seg => seg.startTime < windowEnd && seg.endTime > windowStart,\n  );\n\n  const speakers = [...new Set(\n    matchedSegments.map(s => s.speaker).filter((s): s is string => !!s),\n  )];\n\n  const transcriptSnippet = matchedSegments\n    .map(seg => {\n      const prefix = seg.speaker ? `[${seg.speaker}] ` : '';\n      return `${prefix}${seg.text}`;\n    })\n    .join('\\n');\n\n  return {\n    imagePath,\n    videoTimestamp,\n    alignedOtterTime,\n    transcriptSnippet,\n    speakers,\n  };\n}\n\n/**\n * Get transcript context for all frames from a single video chunk.\n * Uses the chunk's specific offset to align against the day-level Otter transcript.\n */\nexport function getFrameContexts(\n  frames: { imagePath: string; timestamp: number }[],\n  otterSegments: TranscriptSegment[],\n  chunkOffsetSeconds: number,\n  windowSeconds: number = 60,\n): FrameTranscriptContext[] {\n  return frames.map(frame =>\n    getFrameContext(frame.timestamp, frame.imagePath, otterSegments, chunkOffsetSeconds, windowSeconds),\n  );\n}\n\n/**\n * Get transcript context for an artifact by keyword search.\n * Searches for the artifact name/number in Otter transcript.\n */\nexport function getArtifactContext(\n  artifactFilename: string,\n  otterSegments: TranscriptSegment[],\n  additionalKeywords: string[] = [],\n): ArtifactTranscriptContext {\n  // Extract keywords from filename: \"Artifact-1.jpeg\" → [\"artifact\", \"1\"]\n  const filenameKeywords = artifactFilename\n    .replace(/\\.[^.]+$/, '')  // strip extension\n    .split(/[-_\\s]+/)\n    .filter(w => w.length > 0)\n    .map(w => w.toLowerCase());\n\n  const allKeywords = [...filenameKeywords, ...additionalKeywords.map(k => k.toLowerCase())];\n\n  const matchedSegments: TranscriptSegment[] = [];\n  const matchedKeywords: Set<string> = new Set();\n\n  for (const seg of otterSegments) {\n    const lowerText = seg.text.toLowerCase();\n    for (const keyword of allKeywords) {\n      if (lowerText.includes(keyword)) {\n        matchedSegments.push(seg);\n        matchedKeywords.add(keyword);\n        break; // don't double-add the same segment\n      }\n    }\n  }\n\n  const speakers = [...new Set(\n    matchedSegments.map(s => s.speaker).filter((s): s is string => !!s),\n  )];\n\n  const transcriptSnippet = matchedSegments\n    .map(seg => {\n      const prefix = seg.speaker ? `[${seg.speaker}] ` : '';\n      return `${prefix}${seg.text}`;\n    })\n    .join('\\n');\n\n  return {\n    artifactFilename,\n    transcriptSnippet,\n    matchedKeywords: [...matchedKeywords],\n    speakers,\n  };\n}\n\n/**\n * Format frame transcript context for injection into P1 prompt.\n */\nexport function formatFrameContextForPrompt(context: FrameTranscriptContext): string {\n  if (!context.transcriptSnippet) return '';\n  const speakerInfo = context.speakers.length > 0\n    ? `Speakers: ${context.speakers.join(', ')}\\n`\n    : '';\n  return `\\n## TRANSCRIPT CONTEXT\\n\\nTimestamp alignment: video ${formatTime(context.videoTimestamp)} → Otter ${formatTime(context.alignedOtterTime)}\\n${speakerInfo}\\n${context.transcriptSnippet}`;\n}\n\n/**\n * Format artifact transcript context for injection into P2/P3/P4 prompt.\n */\nexport function formatArtifactContextForPrompt(context: ArtifactTranscriptContext): string {\n  if (!context.transcriptSnippet) return '';\n  const kwInfo = context.matchedKeywords.length > 0\n    ? `Matched keywords: ${context.matchedKeywords.join(', ')}\\n`\n    : '';\n  const speakerInfo = context.speakers.length > 0\n    ? `Speakers: ${context.speakers.join(', ')}\\n`\n    : '';\n  return `\\n## TRANSCRIPT CONTEXT\\n\\n${kwInfo}${speakerInfo}\\n${context.transcriptSnippet}`;\n}\n\nfunction formatTime(seconds: number): string {\n  const m = Math.floor(seconds / 60);\n  const s = Math.floor(seconds % 60).toString().padStart(2, '0');\n  return `${m}:${s}`;\n}\n```\n\n#### Tests: `src/lib/pipeline/transcript-context.test.ts`\n\nTest cases:\n1. **getFrameContext** — finds Most common.\nHANDWRITING — A document with significant handwritten content (notes, filled-in forms with handwriting, handwritten annotations that are central to the document's content).\nDENSE_TABLE — A document dominated by a large data table with many rows and columns (spreadsheets, ledgers, pricing matrices, schedules with 10+ rows).\n\nReply in this exact format:\nCLASSIFICATION: [STANDARD|HANDWRITING|DENSE_TABLE]\nCONFIDENCE: [HIGH|MEDIUM|LOW]\nREASONING: [one sentence explaining why]`,\n          },\n        ],\n      },\n    ],\n  });\n\n  return parseClassificationResult(text);\n}\n\nexport function parseClassificationResult(response: string): ClassificationResult {\n  const classMatch = response.match(/CLASSIFICATION:\\s*(STANDARD|HANDWRITING|DENSE_TABLE)/i);\n  const confMatch = response.match(/CONFIDENCE:\\s*(HIGH|MEDIUM|LOW)/i);\n  const reasonMatch = response.match(/REASONING:\\s*(.+)/i);\n\n  const classMap: Record<string, ArtifactClassification> = {\n    'STANDARD': 'artifact_standard',\n    'HANDWRITING': 'artifact_handwriting',\n    'DENSE_TABLE': 'artifact_dense_table',\n  };\n\n  const classification = classMap[classMatch?.[1]?.toUpperCase() ?? 'STANDARD'] ?? 'artifact_standard';\n  const confidenceMap: Record<string, 'high' | 'medium' | 'low'> = {\n    'HIGH': 'high', 'MEDIUM': 'medium', 'LOW': 'low',\n  };\n  const confidence = confidenceMap[confMatch?.[1]?.toUpperCase() ?? 'MEDIUM'] ?? 'medium';\n  const reasoning = reasonMatch?.[1]?.trim() ?? 'No reasoning provided';\n\n  return { classification, confidence, reasoning };\n}\n\n/**\n * Classify multiple artifacts. Returns a map of filename → classification.\n */\nexport async function classifyArtifacts(\n  artifacts: { filename: string; imagePath: string }[],\n): Promise<Map<string, ClassificationResult>> {\n  const results = new Map<string, ClassificationResult>();\n\n  for (const artifact of artifacts) {\n    try {\n      const result = await classifyArtifact(artifact.imagePath);\n      results.set(artifact.filename, result);\n    } catch (error) {\n      console.error(`Artifact classification failed for ${artifact.filename}:`, error);\n      // Default to standard on failure\n      results.set(artifact.filename, {\n        classification: 'artifact_standard',\n        confidence: 'low',\n        reasoning: 'Classification failed, defaulting to standard',\n      });\n    }\n  }\n\n  return results;\n}\n```\n\n#### Tests: `src/lib/pipeline/artifact-classifier.test.ts`\n\nTest cases:\n1. **parseClassificationResult** — parses STANDARD correctly, parses HANDWRITING correctly, parses DENSE_TABLE correctly, defaults to standard on unparseable input, parses confidence levels\n2. **classifyArtifact** — mock Gemini call, verify it sends image and correct prompt\n3. **classifyArtifacts** — classifies multiple artifacts, handles individual failures gracefully (defaults to standard)\n\n---\n\n### Change 5: P1 Prompt Update (`src/lib/pipeline/prompts/p1-screen-page.ts`)\n\nAdd after the first line of the prompt (after \"You are processing a single page...\"):\n\n```\nThis image is extracted from a video recording of a software demonstration. User drops all files for a day: video chunks (.mp4), Otter transcript (.txt), VTT files (.vtt), audio (.m4a), artifact photos (.jpeg)\n2. System auto-classifies by extension\n3. For artifacts: Gemini auto-classifies extraction type (standard/handwriting/dense_table) — user can override\n4. System pairs videos with transcripts\n5. Processing:\n   a. Parse all transcripts (Otter + VTT)\n   b. **VIDEO PHASE** per chunk:\n      - ffmpeg scene detection → raw frames (using existing `extractScenes` from extract.ts)\n      - Frame classification (Gemini: screen vs not-screen)\n      - Frame grouping + multi-select (2-3 best per group)\n      - Offset calculation (VTT↔Otter text match, or Gemini visual↔Otter)\n      - Create synthetic batchFiles rows for each selected frame (extractionType: 'screen_frame', with parentVideoFileId, videoTimestamp, chunkIdentifier)\n   c. **ARTIFACT PHASE:**\n      - Auto-classify (Gemini: standard/handwriting/dense_table) — if not already classified by user\n      - Find transcript context for each artifact\n   d. **PER-IMAGE EXTRACTION:**\n      - screen_frame → C1 → P1 (with per-frame transcript context from offset alignment)\n      - artifact_* → C1 → P2/P3/P4 (with artifact transcript context)\n   e. **ASSEMBLY:** A1 (cross-chunk merge via title-bar grouping) → A2 → V1\n   f. Complete\n\n### One Otter covers many chunks\n\nThe default case is ONE Otter transcript covering the entire day. There are typically 3-6 video chunks per day, each with a different start time. The offset calculator produces a per-chunk offset. `transcript-context.ts` uses each chunk's offset to index into the single day-level Otter transcript — this is how you find the right section of Otter for each frame.\n\n### Offset convention\n\n`otterTime = videoTime + offsetSeconds`. Always. Everywhere. The offset is positive when Otter started before video.\n\n### Existing code that stays\n\n- `extractScenes` from `extract.ts` — already does ffmpeg scene detection, returns `{ timestamps, screenshotPaths }`\n- `correctRotation` from `rotation-corrector.ts` — C1, works on any image\n- `analyzeImages` from `analyze.ts` — Gemini extraction, already handles transcript/screen/project context\n- `assembleScreenCatalog` from `screen-assembler.ts` — A1, already merges by title bar\n- `assembleArtifactCatalog` from `artifact-assembler.ts` — A2, already handles document sets\n- `validateOutputs` from `output-validator.ts` — V1, already reads filesystem catalogs\n- `parseTranscript` from `transcript.ts` — already handles VTT, SRT, and Otter .txt\n\n---\n\n### Change 1: `src/lib/pipeline/batch-worker.ts` — Full Restructure\n\nThe current batch-worker handles per-image extraction with PDF splitting. Everything else -- audit, tooling, pipeline revamp -- serves that goal or comes after it.\n\nThe Golden Inputs (10 files) are delivered and ready to consume. The Requirements Document prompt defines what the output looks like. Your job is to take those inputs and produce that output at a level most companies couldn't dream of.\n\n**Do not rearchitect your pipeline to produce the Requirements Doc.** Use what you have, fill gaps manually where needed, and learn what the process actually requires by doing it. The tooling rebuild comes after the deliverable ships -- not before, not during.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Both Projects Follow the Same Arc\n\n| | Project-Discovery | Tap-Discovery |\n|--|---|---|\n| **Step 1** | Do the work manually to produce golden output | Do the work manually to produce golden output |\n| **Step 2** | Then build tooling to repeat it | Then build tooling to repeat it |\n| **Golden output** | Golden Inputs (10 files) -- DONE | Requirements Document -- IN PROGRESS |\n| **Rebuild starts** | After Golden Inputs proven | After Requirements Doc ships |\n\nProject-discovery didn't plan its pipeline rebuild until after all 3 days of extraction plus full quality passes were done by hand. That manual process revealed what the pipeline actually needs to do -- things we never would have designed for upfront (transcript-only sessions, 133 business rules in a single day, design evolutions across sessions, artifact re-examination patterns). The same will be true for you: the process of manually producing the Requirements Doc will reveal what your pipeline needs that you can't see yet.\n\n---\n\n## 3. What the Golden Inputs Give You\n\nEach day's output follows the Output Architecture spec (with 14 agreed corrections):\n\n- **Screen Catalog** -- PART 1 (new screens) + PART 2 (cross-day enrichments). Field-level extraction with quality flags. Navigation paths. Dialog-over-form relationships. Tab merges.\n- **Artifact Catalog** -- Sequential global numbering. Field extraction. Document set linking. Cross-day enrichments where artifacts reappear.\n- **Processing Summary** -- Classification table, extraction results, quality flags, cross-session validation, downstream notes, quality pass results with enrichments and corrections.\n- **Tim SRD Extraction** -- Post-discovery technical interview. 21 SRD requirements. Tech stack decisions. Architecture evolution documentation.\n\n**Business rules** are embedded in Processing Summaries (Day 3: 133 BRs with IDs, sources, speakers) and in session narratives referenced by the summaries.\n\n**Cross-day enrichments** connect findings across all 3 days. Day 1 has 25 enrichments linking forward to Days 2-3 findings. Day 2 has 32. Day 3 has 19. These are the connective tissue.\n\n---\n\n## 4. What the Golden Inputs Do NOT Give You\n\nThe Golden Inputs are extraction-level output. They document what was observed, discussed, captured, and cross-referenced. They are not:\n\n- **Decomposed into concepts/epics/stories** -- That's your pipeline's job. The raw material is there (screens, artifacts, business rules, stakeholder statements) but the decomposition into requirements hierarchy hasn't happened.\n- **Prioritized** -- Business rules are sourced and attributed but not ranked. Some are CEO mandates, some are operator preferences, some are system constraints. Your pipeline needs to assess priority.\n- **Resolved where stakeholders disagree** -- The Golden Inputs document contradictions and design evolutions (e.g., \"one DB with location IDs\" from Day 2 vs \"3 databases\" from Tim's SRD). They flag these, they don't resolve them. Resolution is a requirements-level decision.\n- **Structured for SRD vs PRD split** -- The Tim SRD extraction covers technical approach. The day-level catalogs cover functional needs. But the PRD/SRD boundary (what vs how) hasn't been drawn through the data. Your pipeline draws that line.\n- **Complete on their own** -- The Golden Inputs capture what happened in 3 days of discovery. There are known gaps: Reports submenu never opened, Management category unexplored, Gadsden facility not visited. The Requirements Doc needs to acknowledge these gaps, not paper over them.\n\n---\n\n## 5. What Project-Discovery Is Planning (High Level)\n\nWe're rebuilding our pipeline to take the same raw inputs (Zoom MP4s, Otter transcripts, artifact photos) and produce output comparable to the Golden Inputs. Push-button, repeatable.\n\n**Key things we learned that inform the rebuild:**\n\n- ~50% of sessions have no screenshots (transcript-only). The pipeline must handle this.\n- Business rule extraction is a first-class output, not a byproduct. Day 3 alone had 133.\n- Quality passes (cross-session, cross-day) catch things single-pass extraction misses: forward references, design evolutions, stakeholder threading, hidden confirmations.\n- The process gets richer as it goes -- each session benefits from everything extracted before it (growing corpus effect).\n- Cross-day enrichment is bidirectional: Day 3 findings enrich Day 1 entries, and vice versa.\n\n**We are not building yet.** We're reviewing the plan, identifying gaps (14 found so far), and incorporating operator feedback before any code changes.\n\n---\n\n## 6. The Two-Mode Vision\n\nThis isn't something to build for now. But it should inform how you evaluate your tooling during the audit.\n\n**Mode 1 -- During Discovery (day-by-day):**\n- Project-discovery processes each day's inputs that evening\n- Produces a \"slightly less golden\" day-level extraction (no full QP, no cross-day backward pass)\n- Hands that extraction to tap-discovery's pipeline\n- Tap-discovery produces intermediate outputs: Daily Brief, Facilitator's Guide, gap analysis\n- These outputs shape the next day's facilitation (what to probe deeper, what was missed, what needs clarification)\n- Repeat each night of the engagement\n\n**Mode 2 -- Post-Discovery (back at HQ):**\n- All days available. Project-discovery runs full extraction with cross-session QP, backward pass, enrichment detection\n- Produces Golden Inputs\n- Tap-discovery produces the Requirements Document from Golden Inputs\n\n**Why this matters for your audit:** Some of your existing tooling (Daily Briefs, Facilitator's Guides, gap analysis) may be exactly what Mode 1 needs. Don't throw it out just because the immediate mission is Mode 2 (Requirements Doc). Evaluate it against both modes.\n\n---\n\n## 7. What This Means for Your Audit\n\n1. **Lead with the Requirements Doc mission.** Evaluate every tool against: does this help me produce the Requirements Document from the Golden Inputs? If yes, keep it. If no, set it aside -- don't delete it.\n\n2. **Understand the gap between Golden Inputs and Requirements Doc.** The Golden Inputs give you extracted, cross-referenced, quality-checked discovery data. The Requirements Doc needs decomposed, prioritized, structured requirements. That gap is your pipeline's core job.\n\n3. **Don't rebuild what project-discovery will provide.** We're handling: raw input processing, session extraction, screen/artifact cataloging, business rule extraction, cross-session QP, cross-day enrichment. If your tooling duplicates this, note it as \"covered by upstream\" rather than \"needs rebuilding.\"\n\n4. **Do flag what you need from us that the Golden Inputs don't provide.** If the Requirements Doc process reveals that you need something structured differently, or additional data we didn't extract, or a different format -- that's valuable feedback for our rebuild.\n\n5. **Preserve Mode 1 tooling.** Anything that produces intermediate deliverables (briefs, guides, facilitation support) has a future even if it's not needed for the Requirements Doc. Tag it, don't trash it.\n\n6. **Stay client-agnostic, day-agnostic, project-agnostic.** This discovery was 3 days with TAP. The next might be 2 days remote with a different client. Neither project should hardcode engagement-specific assumptions.\n\n---\n\n## 8. What's Coming Next (After Both Golden Outputs Exist)\n\nOnce the Requirements Doc is delivered and project-discovery's pipeline rebuild plan is finalized:\n\n1. **Shared vision doc** -- How both projects fit together. What each side owns. Where the handoff happens. How Mode 1 and Mode 2 work end-to-end.\n2. **Boundary spec** -- Formal interface contract between project-discovery output and tap-discovery input. Format, structure, what's guaranteed, what's optional.\n3. **Coordinated rebuild** -- Both projects rebuild their pipelines with shared understanding. No overlap, no gaps, no cross-contamination.\n\nNone of this happens until the Requirements Doc ships. Focus on the deliverable.\n\n---\n\n## 9. Ground Rules for Cross-Project Work\n\nThese protect both projects from the kind of confusion that cost us 3 days when a PDF assumption propagated unchecked:\n\n- **No cross-writing.** Project-discovery does not write to tap-discovery's directories (except at explicit Phase 5 handoff). Tap-discovery does not write to project-discovery's directories.\n- **No shared assumptions without documentation.** If one project assumes something about the other's output format, behavior, or timeline, it goes in a shared doc -- not in a memory file, not in a brain doc, not in a conversation.\n- **Feedback flows through the operator.** If tap-discovery needs something different from project-discovery (or vice versa), that request goes through the operator, not directly between projects. This prevents context pollution.\n- **Each project owns its own context.** Brain docs, memory files, and CLAUDE.md stay within their project. Otter records audio on a phone — different device, different start time. There is typically ONE Otter transcript per day covering ALL video chunks (3-6 chunks). The offset between video time and Otter time must be calculated per-chunk.\n\n**Proven result:** For Day 1 video, the offset is ~56 seconds (Otter started ~56s before video). Convention: `otterTime = videoTime + offsetSeconds`. Offset is positive when Otter recording started before video.\n\n**Frame extraction:** ffmpeg extracts frames using scene detection (`gt(scene,0.15)`) + interval capture (every 30s). These raw frames include software screens, faces, transitions, blanks. Only software screens are useful for P1 extraction.\n\n## Test Data Paths\n\n- Video: `/Users/jasonburks/Downloads/GMT20260316-191615_Recording_1920x1080 (1).mp4` (91 min, muted mic)\n- Otter transcript: `/Users/jasonburks/Documents/_AI_/TEMPORARY-tap-discovery-compare/TAP-Pipeline/04-discovery-outputs/day1/day1-inputs/TAP Contracts.txt`\n- Artifacts: `/Users/jasonburks/Documents/_AI_/TEMPORARY-tap-discovery-compare/TAP-Pipeline/04-discovery-outputs/day1/day1-inputs/Artifacts/` (Artifact-1.jpeg through Artifact-4.jpeg)\n\nUse these paths in integration test comments, but **do not require them at runtime for unit tests**.
