There is no separate migration workstream — each module migrates its own data as it is built, using AI-assisted extraction scripts that pipe Access data into the target database. Tim will run multiple Claude instances simultaneously, each working on a different module's data extraction and mapping, with Kim validating migrated records by comparing what she sees in the new screens against the same records in Access.\n\nThis approach was a deliberate decision, not a default. It reflects Tim's development model: lay out the application structure, discover data mappings as each module is built, and let the migration work serve as a forcing function for understanding the source data. The Access database is the sole source system — a single MDB file per location containing approximately 20 core operational tables alongside an unknown number of temporary and junk tables accumulated over 27 years.\n\n## 15.2 Source Data Inventory\n\n### 15.2.1 Access Database Structure\n\nThe source system is a Microsoft Access 97 MDB file. Two sandbox copies exist for development use:\n\n| Sandbox | Location | Purpose |\n|---------|----------|---------|\n| TAPPgmMP | Mt. Pleasant | Primary sandbox — most complete operational data |\n| Gadsden copy | Gadsden | Second facility — separate database file, same schema |\n\nThe database contains approximately 20 core operational tables spanning receiving, smelting, invoicing, customer management, inventory, and reference data. Beyond these core tables, an unknown number of temporary and junk tables have accumulated since the application's creation in 1998. Many have been dead since approximately 2010. No formal schema documentation exists.\n\nColumn naming is inconsistent. Some tables use descriptive names; others use cryptic identifiers (\"Field 34\") that require investigation to map to their business meaning. The schema reflects 27 years of incremental modification without refactoring.\n\n### 15.2.2 Known Data Quality Issues\n\nThe following data quality problems have been identified during discovery and must be accounted for during migration:\n\n| Issue | Impact | Mitigation |\n|-------|--------|------------|\n| No referential integrity | Orphaned records exist across tables; foreign key relationships are implicit, not enforced | Validate relationships during extraction; log orphans for review |\n| Cryptically named columns | \"Field 34\" and similar names obscure business meaning | Field mapping methodology (§15.4) addresses this systematically |\n| Dead tables (~2010) | Tables exist in schema but have not received writes in 15+ years | Identify and exclude during source inventory phase |\n| Junk/temp tables | Scratch tables from ad hoc queries or one-time operations | Identify by naming pattern and last-modified date; exclude from migration scope |\n| Ghost/dummy contracts | Workaround records created to satisfy system constraints that don't represent real business relationships | Flag during extraction; determine keep/discard per module with Kim's guidance |\n| DEPRECATED fields | EnergySurchargeRate (value: 0.0000, used once) and potentially others | Explicit exclusion list maintained per module |\n| 6-digit foreign key prefix | Location segregation encoded as a record-level prefix rather than database-level separation | Strip during extraction; replaced by database-level location separation in new architecture |\n| Orphaned records | Records referencing nonexistent parents due to missing referential integrity | Log, review with Kim, determine disposition per record type |\n\n### 15.2.3 Data Volume and Scope\n\n**Retention directive:** 7 years of operational data, per CEO (Jared Sweeny) mandate.\n\n**Extraction strategy:** Import everything first. Do not attempt to filter by date during extraction — the Access date formats, storage patterns, and table relationships make pre-filtering unreliable. After all data is loaded into the target database, run queries to identify records outside the 7-year retention window and handle them according to the archival approach defined in §15.7.\n\n**Estimated scope by module area:**\n\n| Module | Data Characteristics | Estimated Table Count |\n|--------|---------------------|----------------------|\n| §4 Aluminum Intake | Receiving notes, BOL records, chemistry readings, inventory tracking | Heavy — multiple core tables |\n| §5 Smelting Operations | Furnace production records, charge sheets, chemistry samples | Moderate — time-series operational data |\n| §6 Financial Management | Invoice records, contract pricing, profitability tracking | Moderate — transactional with lookup references |\n| §7 CRM | Customer records, contracts, source codes | Moderate — shared across locations |\n| §10 User Management | 8 Phase 1 roles | Light — may be created fresh rather than migrated |\n| §11 Admin & Configuration | 9 admin-owned lookup tables, yard location aliases, system defaults | Light — reference data, small row counts |\n\n## 15.3 ETL Approach\n\n### 15.3.1 Tooling\n\n| Component | Technology | Status |\n|-----------|-----------|--------|\n| Source extraction | MDB Tools (command-line utilities for reading Access databases) | **DECIDED** |\n| Script generation | AI (Claude) writes shell scripts to extract and pipe data | **DECIDED** |\n| Target loading | Shell scripts pipe extracted data directly to target database | **DECIDED** |\n| Target database | Turso / libSQL (Tim's choice) vs PostgreSQL (SOW specification) | **CONTRADICTED** — see §15.3.3 |\n\nMDB Tools provides command-line read access to Access MDB files without requiring Microsoft Access or Windows. Claude generates the extraction scripts — shell scripts that read from Access tables, transform data as needed, and pipe results into the target database. Tim executes and validates; the scripts are not black-box automation.\n\n### 15.3.2 Module-by-Module Strategy\n\nMigration is not a phase — it is embedded in the build cycle for each module. The sequence follows the material flow through the plant:\n\n1. **Module development begins** — Tim lays out application structure\n2. **Data discovery** — Tim examines Access tables relevant to the module, maps fields, resolves cryptic names\n3. **Script generation** — Claude writes extraction scripts for the module's tables\n4. **Extraction and load** — Tim runs scripts to move data into the target database\n5. **Screen-level validation** — Kim compares migrated records in the new UI against the same records in Access\n6. **Iterate** — Fix mapping errors, re-extract, re-validate until Kim confirms accuracy\n\n**Parallel execution:** Tim will run multiple Claude instances simultaneously, each working on a different module. One instance handles customer data, another handles receiving, a third handles transfers. This is an explicit part of the development model, not an optimization — each module's data is largely independent.\n\n**Order follows build priority,** which follows material flow: Intake (§4) before Smelting (§5) before Financial (§6). Reference data (§11) may be migrated early as a dependency for operational modules.\n\n### 15.3.3 Target Database Mapping\n\nThe Access database uses a single-file-per-location model (TAPPgmMP for Mt. Pleasant, a separate file for Gadsden). The new architecture separates this into:\n\n| New Database | Content | Maps From |\n|-------------|---------|-----------|\n| Shared database | Users, authentication, cross-location master data | Both Access files (deduplicated) |\n| Mt. Pleasant operational DB | All operational records for Mt. Pleasant | TAPPgmMP |\n| Gadsden operational DB | All operational records for Gadsden | Gadsden Access file |\n\n**Database technology tension:** Tim has selected Turso / libSQL as the target database. The SOW specifies PostgreSQL. This is a **CONTRADICTED** decision requiring resolution before migration scripts are written, as the SQL dialect, data types, and loading mechanisms differ between the two platforms.\n\nThe 6-digit foreign key prefix currently used for location segregation within the shared Access database is stripped during extraction. Location separation is handled at the database level in the new architecture, eliminating the need for prefix-based filtering.\n\n## 15.4 Field Mapping Methodology\n\nThree complementary approaches address the \"Field 34\" problem — cryptically named columns whose business meaning is not apparent from the schema alone.\n\n### 15.4.1 Deductive Approach\n\nThe primary method. Extract data from a known record, display it on the matching screen in the new application, and compare to what Kim sees for the same record in Access. If the value in \"Field 34\" appears in the \"Special Instructions\" box on Kim's screen, the mapping is resolved.\n\n**Process:**\n1. Extract a representative record from Access\n2. Identify all fields with known and unknown mappings\n3. Display in the new UI alongside the Access screen\n4. Kim confirms or corrects each field's placement\n\nThis is the default approach for most field mapping work.\n\n### 15.4.2 Reverse Engineering\n\nAI traces through the Access application logic — VBA code, form data sources, query definitions — to find what reads from and writes to cryptically named fields. This approach works when the deductive method is inconclusive (e.g., a field that is stored but never displayed, or displayed only in certain conditions).\n\n**Process:**\n1. Identify the target field in the Access schema\n2. AI examines VBA modules, form record sources, and query definitions\n3. Trace the data flow: what form control writes to this field, under what conditions\n4. Map the business meaning from the application logic\n\n### 15.4.3 Brute-Force Validation\n\nA programmatic verification method. Insert a unique, identifiable value into every input field on an Access form, then examine which database columns received those values. This creates an unambiguous mapping between UI controls and database fields.\n\n**Process:**\n1. Open the Access sandbox to a blank or test record\n2. Programmatically (or manually) enter unique marker values in every input field\n3. Save the record\n4. Query the database to find which columns contain the marker values\n5. The column-to-field mapping is established definitively\n\nThis approach is most valuable as a verification step after deductive or reverse-engineering mapping, and for forms with many fields where manual tracing is error-prone.\n\n## 15.5 Validation Approach\n\nValidation is module-by-module and screen-level. There is no separate validation phase — validation is the final step of each module's migration cycle.\n\n**Primary validator:** Kim Sproul. She has 16+ years of operational experience and is the only person who can confirm whether migrated data looks correct in context.\n\n**Validation method:**\n1. Tim identifies a representative set of records for the module (including edge cases: oldest records, records with unusual values, records spanning the 7-year boundary)\n2. Kim opens the same record in both Access and the new system, side by side\n3. Kim confirms every visible field matches, or identifies discrepancies\n4. Discrepancies are logged, mapping is corrected, and the affected records are re-extracted\n5. Kim re-validates until she confirms accuracy\n\n**Validation coverage:** Every module that migrates data must pass Kim's screen-level validation before the module is considered complete. There is no automated validation substitute for Kim's domain knowledge — she knows what \"looks right\" in ways that automated checks cannot replicate.\n\n**Desktop AI for Access exploration:** For complex validation scenarios, Tim can use Remote Desktop to Jared's server where the Access sandbox is deployed, sharing his screen with Claude/AI to explore the Access application visually and trace data discrepancies.\n\n## 15.6 Cutover Strategy\n\nThe organic ETL approach simplifies cutover. There is no single cutover event — each module cuts over to the new system as it is built, validated, and approved. This means:\n\n- **No big-bang switchover** requiring a weekend freeze and all-hands migration event\n- **Module-level go/no-go decisions** rather than a single system-level cutover decision\n- **Rollback granularity** at the module level — if a module's migration has problems, only that module reverts to Access while the issue is resolved\n- **Parallel operation** is the natural state during the build phase — some modules run on the new system while others remain in Access\n\nThe final cutover occurs when the last module is migrated, validated, and running in production. At that point, Access transitions from active operational system to read-only archive.\n\n## 15.7 Historical Data and Retention\n\n**Retention policy:** 7 years of operational data must be preserved and queryable. This is a CEO directive (Jared Sweeny), not a regulatory requirement.\n\n**Extraction approach:** Import everything. Do not filter by date during extraction. Tim: *\"I would just import everything anyway, and then just go back and do a query for anything over seven years old.\"*\n\n**Post-import handling of aged data:**\n\n| Data Age | Treatment |\n|----------|-----------|\n| Within 7-year window | Active — fully queryable, visible in all operational screens and reports |\n| Beyond 7-year window | Archive candidate — query to identify, then determine disposition |\n| Pre-2010 dead table data | Exclude from migration entirely — these tables have not received writes in 15+ years |\n\n**Archival approach:** Records beyond the 7-year window are not deleted during migration. They are identified via post-import queries and either archived to a separate store or soft-deleted (flagged as archived but retained in the database). The specific archival mechanism is an open item — it depends on data volume and the target database's capabilities.\n\n## 15.8 Deprecated and Excluded Data\n\nThe following data elements are explicitly excluded from migration or flagged as deprecated:\n\n### Excluded from Migration\n\n| Element | Reason |\n|---------|--------|\n| Dead tables (~2010) | No writes in 15+ years; confirmed inactive during discovery |\n| Junk/temp tables | Scratch data from ad hoc queries; no operational value |\n| EnergySurchargeRate field | DEPRECATED. Value is 0.0000. Element | Reason |\n|---------|--------|\n| Ghost/dummy contracts | Workaround records — Kim must confirm which are safe to exclude |\n| Orphaned records | May indicate data quality issues or may be legitimate historical artifacts |\n| Cryptically named columns with NULL values | May be deprecated fields or may be conditionally populated |\n\nA complete exclusion list will be finalized per module Every pound of aluminum that moves through receiving, processing, and shipping eventually passes through this module as a dollar amount. The module covers lot-based invoicing, invoice quality assurance, purchase order management (new — does not exist in the current system), and profitability tracking across three distinct business work streams.\n     6→\n     7→The current system handles invoicing through a three-step irreversible workflow: Create Invoice > Test Invoices > Process Invoices. Kim creates invoices from processed lots, Treina QA-reviews them via an Access-to-Excel export pipeline (catching weight discrepancies and pricing errors), and the finalized package — PDF invoice, PDF analysis, and Excel analysis — gets pushed to a network share and emailed to customers. This workflow is the financial heart of the system, bridging production completion and customer billing.\n     8→\n     9→The single biggest finding across all three discovery days is the Purchase Order gap. TAP has no PO management in the current Access system. The entire PO workflow — across tolling, buy-sell scrap, and JV partnerships — lives on spreadsheets outside the system. This module must close that gap. Additionally, the CEO has directed a profitability dashboard showing spend vs. revenue by customer and work stream, giving executive visibility into margins across all three business models.\n    10→\n    11→The module serves 5 primary stakeholders across 2 organizations (TAP internal + customers), integrates with an external accounting system (Southware), and must support both file-push and portal-pull output models for invoice delivery. It operates across two TAP facilities (Mt. Pleasant and Gadsden) with isolated financial data per the 3-DB architecture.\n    12→\n    13→## Non-Goals\n    14→\n    15→- **Contract creation and pricing management** — belongs to §7 CRM / Customer Management. §6 consumes contract pricing but does not manage contract lifecycle, pricing terms, or material type hierarchies.\n    16→- **Receiving weight entry and lot creation** — belongs to §4 Aluminum Intake. §6 consumes receiving weight data for invoice calculation but does not manage the receiving workflow.\n    17→- **Smelting and production tracking** — belongs to §5 Smelting Operations. §6 references heat/sow data for invoice detail but does not manage production.\n    18→- **Customer portal self-service** — belongs to §8 Customer Portal. §6 generates documents that the portal may expose, but portal architecture is not §6 scope.\n    19→- **Executive and sales dashboards** — belongs to §9 Reporting & Analytics. §6 provides profitability data; §9 owns dashboard presentation (Bill's sales dashboard, CEO executive dashboard).\n    20→- **External accounting system architecture** — the Southware integration interface is §6 scope, but the accounting system itself is external. Treina receives invoice for QA review (separate workflow — see below).\n    79→\n    80→*Decision Points:*\n    81→- **Lot merge:** If customer requires consolidated billing across multiple lots, Kim uses merge function before Create Invoice step.\n    82→- **Test vs Process:** Test is the quality gate. Processing is irreversible. The deliberate two-step separation is a feature, not a limitation.\n    83→\n    84→*Exceptions & Edge Cases:*\n    85→- Multiple lots merging to one invoice (customer-driven, e.g., JW Aluminum)\n    86→- Invoice number defaults to first lot number (convention, can be overridden)\n    87→- Blended pricing when lots span material types\n    88→- Steel deduction creates dual-weight billing (customer billed on full incoming, recovery on post-steel)\n    89→\n    90→### Invoice QA Review\n    91→\n    92→*Trigger:* Kim generates invoice files.\n    93→*Actors:* Treina (primary), Kim (handoff)\n    94→\n    95→*Process Flow:*\n    96→1. There is no separate migration workstream — each module migrates its own data as it is built, using AI-assisted extraction scripts that pipe Access data into the target database. Tim will run multiple Claude instances simultaneously, each working on a different module's data extraction and mapping, with Kim validating migrated records by comparing what she sees in the new screens against the same records in Access.\n     8→\n     9→This approach was a deliberate decision, not a default. It reflects Tim's development model: lay out the application structure, discover data mappings as each module is built, and let the migration work serve as a forcing function for understanding the source data. The Access database is the sole source system — a single MDB file per location containing approximately 20 core operational tables alongside an unknown number of temporary and junk tables accumulated over 27 years.\n    10→\n    11→## 15.2 Source Data Inventory\n    12→\n    13→### 15.2.1 Access Database Structure\n    14→\n    15→The source system is a Microsoft Access 97 MDB file. Pleasant | Primary sandbox — most complete operational data |\n    20→| Gadsden copy | Gadsden | Second facility — separate database file, same schema |\n    21→\n    22→The database contains approximately 20 core operational tables spanning receiving, smelting, invoicing, customer management, inventory, and reference data. Beyond these core tables, an unknown number of temporary and junk tables have accumulated since the application's creation in 1998. Many have been dead since approximately 2010. No formal schema documentation exists.\n    23→\n    24→Column naming is inconsistent. Some tables use descriptive names; others use cryptic identifiers (\"Field 34\") that require investigation to map to their business meaning. The schema reflects 27 years of incremental modification without refactoring.\n    25→\n    26→### 15.2.2 Known Data Quality Issues\n    27→\n    28→The following data quality problems have been identified during discovery and must be accounted for during migration:\n    29→\n    30→| Issue | Impact | Mitigation |\n    31→|-------|--------|------------|\n    32→| No referential integrity | Orphaned records exist across tables; foreign key relationships are implicit, not enforced | Validate relationships during extraction; log orphans for review |\n    33→| Cryptically named columns | \"Field 34\" and similar names obscure business meaning | Field mapping methodology (§15.4) addresses this systematically |\n    34→| Dead tables (~2010) | Tables exist in schema but have not received writes in 15+ years | Identify and exclude during source inventory phase |\n    35→| Junk/temp tables | Scratch tables from ad hoc queries or one-time operations | Identify by naming pattern and last-modified date; exclude from migration scope |\n    36→| Ghost/dummy contracts | Workaround records created to satisfy system constraints that don't represent real business relationships | Flag during extraction; determine keep/discard per module with Kim's guidance |\n    37→| DEPRECATED fields | EnergySurchargeRate (value: 0.0000, used once) and potentially others | Explicit exclusion list maintained per module |\n    38→| 6-digit foreign key prefix | Location segregation encoded as a record-level prefix rather than database-level separation | Strip during extraction; replaced by database-level location separation in new architecture |\n    39→| Contact Email Y/N flag | Some customer records store Y/N in the email field instead of an address (~273 records need audit) | Data audit during CRM module migration; remap to boolean flag + separate email field |\n    40→\n    41→### 15.2.3 Data Volume and Scope\n    42→\n    43→**Retention directive:** 7 years of operational data, per CEO (Jared Sweeny) mandate.\n    44→\n    45→**Extraction strategy:** Import everything first. Location separation is handled at the database level in the new architecture, eliminating the need for prefix-based filtering.\n    99→\n   100→## 15.4 Field Mapping Methodology\n   101→\n   102→Three complementary approaches address the \"Field 34\" problem — cryptically named columns whose business meaning is not apparent from the schema alone.\n   103→\n   104→### 15.4.1 Deductive Approach\n   105→\n   106→The primary method. Extract data from a known record, display it on the matching screen in the new application, and compare to what Kim sees for the same record in Access. If the value in \"Field 34\" appears in the \"Special Instructions\" box on Kim's screen, the mapping is resolved.\n   107→\n   108→**Process:**\n   109→1. Extract a representative record from Access\n   110→2. Identify all fields with known and unknown mappings\n   111→3. Display in the new UI alongside the Access screen\n   112→4. Kim confirms or corrects each field's placement\n   113→\n   114→This is the default approach for most field mapping work.\n   115→\n   116→### 15.4.2 Reverse Engineering\n   117→\n   118→AI traces through the Access application logic — VBA code, form data sources, query definitions — to find what reads from and writes to cryptically named fields. This approach works when the deductive method is inconclusive (e.g., a field that is stored but never displayed, or displayed only in certain conditions).\n   119→\n   120→**Process:**\n   121→1. Identify the target field in the Access schema\n   122→2. AI examines VBA modules, form record sources, and query definitions\n   123→3. Trace the data flow: what form control writes to this field, under what conditions\n   124→4. Map the business meaning from the application logic\n   125→\n   126→### 15.4.3 Brute-Force Validation\n   127→\n   128→A programmatic verification method. Insert a unique, identifiable value into every input field on an Access form, then examine which database columns received those values. This creates an unambiguous mapping between UI controls and database fields.\n   129→\n   130→**Process:**\n   131→1. Open the Access sandbox to a blank or test record\n   132→2. Programmatically (or manually) enter unique marker values in every input field\n   133→3. Save the record\n   134→4. Query the database to find which columns contain the marker values\n   135→5. The column-to-field mapping is established definitively\n   136→\n   137→This approach is most valuable as a verification step after deductive or reverse-engineering mapping, and for forms with many fields where manual tracing is error-prone.\n   138→\n   139→## 15.5 Validation Approach\n   140→\n   141→Validation is module-by-module and screen-level. There is no separate validation phase — validation is the final step of each module's migration cycle.\n   142→\n   143→**Primary validator:** Kim Sproul. She has 16+ years of operational experience and is the only person who can confirm whether migrated data looks correct in context.\n   144→\n   145→**Validation method:**\n   146→1. There is no single cutover event — each module cuts over to the new system as it is built, validated, and approved. This means:\n   159→\n   160→- **No big-bang switchover** requiring a weekend freeze and all-hands migration event\n   161→- **Module-level go/no-go decisions** rather than a single system-level cutover decision\n   162→- **Rollback granularity** at the module level — if a module's migration has problems, only that module reverts to Access while the issue is resolved\n   163→- **Parallel operation** is the natural state during the build phase — some modules run on the new system while others remain in Access\n   164→\n   165→The final cutover occurs when the last module is migrated, validated, and running in production. At that point, Access transitions from active operational system to read-only archive.\n   166→\n   167→## 15.7 Historical Data and Retention\n   168→\n   169→**Retention policy:** 7 years of operational data must be preserved and queryable. Every pound of aluminum that moves through receiving, processing, and shipping eventually passes through this module as a dollar amount. System displays three-panel layout: Main Grid (top — lot summary with pricing), Sows Panel (left — individual sow details), Pending Invoices Panel (right — queued invoices).\n3. Treina reviews for weight discrepancies between receipt stage and invoice stage.\n4. Treina validates pricing against contract terms.\n5. Treina catches and corrects discrepancies (weight adjustment engine disguised as review).\n6. Treina files approved invoice.\n\n*Exceptions & Edge Cases:*\n- Eight data redundancy points (shadow-record patterns) where Treina manually cross-checks data across multiple sources.\n- This is load-bearing manual work — the new system must systematize this quality gate, not eliminate it.\n\n### Invoice Output & Distribution\n\n*Trigger:* Invoice processing complete.\n*Actors:* Kim (distribution), Treina (QA), Customers (receipt)\n\n*Process Flow:*\n1. System generates three files: PDF invoice, PDF analysis, Excel analysis.\n2. Files pushed to `G:\\PDF\\Invoice\\` network share.\n3. Kim emails files to customer.\n4. Invoice data exported to Southware (external accounting system).\n5. For portal customers: invoice data also feeds customer self-service portal (§8).\n6. For Logan: customer-specific comma-delimited export format (integration debt).\n\n*Decision Points:*\n- **Push vs Pull:** File push model persists alongside any portal/API. Cannot eliminate file generation even when pull model exists.\n- **Customer-specific exports:** Logan's comma-delimited format is an obligation that persists. New system needs configurable export engine, not hardcoded per-customer formats.\n\n### Purchase Order Management (NEW — Does Not Exist Today)\n\n*Trigger:* TAP needs to order material from a vendor, or a customer places a purchase order with TAP.\n*Actors:* Bill (PO creation/approval), Kim (entry), Treina (tracking)\n\n*Process Flow:*\n1. Bill initiates PO based on customer demand or market opportunity.\n2. PO entered into system with: vendor, material type, quantity, price, delivery terms, work stream (tolling/buy-sell/JV).\n3. System tracks PO status: Open > Partially Fulfilled > Fulfilled > Closed.\n4. 30-day delivery window monitored with deadline alerts.\n5. Incoming receipts linked to POs for fulfillment tracking.\n6. PO data feeds profitability tracking.\n\n*Decision Points:*\n- **Work stream classification:** Each PO must be tagged to one of three work streams for profitability tracking.\n- **Market-driven behavior:** Vendors delay delivery in rising commodity markets, cancel in falling markets. System must surface delivery deadline risk.\n\n*Exceptions & Edge Cases:*\n- Currently 100% on spreadsheets — no existing system logic to migrate.\n- Must support all three work streams with different financial models.\n\n## Business Rules\n\n| ID | Rule | Type | Details | Source |\n|----|------|------|---------|--------|\n| BR-06-001 | Toll charge based on weight received | CALC | Toll Charge = Unit Price × Weight Received. Customer billed on received weight, NOT recovered weight. Example: $0.14 × 222,940 lbs = $31,211.60. | [D1-AC-3], [D2-SC-frmLotInvoicing] |\n| BR-06-002 | Invoice total calculation | CALC | InvAmt = (LbsReceived × LotPrice) + AdditionalCharge. Verified: 43,340 × $0.20 + $600 freight = $9,268. | [D1-AC-3], [D2-PS-CSV6] |\n| BR-06-003 | Percent yield calculation | CALC | Recovery % = (Recovered lbs / Weight Received lbs) × 100. Generated from lot processing data through the three-step workflow.\n\n**Key Fields:** Invoice Number, Customer Number, Lot# (primary + consolidated list), Invoice Date, Contract#, Customer PO#, Source, Processed at (location), Weight Received, Processed, Recovered, Contaminated, Percent Yield, Unit Price, Toll Charge Amount, Freight Amount, Invoice Total.\n\n**Sub-records:** Receipt Detail (per-truck lines), Shipment Detail (per-BOL/heat), Invoice Chemistry Detail (per-sow breakdown).\n\n**Output Files:** PDF invoice, PDF analysis, Excel analysis — all pushed to G:\\PDF\\Invoice\\.\n\n**Relationships:**\n- Invoice belongs to Customer (many-to-one)\n- Invoice covers Lots (one-to-many, via merge)\n- Invoice references Contract (many-to-one)\n- Invoice embeds Receipt Detail (one-to-many)\n- Invoice embeds Shipment Detail (one-to-many)\n\n**Volume:** Scales with lots processed per year. Invoice number = lot number convention suggests similar volume to lot creation.\n\n**Data Quality:** Treina's 8 shadow-record points indicate current data quality issues around weight matching and pricing consistency. New system must eliminate shadow records by making validations inline.\n\n### N1: Purchase Order (NEW)\n\nDoes not exist in current system. Biggest gap identified across all three discovery days.\n\n**Key Fields:** PO Number (system-generated), Vendor, Material Type, Quantity (lbs), Price, Delivery Terms, Delivery Date, Work Stream (tolling/buy-sell/JV), Status (Open/Partially Fulfilled/Fulfilled/Closed), Created By, Created Date.\n\n**Relationships:**\n- PO references Vendor/Customer (many-to-one)\n- PO references Material Type (many-to-one)\n- PO linked to Receipts for fulfillment tracking (one-to-many)\n- PO feeds Profitability Record\n\n**Volume:** Unknown — currently on spreadsheets. Estimate based on receiving volume (~4-5 trucks/day).\n\n**Data Quality:** No existing data to migrate. Clean start.\n\n### N2: Profitability Record (NEW)\n\nCEO-directed entity for tracking spend vs. revenue by customer and work stream.\n\n**Key Fields:** Customer, Work Stream (tolling/buy-sell/JV), Period, Revenue (toll charges + additional charges), Costs (material purchase, processing, labor), Margin, Recovery %, Location.\n\n**Relationships:**\n- Profitability Record belongs to Customer (many-to-one)\n- Profitability Record aggregates from Invoices, POs, Lots, Heats\n- Profitability Record belongs to Location (many-to-one)\n\n**Volume:** One record per customer per work stream per period. Scale depends on period granularity (monthly vs. weekly).\n\n**Data Quality:** Requires accurate cost data from §5 (processing costs) and accurate revenue data from §6 (invoicing). Cross-module data quality dependency.\n\n## Reporting Requirements\n\n| Report | Type | Frequency | Users | Parity | Data Sources |\n|--------|------|-----------|-------|--------|-------------|\n| Invoice/Receiving and Processing Report (rptInvoice) | Existing | Per invoice | Customers, Kim, Treina | Replicate | E12, E5, E6, E9, E10 |\n| Invoice Chemistry Detail (rptInvoiceSows) | Existing | Per invoice | Customers | Replicate | E12, E10, E11 |\n| Current Month Production Report | Existing | Monthly | Customers, Jared | Replicate | E5, E12, inventory roll-up |\n| Invoice Analysis (PDF + Excel) | Existing | Per invoice | Treina, Customers | Replicate | E12 |\n| PO Status Report | New | On-demand | Bill, Kim | New | N1 |\n| PO Delivery Deadline Alert | New | Daily/triggered | Bill | New | N1 |\n| Profitability by Customer & Work Stream | New | Monthly/on-demand | Jared, Bill | New | N2, E12, N1 |\n| Weight Variance Report | New | Per invoice batch | Treina | New | E12, E6 (replaces shadow-record manual checks) |\n\n## Current Workarounds to Resolve\n\n| Workaround | Impact | Resolved By (Req ID) |\n|-----------|--------|---------------------|\n| Treina exports Access data to Excel for invoice QA (8 shadow-record points) | Manual effort, error-prone, data redundancy. Consider soft-delete with admin override for genuine errors. |\n| Steel deduction creates dual-weight billing on same lot | Customer sees one weight (full incoming), recovery calc uses another (post-steel). Do not launch without all 8 replaced. |\n| Three work streams have different billing mechanics | Tolling = processing fee on received weight. Buy-sell = margin on purchase vs. recovery value. Lot status flows from §4 (received/processed) into §6 (invoiced/closed). Receipt sequence numbers enable per-truck granularity on invoices. PO fulfillment links receipts to purchase orders.\n- **§5 Smelting Operations:** §6 consumes heat/sow production data for invoice detail. Steel deduction (captured at furnace level) affects dual-weight billing. Cost-per-lot calculation requires heat-level cost data. Chemistry data feeds invoice chemistry detail report (rptInvoiceSows).\n- **§7 CRM / Customer Management:** §6 inherits all pricing from contracts (read-only). Contract terms (payment terms, FOB, additional charges, material type pricing) drive invoice calculation. Customer PO# from contract flows to invoice.\n- **§8 Customer Portal:** §6 generates invoice data that the portal exposes to customers. Push + pull delivery model means §6 must feed both file output and portal data.\n- **§9 Reporting & Analytics:** §6 provides profitability data that §9 consumes for executive dashboard, sales dashboard, and operational reports. Every pound of aluminum that moves through receiving, processing, and shipping eventually passes through this module as a dollar amount. The module covers lot-based invoicing, invoice quality assurance, purchase order management (new — does not exist in the current system), and profitability tracking across three distinct business work streams.\n\nThe current system handles invoicing through a three-step irreversible workflow: Create Invoice > Test Invoices > Process Invoices. Kim creates invoices from processed lots, Treina QA-reviews them via an Access-to-Excel export pipeline (catching weight discrepancies and pricing errors), and the finalized package — PDF invoice, PDF analysis, and Excel analysis — gets pushed to a network share and emailed to customers. This workflow is the financial heart of the system, bridging production completion and customer billing.\n\nThe single biggest finding across all three discovery days is the Purchase Order gap. TAP has no PO management in the current Access system. The entire PO workflow — across tolling, buy-sell scrap, and JV partnerships — lives on spreadsheets outside the system. This module must close that gap. Additionally, the CEO has directed a profitability dashboard showing spend vs. revenue by customer and work stream, giving executive visibility into margins across all three business models.\n\nThe module serves 5 primary stakeholders across 2 organizations (TAP internal + customers), integrates with an external accounting system (Southware), and must support both file-push and portal-pull output models for invoice delivery. It operates across two TAP facilities (Mt. Pleasant and Gadsden) with isolated financial data per the 3-DB architecture.\n\n## Non-Goals\n\n- **Contract creation and pricing management** — belongs to §7 CRM / Customer Management. §6 consumes contract pricing but does not manage contract lifecycle, pricing terms, or material type hierarchies.\n- **Receiving weight entry and lot creation** — belongs to §4 Aluminum Intake. §6 consumes receiving weight data for invoice calculation but does not manage the receiving workflow.\n- **Smelting and production tracking** — belongs to §5 Smelting Operations. §6 references heat/sow data for invoice detail but does not manage production.\n- **Customer portal self-service** — belongs to §8 Customer Portal. §6 generates documents that the portal may expose, but portal architecture is not §6 scope.\n- **Executive and sales dashboards** — belongs to §9 Reporting & Analytics. §6 provides profitability data; §9 owns dashboard presentation (Bill's sales dashboard, CEO executive dashboard).\n- **External accounting system architecture** — the Southware integration interface is §6 scope, but the accounting system itself is external. Database design and hosting decisions belong in Part 2 (SRD).\n- **Real-time market pricing integration** — discussed during discovery as a Bill dashboard feature, belongs to §9 Reporting & Analytics. §6 tracks historical pricing via contracts.\n- **Power BI / Grafana dashboard infrastructure** — technical implementation decisions belong in Part 2 (SRD). §6 specifies what financial data must be reportable.\n\n## Vocabulary\n\n| Term | Definition | Notes |\n|------|-----------|-------|\n| Invoice | The billing document generated from lot processing data. Covers one or more lots merged for a single customer. Three-step lifecycle: Create > Test > Process. | Invoice number = first lot number by convention (not hard rule). |\n| Toll Charge | The processing fee charged to the customer, calculated as Unit Price × Weight Received. | Based on RECEIVED weight, NOT recovered weight. Core revenue calculation. |\n| Invoice Total | Toll Charge + Additional Charges (freight, surcharges). The amount billed to the customer. | Verified: 43,340 lbs × $0.20 + $600 freight = $9,268. |\n| Percent Yield | Recovery percentage: (Recovered lbs / Weight Received lbs) × 100. | Displayed on invoices and contract summary views. Customer-facing metric. |\n| Weight Reconciliation Chain | The complete weight trail visible on an invoice: received > processed > recovered > yield %. | Customer verification mechanism. |\n| Steel Deduction | Weight of steel removed from incoming material before smelting. Creates dual-weight billing: customer billed on full incoming weight, recovery calculated on post-steel weight. | Documented on furnace production sheets. |\n| Lot Merge | Consolidating multiple lots onto a single invoice for billing. Customer-driven (e.g., JW requires individual lot per load but wants consolidated billing). | Kim's merge function in frmLotInvoicing. |\n| Purchase Order (PO) | A formal order for material or services. Does NOT exist in current system — biggest gap identified. Entire PO process lives on spreadsheets. | Must support all three work streams. |\n| Work Stream | One of three distinct business models: (1) tolling/recycling, (2) buy-sell scrap for profit, (3) JV/partnership. Type L = per lot (per truckload), Type U = per unit (per pound). | Freight is the most common additional charge. |\n| Energy Surcharge | A per-contract surcharge field. DEPRECATED — used once for high energy costs. Can be dropped in new system. | EnergySurchgRate field exists but is 0.0000 on all observed contracts. |\n| Blended Price | A contract-level flag indicating the price is a blend of multiple material rates rather than a single rate. | Checkbox on contract form. Kim opens frmLotInvoicing, enters lot number or uses \"Uninvoiced Processed Lots Only\" filter.\n2. System displays three-panel layout: Main Grid (top — lot summary with pricing), Sows Panel (left — individual sow details), Pending Invoices Panel (right — queued invoices).\n3. Kim reviews lot data: LbsReceived, WeightOut, ContamWgt, LotPrice, Calc, InvAmt, Additional Charge info, Energy Rate/Chg.\n4. Kim clicks **Create Invoice** — system updates sows, closes receipts, updates lot. Confirmation: \"5 updated sows. 1 receipts were closed. 1 Lot updated.\" Invoice moves to Pending Invoices panel.\n5. Kim clicks **Test Invoices** — system generates preview reports (rptInvoice + rptInvoiceSows) for QA review.\n6. Test output reviewed with customer contact (Kim calls or emails preview).\n7. Kim clicks **Process Invoices** — **IRREVERSIBLE**. Lot is permanently closed. Inventory moves from unprocessed to processed.\n8. System generates three output files: PDF invoice, PDF analysis, Excel analysis. Saved to `G:\\PDF\\Invoice\\{CustNo}_{date}_{LotNo}_INV.xls` (and PDF equivalents).\n9. Kim emails files to customer for approval.\n10. Treina receives invoice for QA review (separate workflow — see below).\n\n*Decision Points:*\n- **Lot merge:** If customer requires consolidated billing across multiple lots, Kim uses merge function before Create Invoice step.\n- **Test vs Process:** Test is the quality gate. Processing is irreversible. The deliberate two-step separation is a feature, not a limitation.\n\n*Exceptions & Edge Cases:*\n- Multiple lots merging to one invoice (customer-driven, e.g., JW Aluminum)\n- Invoice number defaults to first lot number (convention, can be overridden)\n- Blended pricing when lots span material types\n- Steel deduction creates dual-weight billing (customer billed on full incoming, recovery on post-steel)\n\n### Invoice QA Review\n\n*Trigger:* Kim generates invoice files.\n*Actors:* Treina (primary), Kim (handoff)\n\n*Process Flow:*\n1. Treina receives invoice files (PDF + Excel) from Kim's processing.\n2. Treina exports invoice data from Access to Excel.\n3. Treina reviews for weight discrepancies between receipt stage and invoice stage.\n4. Treina validates pricing against contract terms.\n5. Treina catches and corrects discrepancies (weight adjustment engine disguised as review).\n6. Treina files approved invoice.\n\n*Exceptions & Edge Cases:*\n- Eight data redundancy points (shadow-record patterns) where Treina manually cross-checks data across multiple sources.\n- This is load-bearing manual work — the new system must systematize this quality gate, not eliminate it.\n\n### Invoice Output & Distribution\n\n*Trigger:* Invoice processing complete.\n*Actors:* Kim (distribution), Treina (QA), Customers (receipt)\n\n*Process Flow:*\n1. System generates three files: PDF invoice, PDF analysis, Excel analysis.\n2. Files pushed to `G:\\PDF\\Invoice\\` network share.\n3. Kim emails files to customer.\n4. Invoice data exported to Southware (external accounting system).\n5. For portal customers: invoice data also feeds customer self-service portal (§8).\n6. For Logan: customer-specific comma-delimited export format (integration debt).\n\n*Decision Points:*\n- **Push vs Pull:** File push model persists alongside any portal/API. Cannot eliminate file generation even when pull model exists.\n- **Customer-specific exports:** Logan's comma-delimited format is an obligation that persists. New system needs configurable export engine, not hardcoded per-customer formats.\n\n### Purchase Order Management (NEW — Does Not Exist Today)\n\n*Trigger:* TAP needs to order material from a vendor, or a customer places a purchase order with TAP.\n*Actors:* Bill (PO creation/approval), Kim (entry), Treina (tracking)\n\n*Process Flow:*\n1. Bill initiates PO based on customer demand or market opportunity.\n2. PO entered into system with: vendor, material type, quantity, price, delivery terms, work stream (tolling/buy-sell/JV).\n3. System tracks PO status: Open > Partially Fulfilled > Fulfilled > Closed.\n4. 30-day delivery window monitored with deadline alerts.\n5. Incoming receipts linked to POs for fulfillment tracking.\n6. PO data feeds profitability tracking.\n\n*Decision Points:*\n- **Work stream classification:** Each PO must be tagged to one of three work streams for profitability tracking.\n- **Market-driven behavior:** Vendors delay delivery in rising commodity markets, cancel in falling markets. System must surface delivery deadline risk.\n\n*Exceptions & Edge Cases:*\n- Currently 100% on spreadsheets — no existing system logic to migrate.\n- Must support all three work streams with different financial models.\n\n## Business Rules\n\n| ID | Rule | Type | Details | Source |\n|----|------|------|---------|--------|\n| BR-06-001 | Toll charge based on weight received | CALC | Toll Charge = Unit Price × Weight Received. Every pound of aluminum that moves through receiving, processing, and shipping eventually passes through this module as a dollar amount. The module covers lot-based invoicing, invoice quality assurance, purchase order management (new — does not exist in the current system), and profitability tracking across three distinct business work streams.\n\nThe current system handles invoicing through a three-step irreversible workflow: Create Invoice > Test Invoices > Process Invoices. Kim creates invoices from processed lots, Treina QA-reviews them via an Access-to-Excel export pipeline (catching weight discrepancies and pricing errors), and the finalized package — PDF invoice, PDF analysis, and Excel analysis — gets pushed to a network share and emailed to customers. This workflow is the financial heart of the system, bridging production completion and customer billing.\n\nThe single biggest finding across all three discovery days is the Purchase Order gap. TAP has no PO management in the current Access system. The entire PO workflow — across tolling, buy-sell scrap, and JV partnerships — lives on spreadsheets outside the system. This module must close that gap. Additionally, the CEO has directed a profitability dashboard showing spend vs. revenue by customer and work stream, giving executive visibility into margins across all three business models.\n\nThe module serves 5 primary stakeholders across 2 organizations (TAP internal + customers), integrates with an external accounting system (Southware), and must support both file-push and portal-pull output models for invoice delivery. It operates across two TAP facilities (Mt. Pleasant and Gadsden) with isolated financial data per the 3-DB architecture.\n\n## Non-Goals\n\n- **Contract creation and pricing management** — belongs to §7 CRM / Customer Management. §6 consumes contract pricing but does not manage contract lifecycle, pricing terms, or material type hierarchies.\n- **Receiving weight entry and lot creation** — belongs to §4 Aluminum Intake. §6 consumes receiving weight data for invoice calculation but does not manage the receiving workflow.\n- **Smelting and production tracking** — belongs to §5 Smelting Operations. §6 references heat/sow data for invoice detail but does not manage production.\n- **Customer portal self-service** — belongs to §8 Customer Portal. §6 generates documents that the portal may expose, but portal architecture is not §6 scope.\n- **Executive and sales dashboards** — belongs to §9 Reporting & Analytics. §6 provides profitability data; §9 owns dashboard presentation (Bill's sales dashboard, CEO executive dashboard).\n- **External accounting system architecture** — the Southware integration interface is §6 scope, but the accounting system itself is external. Database design and hosting decisions belong in Part 2 (SRD).\n- **Real-time market pricing integration** — discussed during discovery as a Bill dashboard feature, belongs to §9 Reporting & Analytics. §6 tracks historical pricing via contracts.\n- **Power BI / Grafana dashboard infrastructure** — technical implementation decisions belong in Part 2 (SRD). §6 specifies what financial data must be reportable.\n\n## Vocabulary\n\n| Term | Definition | Notes |\n|------|-----------|-------|\n| Invoice | The billing document generated from lot processing data. Covers one or more lots merged for a single customer. Three-step lifecycle: Create > Test > Process. | Invoice number = first lot number by convention (not hard rule). |\n| Toll Charge | The processing fee charged to the customer, calculated as Unit Price × Weight Received. | Based on RECEIVED weight, NOT recovered weight. Core revenue calculation. |\n| Invoice Total | Toll Charge + Additional Charges (freight, surcharges). The amount billed to the customer. | Verified: 43,340 lbs × $0.20 + $600 freight = $9,268. |\n| Percent Yield | Recovery percentage: (Recovered lbs / Weight Received lbs) × 100. | Displayed on invoices and contract summary views. Customer-facing metric. |\n| Weight Reconciliation Chain | The complete weight trail visible on an invoice: received > processed > recovered > yield %. | Customer verification mechanism. |\n| Steel Deduction | Weight of steel removed from incoming material before smelting. Creates dual-weight billing: customer billed on full incoming weight, recovery calculated on post-steel weight. | Documented on furnace production sheets. |\n| Lot Merge | Consolidating multiple lots onto a single invoice for billing. Customer-driven (e.g., JW requires individual lot per load but wants consolidated billing). | Kim's merge function in frmLotInvoicing. |\n| Purchase Order (PO) | A formal order for material or services. Does NOT exist in current system — biggest gap identified. Entire PO process lives on spreadsheets. | Must support all three work streams. |\n| Work Stream | One of three distinct business models: (1) tolling/recycling, (2) buy-sell scrap for profit, (3) JV/partnership. Each has different billing mechanics and margin structures. | CEO requires profitability visibility across all three. |\n| Profitability Record | Spend vs. revenue tracking by customer and work stream. New entity — CEO directive. | Feeds profitability dashboard. |\n| Invoice QA | Treina's quality assurance review: Access > Excel export > review for weight discrepancies and pricing > file approved. | Eight data redundancy points identified (shadow-record patterns). |\n| Shadow Record | A manual data entry pattern where the same information is maintained in multiple places (system + spreadsheet, or person's memory). | Treina has 8 identified shadow-record points. Bill's pricing knowledge is another. |\n| Pending Invoice | An invoice that has been created but not yet processed. Visible in the Pending Invoices panel of frmLotInvoicing. | Intermediate state between Create and Process. |\n| Test Invoice | A preview invoice generated for QA review before final processing. | Generates same reports as final but does not close the lot. |\n| Remittance Address | The payment destination address (TAP, DEPT# 318, P.O. BOX 1000, MEMPHIS, TN 38148-0318). Separate from facility addresses. | Must appear on all invoices and payment documents. |\n| Southware | TAP's external accounting system (AP/AR). Invoices are exported to Southware as part of the invoice processing workflow. | Integration interface, not replacement. |\n| Additional Charge | Line-item or header-level surcharge on a contract/invoice. Type L = per lot (per truckload), Type U = per unit (per pound). | Freight is the most common additional charge. |\n| Energy Surcharge | A per-contract surcharge field. DEPRECATED — used once for high energy costs. Can be dropped in new system. | EnergySurchgRate field exists but is 0.0000 on all observed contracts. |\n| Blended Price | A contract-level flag indicating the price is a blend of multiple material rates rather than a single rate. | Checkbox on contract form. Affects invoice calculation when lots span material types. |\n| Three-Tier Hierarchy | Seq# (per truck/event) > Lot# (consolidation group) > Invoice (billing unit). Enables per-truck granularity, customer-facing grouping, and billing aggregation. | Architectural pattern bridging §4 receiving and §6 invoicing. |\n\n## User Roles & Access\n\n| Role | Organization(s) | Access Level | Key Activities |\n|------|-----------------|-------------|----------------|\n| Kim Sproul | TAP — Mt. Pleasant | Full operational | Invoice creation, lot merge, invoice processing, file distribution, invoice lookup. Primary operator. SPOF. |\n| Treina | TAP — Finance | Read + QA review | Invoice QA workflow (Access > Excel > review > file), weight discrepancy validation, 8 shadow-record reconciliation points. Needs read-only dashboard without operational edit permissions. |\n| Bill Crawford | TAP — Sales | Read + pricing authority | Pricing knowledge (tacit — 20-25 material types in his head), deal evaluation, weight discrepancy notifications, PO delivery deadline management. |\n| Jared | TAP — CEO | Executive read | Profitability dashboard access via customer website (not TAP Access). Cross-location financial visibility. |\n| Fayla | TAP — Gadsden | Full operational | Replicates Kim's invoicing role at Gadsden facility. |\n| Jason Bracket | TAP — Plant Manager | Read + notifications | Oversees financial operations at both facilities. Receives weight tolerance alerts. |\n| Customers | External | Receives documents | Receives invoice packages (PDF + Excel), monthly production reports. Reviews weight reconciliation and chemistry data for payment approval. |\n\n## Key Workflows\n\n### Lot Invoicing (Three-Step Workflow)\n\n*Trigger:* Lot processing is complete and sows have been produced, weighed, and (optionally) chemistry-analyzed.\n*Actors:* Kim (creation), Treina (QA), Customer (receives)\n\n*Process Flow:*\n1. Kim opens frmLotInvoicing, enters lot number or uses \"Uninvoiced Processed Lots Only\" filter.\n2. System displays three-panel layout: Main Grid (top — lot summary with pricing), Sows Panel (left — individual sow details), Pending Invoices Panel (right — queued invoices).\n3. Kim reviews lot data: LbsReceived, WeightOut, ContamWgt, LotPrice, Calc, InvAmt, Additional Charge info, Energy Rate/Chg.\n4. Kim clicks **Create Invoice** — system updates sows, closes receipts, updates lot. Confirmation: \"5 updated sows. 1 receipts were closed. 1 Lot updated.\" Invoice moves to Pending Invoices panel.\n5. Kim clicks **Test Invoices** — system generates preview reports (rptInvoice + rptInvoiceSows) for QA review.\n6. Test output reviewed with customer contact (Kim calls or emails preview).\n7. Kim clicks **Process Invoices** — **IRREVERSIBLE**. Lot is permanently closed. Inventory moves from unprocessed to processed.\n8. System generates three output files: PDF invoice, PDF analysis, Excel analysis. Saved to `G:\\PDF\\Invoice\\{CustNo}_{date}_{LotNo}_INV.xls` (and PDF equivalents).\n9. Kim emails files to customer for approval.\n10. Treina receives invoice for QA review (separate workflow — see below).\n\n*Decision Points:*\n- **Lot merge:** If customer requires consolidated billing across multiple lots, Kim uses merge function before Create Invoice step.\n- **Test vs Process:** Test is the quality gate. Processing is irreversible. The deliberate two-step separation is a feature, not a limitation.\n\n*Exceptions & Edge Cases:*\n- Multiple lots merging to one invoice (customer-driven, e.g., JW Aluminum)\n- Invoice number defaults to first lot number (convention, can be overridden)\n- Blended pricing when lots span material types\n- Steel deduction creates dual-weight billing (customer billed on full incoming, recovery on post-steel)\n\n### Invoice QA Review\n\n*Trigger:* Kim generates invoice files.\n*Actors:* Treina (primary), Kim (handoff)\n\n*Process Flow:*\n1. Treina receives invoice files (PDF + Excel) from Kim's processing.\n2. Treina exports invoice data from Access to Excel.\n3. Treina reviews for weight discrepancies between receipt stage and invoice stage.\n4. Treina validates pricing against contract terms.\n5. Treina catches and corrects discrepancies (weight adjustment engine disguised as review).\n6. Treina files approved invoice.\n\n*Exceptions & Edge Cases:*\n- Eight data redundancy points (shadow-record patterns) where Treina manually cross-checks data across multiple sources.\n- This is load-bearing manual work — the new system must systematize this quality gate, not eliminate it.\n\n### Invoice Output & Distribution\n\n*Trigger:* Invoice processing complete.\n*Actors:* Kim (distribution), Treina (QA), Customers (receipt)\n\n*Process Flow:*\n1. System generates three files: PDF invoice, PDF analysis, Excel analysis.\n2. Files pushed to `G:\\PDF\\Invoice\\` network share.\n3. Kim emails files to customer.\n4. Invoice data exported to Southware (external accounting system).\n5. For portal customers: invoice data also feeds customer self-service portal (§8).\n6. For Logan: customer-specific comma-delimited export format (integration debt).\n\n*Decision Points:*\n- **Push vs Pull:** File push model persists alongside any portal/API. Cannot eliminate file generation even when pull model exists.\n- **Customer-specific exports:** Logan's comma-delimited format is an obligation that persists. New system needs configurable export engine, not hardcoded per-customer formats.\n\n### Purchase Order Management (NEW — Does Not Exist Today)\n\n*Trigger:* TAP needs to order material from a vendor, or a customer places a purchase order with TAP.\n*Actors:* Bill (PO creation/approval), Kim (entry), Treina (tracking)\n\n*Process Flow:*\n1. Bill initiates PO based on customer demand or market opportunity.\n2. PO entered into system with: vendor, material type, quantity, price, delivery terms, work stream (tolling/buy-sell/JV).\n3. System tracks PO status: Open > Partially Fulfilled > Fulfilled > Closed.\n4. 30-day delivery window monitored with deadline alerts.\n5. Incoming receipts linked to POs for fulfillment tracking.\n6. PO data feeds profitability tracking.\n\n*Decision Points:*\n- **Work stream classification:** Each PO must be tagged to one of three work streams for profitability tracking.\n- **Market-driven behavior:** Vendors delay delivery in rising commodity markets, cancel in falling markets. System must surface delivery deadline risk.\n\n*Exceptions & Edge Cases:*\n- Currently 100% on spreadsheets — no existing system logic to migrate.\n- Must support all three work streams with different financial models.\n\n## Business Rules\n\n| ID | Rule | Type | Details | Source |\n|----|------|------|---------|--------|\n| BR-06-001 | Toll charge based on weight received | CALC | Toll Charge = Unit Price × Weight Received. Customer billed on received weight, NOT recovered weight. Example: $0.14 × 222,940 lbs = $31,211.60. | [D1-AC-3], [D2-SC-frmLotInvoicing] |\n| BR-06-002 | Invoice total calculation | CALC | InvAmt = (LbsReceived × LotPrice) + AdditionalCharge. Verified: 43,340 × $0.20 + $600 freight = $9,268. | [D1-AC-3], [D2-PS-CSV6] |\n| BR-06-003 | Percent yield calculation | CALC | Recovery % = (Recovered lbs / Weight Received lbs) × 100. Example: 46,073 / 222,940 = 20.67%. | [D1-AC-3], [D1-SC-4] |\n| BR-06-004 | Invoice three-step workflow | WORKFLOW | Create Invoice > Test Invoices > Process Invoices. Kim reviews with customer contact between Test and Process. | [D2-SC-frmLotInvoicing] |\n| BR-06-005 | Invoice processing is irreversible | CONSTRAINT | Once processed, lot is closed and inventory moves from unprocessed to processed. No undo. Permanent state change. | [D2-SC-frmLotInvoicing] |\n| BR-06-006 | Invoice generates three output files | WORKFLOW | PDF invoice + PDF analysis + Excel analysis. Saved to G:\\PDF\\Invoice\\{CustNo}_{date}_{LotNo}_INV.xls. | [D2-SC-frmLotInvoicing] |\n| BR-06-007 | Multiple lots can merge to one invoice | CONSTRAINT | Lot merge function consolidates multiple lots. Customer-driven. Weight reconciliation across merged lots required. | [D1-AC-3], [D3-PS-W4] |\n| BR-06-008 | Invoice number convention | FORMAT | Invoice number = first lot number in merged set. Convention, not hard requirement. | [D3-PS-W4] |\n| BR-06-009 | Invoicing is per-heat | CONSTRAINT | Each heat generates its own billable unit. Billing traces back to individual heats. Affects cost allocation. | [D3-PS-W5A] |\n| BR-06-010 | Uninvoiced processed lots filter | WORKFLOW | Lot invoicing lookup supports \"Uninvoiced Processed Lots Only\" checkbox to filter ready-to-invoice lots. | [D2-SC-frmLotInvoicing] |\n| BR-06-011 | Invoice QA workflow | WORKFLOW | Treina's QA: Access > Excel > review for weight discrepancies and pricing > file. Eight shadow-record data redundancy points. | [D2-PS-W7] |\n| BR-06-012 | Invoice file push model persists | INTEGRATION | File push to G:\\PDF\\Invoice\\ continues alongside any portal/API. Cannot eliminate file generation. | [D2-PS-W5] |\n| BR-06-013 | Weight reconciliation chain on invoice | CALC | Invoice shows: received weight > processed weight > recovered weight > yield %. Customer-facing verification. | [D3-PS-W4], [D1-AC-3] |\n| BR-06-014 | Three-tier hierarchy | CONSTRAINT | Seq# (per truck) > Lot# (consolidation) > Invoice (billing). Bridges §4 receiving architecture and §6 invoicing. | [D3-PS-W4] |\n| BR-06-015 | Purchase order gap | CONSTRAINT | Entire PO process on spreadsheets. No PO management in current Access. Must support tolling, buy-sell, JV. Confirmed by Kim, Treina, Bill. | [D2-PS-W7], [D3-PS-W1], [D1-AC-1] |\n| BR-06-016 | Profitability dashboard (CEO directive) | CONSTRAINT | Spend vs revenue by customer and work stream. CEO accesses via customer website. Three streams trackable. | [D3-PS-W1-QP2], [D2-PS-W8] |\n| BR-06-017 | Delivery deadline alerts for POs | NOTIFY | 30-day delivery terms. Vendors delay in rising markets, cancel in falling. Alert when window expiring. | [D2-PS-W8] |\n| BR-06-018 | Remittance address separate from facility | FORMAT | Payment goes to corporate/billing (TAP, DEPT# 318, P.O. Generated from lot processing data through the three-step workflow.\n\n**Key Fields:** Invoice Number, Customer Number, Lot# (primary + consolidated list), Invoice Date, Contract#, Customer PO#, Source, Processed at (location), Weight Received, Processed, Recovered, Contaminated, Percent Yield, Unit Price, Toll Charge Amount, Freight Amount, Invoice Total.\n\n**Sub-records:** Receipt Detail (per-truck lines), Shipment Detail (per-BOL/heat), Invoice Chemistry Detail (per-sow breakdown).\n\n**Output Files:** PDF invoice, PDF analysis, Excel analysis — all pushed to G:\\PDF\\Invoice\\.\n\n**Relationships:**\n- Invoice belongs to Customer (many-to-one)\n- Invoice covers Lots (one-to-many, via merge)\n- Invoice references Contract (many-to-one)\n- Invoice embeds Receipt Detail (one-to-many)\n- Invoice embeds Shipment Detail (one-to-many)\n\n**Volume:** Scales with lots processed per year. Invoice number = lot number convention suggests similar volume to lot creation.\n\n**Data Quality:** Treina's 8 shadow-record points indicate current data quality issues around weight matching and pricing consistency. New system must eliminate shadow records by making validations inline.\n\n### N1: Purchase Order (NEW)\n\nDoes not exist in current system. Biggest gap identified across all three discovery days.\n\n**Key Fields:** PO Number (system-generated), Vendor, Material Type, Quantity (lbs), Price, Delivery Terms, Delivery Date, Work Stream (tolling/buy-sell/JV), Status (Open/Partially Fulfilled/Fulfilled/Closed), Created By, Created Date.\n\n**Relationships:**\n- PO references Vendor/Customer (many-to-one)\n- PO references Material Type (many-to-one)\n- PO linked to Receipts for fulfillment tracking (one-to-many)\n- PO feeds Profitability Record\n\n**Volume:** Unknown — currently on spreadsheets. There is no separate migration workstream — each module migrates its own data as it is built, using AI-assisted extraction scripts that pipe Access data into the target database. Tim will run multiple Claude instances simultaneously, each working on a different module's data extraction and mapping, with Kim validating migrated records by comparing what she sees in the new screens against the same records in Access.\n\nThis approach was a deliberate decision, not a default. It reflects Tim's development model: lay out the application structure, discover data mappings as each module is built, and let the migration work serve as a forcing function for understanding the source data. The Access database is the sole source system — a single MDB file per location containing approximately 20 core operational tables alongside an unknown number of temporary and junk tables accumulated over 27 years.\n\n## 15.2 Source Data Inventory\n\n### 15.2.1 Access Database Structure\n\nThe source system is a Microsoft Access 97 MDB file. Two sandbox copies exist for development use:\n\n| Sandbox | Location | Purpose |\n|---------|----------|---------|\n| TAPPgmMP | Mt. Pleasant | Primary sandbox — most complete operational data |\n| Gadsden copy | Gadsden | Second facility — separate database file, same schema |\n\nThe database contains approximately 20 core operational tables spanning receiving, smelting, invoicing, customer management, inventory, and reference data. Beyond these core tables, an unknown number of temporary and junk tables have accumulated since the application's creation in 1998. Many have been dead since approximately 2010. No formal schema documentation exists.\n\nColumn naming is inconsistent. Some tables use descriptive names; others use cryptic identifiers (\"Field 34\") that require investigation to map to their business meaning. The schema reflects 27 years of incremental modification without refactoring.\n\n### 15.2.2 Known Data Quality Issues\n\nThe following data quality problems have been identified during discovery and must be accounted for during migration:\n\n| Issue | Impact | Mitigation |\n|-------|--------|------------|\n| No referential integrity | Orphaned records exist across tables; foreign key relationships are implicit, not enforced | Validate relationships during extraction; log orphans for review |\n| Cryptically named columns | \"Field 34\" and similar names obscure business meaning | Field mapping methodology (§15.4) addresses this systematically |\n| Dead tables (~2010) | Tables exist in schema but have not received writes in 15+ years | Identify and exclude during source inventory phase |\n| Junk/temp tables | Scratch tables from ad hoc queries or one-time operations | Identify by naming pattern and last-modified date; exclude from migration scope |\n| Ghost/dummy contracts | Workaround records created to satisfy system constraints that don't represent real business relationships | Flag during extraction; determine keep/discard per module with Kim's guidance |\n| DEPRECATED fields | EnergySurchargeRate (value: 0.0000, used once) and potentially others | Explicit exclusion list maintained per module |\n| 6-digit foreign key prefix | Location segregation encoded as a record-level prefix rather than database-level separation | Strip during extraction; replaced by database-level location separation in new architecture |\n| Contact Email Y/N flag | Some customer records store Y/N in the email field instead of an address (~273 records need audit) | Data audit during CRM module migration; remap to boolean flag + separate email field |\n\n### 15.2.3 Data Volume and Scope\n\n**Retention directive:** 7 years of operational data, per CEO (Jared Sweeny) mandate.\n\n**Extraction strategy:** Import everything first. Do not attempt to filter by date during extraction — the Access date formats, storage patterns, and table relationships make pre-filtering unreliable. After all data is loaded into the target database, run queries to identify records outside the 7-year retention window and handle them according to the archival approach defined in §15.7.\n\n**Estimated scope by module area:**\n\n| Module | Data Characteristics | Estimated Table Count |\n|--------|---------------------|----------------------|\n| §4 Aluminum Intake | Receiving notes, BOL records, chemistry readings, inventory tracking | Heavy — multiple core tables |\n| §5 Smelting Operations | Furnace production records, charge sheets, chemistry samples | Moderate — time-series operational data |\n| §6 Financial Management | Invoice records, contract pricing, profitability tracking | Moderate — transactional with lookup references |\n| §7 CRM | Customer records, contracts, source codes | Moderate — shared across locations |\n| §10 User Management | 8 Phase 1 roles | Light — may be created fresh rather than migrated |\n| §11 Admin & Configuration | 9 admin-owned lookup tables, yard location aliases, system defaults | Light — reference data, small row counts |\n\n## 15.3 ETL Approach\n\n### 15.3.1 Tooling\n\n| Component | Technology | Status |\n|-----------|-----------|--------|\n| Source extraction | MDB Tools (command-line utilities for reading Access databases) | **DECIDED** |\n| Script generation | AI (Claude) writes shell scripts to extract and pipe data | **DECIDED** |\n| Target loading | Shell scripts pipe extracted data directly to target database | **DECIDED** |\n| Target database | Turso / libSQL (Tim's choice) vs PostgreSQL (SOW specification) | **CONTRADICTED** — see §15.3.3 |\n\nMDB Tools provides command-line read access to Access MDB files without requiring Microsoft Access or Windows. Claude generates the extraction scripts — shell scripts that read from Access tables, transform data as needed, and pipe results into the target database. Tim executes and validates; the scripts are not black-box automation.\n\n### 15.3.2 Module-by-Module Strategy\n\nMigration is not a phase — it is embedded in the build cycle for each module. The sequence follows the material flow through the plant:\n\n1. **Module development begins** — Tim lays out application structure\n2. **Data discovery** — Tim examines Access tables relevant to the module, maps fields, resolves cryptic names\n3. **Script generation** — Claude writes extraction scripts for the module's tables\n4. **Extraction and load** — Tim runs scripts to move data into the target database\n5. **Screen-level validation** — Kim compares migrated records in the new UI against the same records in Access\n6. **Iterate** — Fix mapping errors, re-extract, re-validate until Kim confirms accuracy\n\n**Parallel execution:** Tim will run multiple Claude instances simultaneously, each working on a different module. One instance handles customer data, another handles receiving, a third handles transfers. This is an explicit part of the development model, not an optimization — each module's data is largely independent.\n\n**Order follows build priority,** which follows material flow: Intake (§4) before Smelting (§5) before Financial (§6). Reference data (§11) may be migrated early as a dependency for operational modules.\n\n### 15.3.3 Target Database Mapping\n\nThe Access database uses a single-file-per-location model (TAPPgmMP for Mt. Pleasant, a separate file for Gadsden). The new architecture separates this into:\n\n| New Database | Content | Maps From |\n|-------------|---------|-----------|\n| Shared database | Users, authentication, cross-location master data | Both Access files (deduplicated) |\n| Mt. Pleasant operational DB | All operational records for Mt. Pleasant | TAPPgmMP |\n| Gadsden operational DB | All operational records for Gadsden | Gadsden Access file |\n\n**Database technology tension:** Tim has selected Turso / libSQL as the target database. The SOW specifies PostgreSQL. This is a **CONTRADICTED** decision requiring resolution before migration scripts are written, as the SQL dialect, data types, and loading mechanisms differ between the two platforms.\n\nThe 6-digit foreign key prefix currently used for location segregation within the shared Access database is stripped during extraction. Location separation is handled at the database level in the new architecture, eliminating the need for prefix-based filtering.\n\n## 15.4 Field Mapping Methodology\n\nThree complementary approaches address the \"Field 34\" problem — cryptically named columns whose business meaning is not apparent from the schema alone.\n\n### 15.4.1 Deductive Approach\n\nThe primary method. Extract data from a known record, display it on the matching screen in the new application, and compare to what Kim sees for the same record in Access. If the value in \"Field 34\" appears in the \"Special Instructions\" box on Kim's screen, the mapping is resolved.\n\n**Process:**\n1. Extract a representative record from Access\n2. Identify all fields with known and unknown mappings\n3. Display in the new UI alongside the Access screen\n4. Kim confirms or corrects each field's placement\n\nThis is the default approach for most field mapping work.\n\n### 15.4.2 Reverse Engineering\n\nAI traces through the Access application logic — VBA code, form data sources, query definitions — to find what reads from and writes to cryptically named fields. This approach works when the deductive method is inconclusive (e.g., a field that is stored but never displayed, or displayed only in certain conditions).\n\n**Process:**\n1. Identify the target field in the Access schema\n2. AI examines VBA modules, form record sources, and query definitions\n3. Trace the data flow: what form control writes to this field, under what conditions\n4. Map the business meaning from the application logic\n\n### 15.4.3 Brute-Force Validation\n\nA programmatic verification method. Insert a unique, identifiable value into every input field on an Access form, then examine which database columns received those values. This creates an unambiguous mapping between UI controls and database fields.\n\n**Process:**\n1. Open the Access sandbox to a blank or test record\n2. Programmatically (or manually) enter unique marker values in every input field\n3. Save the record\n4. Query the database to find which columns contain the marker values\n5. The column-to-field mapping is established definitively\n\nThis approach is most valuable as a verification step after deductive or reverse-engineering mapping, and for forms with many fields where manual tracing is error-prone.\n\n## 15.5 Validation Approach\n\nValidation is module-by-module and screen-level. There is no separate validation phase — validation is the final step of each module's migration cycle.\n\n**Primary validator:** Kim Sproul. She has 16+ years of operational experience and is the only person who can confirm whether migrated data looks correct in context.\n\n**Validation method:**\n1. Tim identifies a representative set of records for the module (including edge cases: oldest records, records with unusual values, records spanning the 7-year boundary)\n2. Kim opens the same record in both Access and the new system, side by side\n3. Kim confirms every visible field matches, or identifies discrepancies\n4. Discrepancies are logged, mapping is corrected, and the affected records are re-extracted\n5. Kim re-validates until she confirms accuracy\n\n**Validation coverage:** Every module that migrates data must pass Kim's screen-level validation before the module is considered complete. There is no automated validation substitute for Kim's domain knowledge — she knows what \"looks right\" in ways that automated checks cannot replicate.\n\n**Desktop AI for Access exploration:** For complex validation scenarios, Tim can use Remote Desktop to Jared's server where the Access sandbox is deployed, sharing his screen with Claude/AI to explore the Access application visually and trace data discrepancies.\n\n## 15.6 Cutover Strategy\n\nThe organic ETL approach simplifies cutover. There is no single cutover event — each module cuts over to the new system as it is built, validated, and approved. This means:\n\n- **No big-bang switchover** requiring a weekend freeze and all-hands migration event\n- **Module-level go/no-go decisions** rather than a single system-level cutover decision\n- **Rollback granularity** at the module level — if a module's migration has problems, only that module reverts to Access while the issue is resolved\n- **Parallel operation** is the natural state during the build phase — some modules run on the new system while others remain in Access\n\nThe final cutover occurs when the last module is migrated, validated, and running in production. At that point, Access transitions from active operational system to read-only archive.\n\n## 15.7 Historical Data and Retention\n\n**Retention policy:** 7 years of operational data must be preserved and queryable. This is a CEO directive (Jared Sweeny), not a regulatory requirement.\n\n**Extraction approach:** Import everything. Do not filter by date during extraction. Tim: *\"I would just import everything anyway, and then just go back and do a query for anything over seven years old.\"*\n\n**Post-import handling of aged data:**\n\n| Data Age | Treatment |\n|----------|-----------|\n| Within 7-year window | Active — fully queryable, visible in all operational screens and reports |\n| Beyond 7-year window | Archive candidate — query to identify, then determine disposition |\n| Pre-2010 dead table data | Exclude from migration entirely — these tables have not received writes in 15+ years |\n\n**Archival approach:** Records beyond the 7-year window are not deleted during migration. They are identified via post-import queries and either archived to a separate store or soft-deleted (flagged as archived but retained in the database). The specific archival mechanism is an open item — it depends on data volume and the target database's capabilities.\n\n## 15.8 Deprecated and Excluded Data\n\nThe following data elements are explicitly excluded from migration or flagged as deprecated:\n\n### Excluded from Migration\n\n| Element | Reason |\n|---------|--------|\n| Dead tables (~2010) | No writes in 15+ years; confirmed inactive during discovery |\n| Junk/temp tables | Scratch data from ad hoc queries; no operational value |\n| EnergySurchargeRate field | DEPRECATED. Value is 0.0000. Used once in the system's history. |\n| 6-digit location prefix | Replaced by database-level location separation; stripped during extraction |\n\n### Requires Investigation Before Exclusion\n\n| Element | Reason |\n|---------|--------|\n| Ghost/dummy contracts | Workaround records — Kim must confirm which are safe to exclude |\n| Orphaned records | May indicate data quality issues or may be legitimate historical artifacts |\n| Cryptically named columns with NULL values | May be deprecated fields or may be conditionally populated |\n\nA complete exclusion list will be finalized per module
