|\n\n**Summary:** 42 requirements. 37 Must-Have, 5 Should-Have.\n\n## Data Entities\n\n### E12: Invoice\n\nThe primary billing entity. Generated from lot processing data through the three-step workflow.\n\n**Key Fields:** Invoice Number, Customer Number, Lot# (primary + consolidated list), Invoice Date, Contract#, Customer PO#, Source, Processed at (location), Weight Received, Processed, Recovered, Contaminated, Percent Yield, Unit Price, Toll Charge Amount, Freight Amount, Invoice Total.\n\n**Sub-records:** Receipt Detail (per-truck lines), Shipment Detail (per-BOL/heat), Invoice Chemistry Detail (per-sow breakdown).\n\n**Output Files:** PDF invoice, PDF analysis, Excel analysis — all pushed to G:\\PDF\\Invoice\\.\n\n**Relationships:**\n- Invoice belongs to Customer (many-to-one)\n- Invoice covers Lots (one-to-many, via merge)\n- Invoice references Contract (many-to-one)\n- Invoice embeds Receipt Detail (one-to-many)\n- Invoice embeds Shipment Detail (one-to-many)\n\n**Volume:** Scales with lots processed per year. Invoice number = lot number convention suggests similar volume to lot creation.\n\n**Data Quality:** Treina's 8 shadow-record points indicate current data quality issues around weight matching and pricing consistency. New system must eliminate shadow records by making validations inline.\n\n### N1: Purchase Order (NEW)\n\nDoes not exist in current system. Biggest gap identified across all three discovery days.\n\n**Key Fields:** PO Number (system-generated), Vendor, Material Type, Quantity (lbs), Price, Delivery Terms, Delivery Date, Work Stream (tolling/buy-sell/JV), Status (Open/Partially Fulfilled/Fulfilled/Closed), Created By, Created Date.\n\n**Relationships:**\n- PO references Vendor/Customer (many-to-one)\n- PO references Material Type (many-to-one)\n- PO linked to Receipts for fulfillment tracking (one-to-many)\n- PO feeds Profitability Record\n\n**Volume:** Unknown — currently on spreadsheets. Estimate based on receiving volume (~4-5 trucks/day).\n\n**Data Quality:** No existing data to migrate. Clean start.\n\n### N2: Profitability Record (NEW)\n\nCEO-directed entity for tracking spend vs. revenue by customer and work stream.\n\n**Key Fields:** Customer, Work Stream (tolling/buy-sell/JV), Period, Revenue (toll charges + additional charges), Costs (material purchase, processing, labor), Margin, Recovery %, Location.\n\n**Relationships:**\n- Profitability Record belongs to Customer (many-to-one)\n- Profitability Record aggregates from Invoices, POs, Lots, Heats\n- Profitability Record belongs to Location (many-to-one)\n\n**Volume:** One record per customer per work stream per period. Scale depends on period granularity (monthly vs. weekly).\n\n**Data Quality:** Requires accurate cost data from §5 (processing costs) and accurate revenue data from §6 (invoicing). Cross-module data quality dependency.\n\n## Reporting Requirements\n\n| Report | Type | Frequency | Users | Parity | Data Sources |\n|--------|------|-----------|-------|--------|-------------|\n| Invoice/Receiving and Processing Report (rptInvoice) | Existing | Per invoice | Customers, Kim, Treina | Replicate | E12, E5, E6, E9, E10 |\n| Invoice Chemistry Detail (rptInvoiceSows) | Existing | Per invoice | Customers | Replicate | E12, E10, E11 |\n| Current Month Production Report | Existing | Monthly | Customers, Jared | Replicate | E5, E12, inventory roll-up |\n| Invoice Analysis (PDF + Excel) | Existing | Per invoice | Treina, Customers | Replicate | E12 |\n| PO Status Report | New | On-demand | Bill, Kim | New | N1 |\n| PO Delivery Deadline Alert | New | Daily/triggered | Bill | New | N1 |\n| Profitability by Customer & Work Stream | New | Monthly/on-demand | Jared, Bill | New | N2, E12, N1 |\n| Weight Variance Report | New | Per invoice batch | Treina | New | E12, E6 (replaces shadow-record manual checks) |\n\n## Current Workarounds to Resolve\n\n| Workaround | Impact | Resolved By (Req ID) |\n|-----------|--------|---------------------|\n| Treina exports Access data to Excel for invoice QA (8 shadow-record points) | Manual effort, error-prone, data redundancy. Lot status flows from §4 (received/processed) into §6 (invoiced/closed). Receipt sequence numbers enable per-truck granularity on invoices. PO fulfillment links receipts to purchase orders.\n- **§5 Smelting Operations:** §6 consumes heat/sow production data for invoice detail. Steel deduction (captured at furnace level) affects dual-weight billing. Cost-per-lot calculation requires heat-level cost data. Chemistry data feeds invoice chemistry detail report (rptInvoiceSows).\n- **§7 CRM / Customer Management:** §6 inherits all pricing from contracts (read-only). Contract terms (payment terms, FOB, additional charges, material type pricing) drive invoice calculation. Customer PO# from contract flows to invoice.\n- **§8 Customer Portal:** §6 generates invoice data that the portal exposes to customers. Push + pull delivery model means §6 must feed both file output and portal data.\n- **§9 Reporting & Analytics:** §6 provides profitability data that §9 consumes for executive dashboard, sales dashboard, and operational reports. Monthly inventory roll-up feeds reporting. Cost-per-lot feeds analytics.\n- **§10 User Management:** §6 requires role-based access control: Kim = full operational, Treina = read-only QA, Bill = read + PO creation, Jared = executive read. Finance role is architectural, not a feature flag.\n- **§11 Admin & Configuration:** Payment terms, FOB codes, and other lookup tables managed in §11 are consumed by §6 via contract inheritance.\n\n## Scope Decomposition\n\n- **Lot Invoicing Engine:** Core three-step workflow (Create > Test > Process), toll calculation, lot merge, invoice file generation. Depends on §4 (receiving weight data) and §5 (heat/sow production data). Constrained by irreversibility requirement (FM-R-005). Highest priority — this is the financial heart of the system.\n\n- **Invoice Distribution:** File push to configurable storage, email distribution, Southware export, configurable per-customer export formats. Depends on Lot Invoicing Engine for output. Logan comma-delimited format is the integration debt forcing configurable exports.\n\n- **Invoice QA:** Read-only dashboard for Treina, weight discrepancy flagging, approval/rejection workflow. Depends on Lot Invoicing Engine for data. Must replace all 8 of Treina's shadow-record validation points before launch.\n\n- **Purchase Order Management:** New feature — no existing system logic. PO CRUD, lifecycle tracking, receipt linkage, delivery deadline alerts. Depends on §4 (receipt linkage) and §7 (vendor/customer data). Independent of invoicing — can be built in parallel.\n\n- **Profitability Tracking:** New feature — CEO directive. Spend vs. revenue by customer and work stream. Depends on invoicing data + PO data + cost data from §5. Monthly inventory roll-up logic. Should be built after invoicing and PO management are functional.\n\n- **Cross-Location Financial Isolation:** Zero cross-contamination between Mt. Pleasant and Gadsden financial data. Cross-location reporting via read-only views. Depends on SRD 3-DB architecture. Architectural constraint that affects all other work areas.\n\n## Success Criteria\n\n| # | Criterion | Measure | Current State | Target | Source There is no separate migration workstream — each module migrates its own data as it is built, using AI-assisted extraction scripts that pipe Access data into the target database. Tim will run multiple Claude instances simultaneously, each working on a different module's data extraction and mapping, with Kim validating migrated records by comparing what she sees in the new screens against the same records in Access.\n\nThis approach was a deliberate decision, not a default. It reflects Tim's development model: lay out the application structure, discover data mappings as each module is built, and let the migration work serve as a forcing function for understanding the source data. The Access database is the sole source system — a single MDB file per location containing approximately 20 core operational tables alongside an unknown number of temporary and junk tables accumulated over 27 years.\n\n## 15.2 Source Data Inventory\n\n### 15.2.1 Access Database Structure\n\nThe source system is a Microsoft Access 97 MDB file. Two sandbox copies exist for development use:\n\n| Sandbox | Location | Purpose |\n|---------|----------|---------|\n| TAPPgmMP | Mt. Pleasant | Primary sandbox — most complete operational data |\n| Gadsden copy | Gadsden | Second facility — separate database file, same schema |\n\nThe database contains approximately 20 core operational tables spanning receiving, smelting, invoicing, customer management, inventory, and reference data. Beyond these core tables, an unknown number of temporary and junk tables have accumulated since the application's creation in 1998. Many have been dead since approximately 2010. No formal schema documentation exists.\n\nColumn naming is inconsistent. Some tables use descriptive names; others use cryptic identifiers (\"Field 34\") that require investigation to map to their business meaning. The schema reflects 27 years of incremental modification without refactoring.\n\n### 15.2.2 Known Data Quality Issues\n\nThe following data quality problems have been identified during discovery and must be accounted for during migration:\n\n| Issue | Impact | Mitigation |\n|-------|--------|------------|\n| No referential integrity | Orphaned records exist across tables; foreign key relationships are implicit, not enforced | Validate relationships during extraction; log orphans for review |\n| Cryptically named columns | \"Field 34\" and similar names obscure business meaning | Field mapping methodology (§15.4) addresses this systematically |\n| Dead tables (~2010) | Tables exist in schema but have not received writes in 15+ years | Identify and exclude during source inventory phase |\n| Junk/temp tables | Scratch tables from ad hoc queries or one-time operations | Identify by naming pattern and last-modified date; exclude from migration scope |\n| Ghost/dummy contracts | Workaround records created to satisfy system constraints that don't represent real business relationships | Flag during extraction; determine keep/discard per module with Kim's guidance |\n| DEPRECATED fields | EnergySurchargeRate (value: 0.0000, used once) and potentially others | Explicit exclusion list maintained per module |\n| 6-digit foreign key prefix | Location segregation encoded as a record-level prefix rather than database-level separation | Strip during extraction; replaced by database-level location separation in new architecture |\n| Contact Email Y/N flag | Some customer records store Y/N in the email field instead of an address (~273 records need audit) | Data audit during CRM module migration; remap to boolean flag + separate email field |\n\n### 15.2.3 Data Volume and Scope\n\n**Retention directive:** 7 years of operational data, per CEO (Jared Sweeny) mandate.\n\n**Extraction strategy:** Import everything first. Do not attempt to filter by date during extraction — the Access date formats, storage patterns, and table relationships make pre-filtering unreliable. After all data is loaded into the target database, run queries to identify records outside the 7-year retention window and handle them according to the archival approach defined in §15.7.\n\n**Estimated scope by module area:**\n\n| Module | Data Characteristics | Estimated Table Count |\n|--------|---------------------|----------------------|\n| §4 Aluminum Intake | Receiving notes, BOL records, chemistry readings, inventory tracking | Heavy — multiple core tables |\n| §5 Smelting Operations | Furnace production records, charge sheets, chemistry samples | Moderate — time-series operational data |\n| §6 Financial Management | Invoice records, contract pricing, profitability tracking | Moderate — transactional with lookup references |\n| §7 CRM | Customer records, contracts, source codes | Moderate — shared across locations |\n| §10 User Management | 8 Phase 1 roles | Light — may be created fresh rather than migrated |\n| §11 Admin & Configuration | 9 admin-owned lookup tables, yard location aliases, system defaults | Light — reference data, small row counts |\n\n## 15.3 ETL Approach\n\n### 15.3.1 Tooling\n\n| Component | Technology | Status |\n|-----------|-----------|--------|\n| Source extraction | MDB Tools (command-line utilities for reading Access databases) | **DECIDED** |\n| Script generation | AI (Claude) writes shell scripts to extract and pipe data | **DECIDED** |\n| Target loading | Shell scripts pipe extracted data directly to target database | **DECIDED** |\n| Target database | Turso / libSQL (Tim's choice) vs PostgreSQL (SOW specification) | **CONTRADICTED** — see §15.3.3 |\n\nMDB Tools provides command-line read access to Access MDB files without requiring Microsoft Access or Windows. Claude generates the extraction scripts — shell scripts that read from Access tables, transform data as needed, and pipe results into the target database. Tim executes and validates; the scripts are not black-box automation.\n\n### 15.3.2 Module-by-Module Strategy\n\nMigration is not a phase — it is embedded in the build cycle for each module. The sequence follows the material flow through the plant:\n\n1. **Module development begins** — Tim lays out application structure\n2. **Data discovery** — Tim examines Access tables relevant to the module, maps fields, resolves cryptic names\n3. **Script generation** — Claude writes extraction scripts for the module's tables\n4. **Extraction and load** — Tim runs scripts to move data into the target database\n5. **Screen-level validation** — Kim compares migrated records in the new UI against the same records in Access\n6. **Iterate** — Fix mapping errors, re-extract, re-validate until Kim confirms accuracy\n\n**Parallel execution:** Tim will run multiple Claude instances simultaneously, each working on a different module. One instance handles customer data, another handles receiving, a third handles transfers. This is an explicit part of the development model, not an optimization — each module's data is largely independent.\n\n**Order follows build priority,** which follows material flow: Intake (§4) before Smelting (§5) before Financial (§6). Reference data (§11) may be migrated early as a dependency for operational modules.\n\n### 15.3.3 Target Database Mapping\n\nThe Access database uses a single-file-per-location model (TAPPgmMP for Mt. Pleasant, a separate file for Gadsden). The new architecture separates this into:\n\n| New Database | Content | Maps From |\n|-------------|---------|-----------|\n| Shared database | Users, authentication, cross-location master data | Both Access files (deduplicated) |\n| Mt. Pleasant operational DB | All operational records for Mt. Pleasant | TAPPgmMP |\n| Gadsden operational DB | All operational records for Gadsden | Gadsden Access file |\n\n**Database technology tension:** Tim has selected Turso / libSQL as the target database. The SOW specifies PostgreSQL. This is a **CONTRADICTED** decision requiring resolution before migration scripts are written, as the SQL dialect, data types, and loading mechanisms differ between the two platforms.\n\nThe 6-digit foreign key prefix currently used for location segregation within the shared Access database is stripped during extraction. Location separation is handled at the database level in the new architecture, eliminating the need for prefix-based filtering.\n\n## 15.4 Field Mapping Methodology\n\nThree complementary approaches address the \"Field 34\" problem — cryptically named columns whose business meaning is not apparent from the schema alone.\n\n### 15.4.1 Deductive Approach\n\nThe primary method. Extract data from a known record, display it on the matching screen in the new application, and compare to what Kim sees for the same record in Access. If the value in \"Field 34\" appears in the \"Special Instructions\" box on Kim's screen, the mapping is resolved.\n\n**Process:**\n1. Extract a representative record from Access\n2. Identify all fields with known and unknown mappings\n3. Display in the new UI alongside the Access screen\n4. Kim confirms or corrects each field's placement\n\nThis is the default approach for most field mapping work.\n\n### 15.4.2 Reverse Engineering\n\nAI traces through the Access application logic — VBA code, form data sources, query definitions — to find what reads from and writes to cryptically named fields. This approach works when the deductive method is inconclusive (e.g., a field that is stored but never displayed, or displayed only in certain conditions).\n\n**Process:**\n1. Identify the target field in the Access schema\n2. AI examines VBA modules, form record sources, and query definitions\n3. Trace the data flow: what form control writes to this field, under what conditions\n4. Map the business meaning from the application logic\n\n### 15.4.3 Brute-Force Validation\n\nA programmatic verification method. Insert a unique, identifiable value into every input field on an Access form, then examine which database columns received those values. This creates an unambiguous mapping between UI controls and database fields.\n\n**Process:**\n1. Open the Access sandbox to a blank or test record\n2. Programmatically (or manually) enter unique marker values in every input field\n3. Save the record\n4. Query the database to find which columns contain the marker values\n5. The column-to-field mapping is established definitively\n\nThis approach is most valuable as a verification step after deductive or reverse-engineering mapping, and for forms with many fields where manual tracing is error-prone.\n\n## 15.5 Validation Approach\n\nValidation is module-by-module and screen-level. There is no separate validation phase — validation is the final step of each module's migration cycle.\n\n**Primary validator:** Kim Sproul. She has 16+ years of operational experience and is the only person who can confirm whether migrated data looks correct in context.\n\n**Validation method:**\n1. Tim identifies a representative set of records for the module (including edge cases: oldest records, records with unusual values, records spanning the 7-year boundary)\n2. Kim opens the same record in both Access and the new system, side by side\n3. Kim confirms every visible field matches, or identifies discrepancies\n4. Discrepancies are logged, mapping is corrected, and the affected records are re-extracted\n5. Kim re-validates until she confirms accuracy\n\n**Validation coverage:** Every module that migrates data must pass Kim's screen-level validation before the module is considered complete. There is no automated validation substitute for Kim's domain knowledge — she knows what \"looks right\" in ways that automated checks cannot replicate.\n\n**Desktop AI for Access exploration:** For complex validation scenarios, Tim can use Remote Desktop to Jared's server where the Access sandbox is deployed, sharing his screen with Claude/AI to explore the Access application visually and trace data discrepancies.\n\n## 15.6 Cutover Strategy\n\nThe organic ETL approach simplifies cutover. There is no single cutover event — each module cuts over to the new system as it is built, validated, and approved. This means:\n\n- **No big-bang switchover** requiring a weekend freeze and all-hands migration event\n- **Module-level go/no-go decisions** rather than a single system-level cutover decision\n- **Rollback granularity** at the module level — if a module's migration has problems, only that module reverts to Access while the issue is resolved\n- **Parallel operation** is the natural state during the build phase — some modules run on the new system while others remain in Access\n\nThe final cutover occurs when the last module is migrated, validated, and running in production. At that point, Access transitions from active operational system to read-only archive.\n\n## 15.7 Historical Data and Retention\n\n**Retention policy:** 7 years of operational data must be preserved and queryable. This is a CEO directive (Jared Sweeny), not a regulatory requirement.\n\n**Extraction approach:** Import everything. Do not filter by date during extraction. Tim: *\"I would just import everything anyway, and then just go back and do a query for anything over seven years old.\"*\n\n**Post-import handling of aged data:**\n\n| Data Age | Treatment |\n|----------|-----------|\n| Within 7-year window | Active — fully queryable, visible in all operational screens and reports |\n| Beyond 7-year window | Archive candidate — query to identify, then determine disposition |\n| Pre-2010 dead table data | Exclude from migration entirely — these tables have not received writes in 15+ years |\n\n**Archival approach:** Records beyond the 7-year window are not deleted during migration. They are identified via post-import queries and either archived to a separate store or soft-deleted (flagged as archived but retained in the database). The specific archival mechanism is an open item — it depends on data volume and the target database's capabilities.\n\n## 15.8 Deprecated and Excluded Data\n\nThe following data elements are explicitly excluded from migration or flagged as deprecated:\n\n### Excluded from Migration\n\n| Element | Reason |\n|---------|--------|\n| Dead tables (~2010) | No writes in 15+ years; confirmed inactive during discovery |\n| Junk/temp tables | Scratch data from ad hoc queries; no operational value |\n| EnergySurchargeRate field | DEPRECATED. BOX 1000, MEMPHIS, TN 38148-0318). Separate from facility addresses. | Must appear on all invoices and payment documents. |\n    43→| Southware | TAP's external accounting system (AP/AR). Invoices are exported to Southware as part of the invoice processing workflow. | Integration interface, not replacement. |\n    44→| Additional Charge | Line-item or header-level surcharge on a contract/invoice. Type L = per lot (per truckload), Type U = per unit (per pound). | Freight is the most common additional charge. |\n    45→| Energy Surcharge | A per-contract surcharge field. DEPRECATED — used once for high energy costs. Can be dropped in new system. | EnergySurchgRate field exists but is 0.0000 on all observed contracts. |\n    46→| Blended Price | A contract-level flag indicating the price is a blend of multiple material rates rather than a single rate. | Checkbox on contract form. Affects invoice calculation when lots span material types. |\n    47→| Three-Tier Hierarchy | Seq# (per truck/event) > Lot# (consolidation group) > Invoice (billing unit). Enables per-truck granularity, customer-facing grouping, and billing aggregation. | Architectural pattern bridging §4 receiving and §6 invoicing. |\n    48→\n    49→## User Roles & Access\n    50→\n    51→| Role | Organization(s) | Access Level | Key Activities |\n    52→|------|-----------------|-------------|----------------|\n    53→| Kim Sproul | TAP — Mt. Pleasant | Full operational | Invoice creation, lot merge, invoice processing, file distribution, invoice lookup. Primary operator. SPOF. |\n    54→| Treina | TAP — Finance | Read + QA review | Invoice QA workflow (Access > Excel > review > file), weight discrepancy validation, 8 shadow-record reconciliation points. Needs read-only dashboard without operational edit permissions. |\n    55→| Bill Crawford | TAP — Sales | Read + pricing authority | Pricing knowledge (tacit — 20-25 material types in his head), deal evaluation, weight discrepancy notifications, PO delivery deadline management. |\n    56→| Jared | TAP — CEO | Executive read | Profitability dashboard access via customer website (not TAP Access). Cross-location financial visibility. |\n    57→| Fayla | TAP — Gadsden | Full operational | Replicates Kim's invoicing role at Gadsden facility. |\n    58→| Jason Bracket | TAP — Plant Manager | Read + notifications | Oversees financial operations at both facilities. Receives weight tolerance alerts. |\n    59→| Customers | External | Receives documents | Receives invoice packages (PDF + Excel), monthly production reports. Reviews weight reconciliation and chemistry data for payment approval. |\n    60→\n    61→## Key Workflows\n    62→\n    63→### Lot Invoicing (Three-Step Workflow)\n    64→\n    65→*Trigger:* Lot processing is complete and sows have been produced, weighed, and (optionally) chemistry-analyzed.\n    66→*Actors:* Kim (creation), Treina (QA), Customer (receives)\n    67→\n    68→*Process Flow:*\n    69→1. Kim opens frmLotInvoicing, enters lot number or uses \"Uninvoiced Processed Lots Only\" filter.\n    70→2. System displays three-panel layout: Main Grid (top — lot summary with pricing), Sows Panel (left — individual sow details), Pending Invoices Panel (right — queued invoices).\n    71→3. Kim reviews lot data: LbsReceived, WeightOut, ContamWgt, LotPrice, Calc, InvAmt, Additional Charge info, Energy Rate/Chg.\n    72→4. Kim clicks **Create Invoice** — system updates sows, closes receipts, updates lot. Confirmation: \"5 updated sows. 1 receipts were closed. 1 Lot updated.\" Invoice moves to Pending Invoices panel.\n    73→5. Kim clicks **Test Invoices** — system generates preview reports (rptInvoice + rptInvoiceSows) for QA review.\n    74→6. Test output reviewed with customer contact (Kim calls or emails preview).\n    75→7. Kim clicks **Process Invoices** — **IRREVERSIBLE**. Lot is permanently closed. Inventory moves from unprocessed to processed.\n    76→8. System generates three output files: PDF invoice, PDF analysis, Excel analysis. Saved to `G:\\PDF\\Invoice\\{CustNo}_{date}_{LotNo}_INV.xls` (and PDF equivalents).\n    77→9. Kim emails files to customer for approval.\n    78→10. Treina receives invoice for QA review (separate workflow — see below).\n    79→\n    80→*Decision Points:*\n    81→- **Lot merge:** If customer requires consolidated billing across multiple lots, Kim uses merge function before Create Invoice step.\n    82→- **Test vs Process:** Test is the quality gate. Processing is irreversible. The deliberate two-step separation is a feature, not a limitation.\n    83→\n    84→*Exceptions & Edge Cases:*\n    85→- Multiple lots merging to one invoice (customer-driven, e.g., JW Aluminum)\n    86→- Invoice number defaults to first lot number (convention, can be overridden)\n    87→- Blended pricing when lots span material types\n    88→- Steel deduction creates dual-weight billing (customer billed on full incoming, recovery on post-steel)\n    89→\n    90→### Invoice QA Review\n    91→\n    92→*Trigger:* Kim generates invoice files.\n    93→*Actors:* Treina (primary), Kim (handoff)\n    94→\n    95→*Process Flow:*\n    96→1. Treina receives invoice files (PDF + Excel) from Kim's processing.\n    97→2. Treina exports invoice data from Access to Excel.\n    98→3. Treina reviews for weight discrepancies between receipt stage and invoice stage.\n    99→4. Treina validates pricing against contract terms.\n   100→5. Treina catches and corrects discrepancies (weight adjustment engine disguised as review).\n   101→6. Treina files approved invoice.\n   102→\n   103→*Exceptions & Edge Cases:*\n   104→- Eight data redundancy points (shadow-record patterns) where Treina manually cross-checks data across multiple sources.\n   105→- This is load-bearing manual work — the new system must systematize this quality gate, not eliminate it.\n   106→\n   107→### Invoice Output & Distribution\n   108→\n   109→*Trigger:* Invoice processing complete.\n   110→*Actors:* Kim (distribution), Treina (QA), Customers (receipt)\n   111→\n   112→*Process Flow:*\n   113→1. System generates three files: PDF invoice, PDF analysis, Excel analysis.\n   114→2. Files pushed to `G:\\PDF\\Invoice\\` network share.\n   115→3. Kim emails files to customer.\n   116→4. Invoice data exported to Southware (external accounting system).\n   117→5. For portal customers: invoice data also feeds customer self-service portal (§8).\n   118→6. For Logan: customer-specific comma-delimited export format (integration debt).\n   119→\n   120→*Decision Points:*\n   121→- **Push vs Pull:** File push model persists alongside any portal/API. Cannot eliminate file generation even when pull model exists.\n   122→- **Customer-specific exports:** Logan's comma-delimited format is an obligation that persists. New system needs configurable export engine, not hardcoded per-customer formats.\n   123→\n   124→### Purchase Order Management (NEW — Does Not Exist Today)\n   125→\n   126→*Trigger:* TAP needs to order material from a vendor, or a customer places a purchase order with TAP.\n   127→*Actors:* Bill (PO creation/approval), Kim (entry), Treina (tracking)\n   128→\n   129→*Process Flow:*\n   130→1. Bill initiates PO based on customer demand or market opportunity.\n   131→2. PO entered into system with: vendor, material type, quantity, price, delivery terms, work stream (tolling/buy-sell/JV).\n   132→3. System tracks PO status: Open > Partially Fulfilled > Fulfilled > Closed.\n   133→4. 30-day delivery window monitored with deadline alerts.\n   134→5. Incoming receipts linked to POs for fulfillment tracking.\n   135→6. PO data feeds profitability tracking.\n   136→\n   137→*Decision Points:*\n   138→- **Work stream classification:** Each PO must be tagged to one of three work streams for profitability tracking.\n   139→- **Market-driven behavior:** Vendors delay delivery in rising commodity markets, cancel in falling markets. System must surface delivery deadline risk.\n   140→\n   141→*Exceptions & Edge Cases:*\n   142→- Currently 100% on spreadsheets — no existing system logic to migrate.\n   143→- Must support all three work streams with different financial models.\n   144→\n   145→## Business Rules\n   146→\n   147→| ID | Rule | Type | Details | Source |\n   148→|----|------|------|---------|--------|\n   149→| BR-06-001 | Toll charge based on weight received | CALC | Toll Charge = Unit Price × Weight Received. Customer billed on received weight, NOT recovered weight. Example: $0.14 × 222,940 lbs = $31,211.60. | [D1-AC-3], [D2-SC-frmLotInvoicing] |\n   150→| BR-06-002 | Invoice total calculation | CALC | InvAmt = (LbsReceived × LotPrice) + AdditionalCharge. Verified: 43,340 × $0.20 + $600 freight = $9,268. | [D1-AC-3], [D2-PS-CSV6] |\n   151→| BR-06-003 | Percent yield calculation | CALC | Recovery % = (Recovered lbs / Weight Received lbs) × 100. Example: 46,073 / 222,940 = 20.67%. | [D1-AC-3], [D1-SC-4] |\n   152→| BR-06-004 | Invoice three-step workflow | WORKFLOW | Create Invoice > Test Invoices > Process Invoices. Kim reviews with customer contact between Test and Process. | [D2-SC-frmLotInvoicing] |\n   153→| BR-06-005 | Invoice processing is irreversible | CONSTRAINT | Once processed, lot is closed and inventory moves from unprocessed to processed. No undo. Permanent state change. | [D2-SC-frmLotInvoicing] |\n   154→| BR-06-006 | Invoice generates three output files | WORKFLOW | PDF invoice + PDF analysis + Excel analysis. Saved to G:\\PDF\\Invoice\\{CustNo}_{date}_{LotNo}_INV.xls. | [D2-SC-frmLotInvoicing] |\n   155→| BR-06-007 | Multiple lots can merge to one invoice | CONSTRAINT | Lot merge function consolidates multiple lots. Customer-driven. Weight reconciliation across merged lots required. | [D1-AC-3], [D3-PS-W4] |\n   156→| BR-06-008 | Invoice number convention | FORMAT | Invoice number = first lot number in merged set. Convention, not hard requirement. | [D3-PS-W4] |\n   157→| BR-06-009 | Invoicing is per-heat | CONSTRAINT | Each heat generates its own billable unit. Billing traces back to individual heats. Affects cost allocation. | [D3-PS-W5A] |\n   158→| BR-06-010 | Uninvoiced processed lots filter | WORKFLOW | Lot invoicing lookup supports \"Uninvoiced Processed Lots Only\" checkbox to filter ready-to-invoice lots. | [D2-SC-frmLotInvoicing] |\n   159→| BR-06-011 | Invoice QA workflow | WORKFLOW | Treina's QA: Access > Excel > review for weight discrepancies and pricing > file. Eight shadow-record data redundancy points. | [D2-PS-W7] |\n   160→| BR-06-012 | Invoice file push model persists | INTEGRATION | File push to G:\\PDF\\Invoice\\ continues alongside any portal/API. Cannot eliminate file generation. | [D2-PS-W5] |\n   161→| BR-06-013 | Weight reconciliation chain on invoice | CALC | Invoice shows: received weight > processed weight > recovered weight > yield %. Customer-facing verification. | [D3-PS-W4], [D1-AC-3] |\n   162→| BR-06-014 | Three-tier hierarchy | CONSTRAINT | Seq# (per truck) > Lot# (consolidation) > Invoice (billing). Bridges §4 receiving architecture and §6 invoicing. | [D3-PS-W4] |\n   163→| BR-06-015 | Purchase order gap | CONSTRAINT | Entire PO process on spreadsheets. No PO management in current Access. Must support tolling, buy-sell, JV. Confirmed by Kim, Treina, Bill. | [D2-PS-W7], [D3-PS-W1], [D1-AC-1] |\n   164→| BR-06-016 | Profitability dashboard (CEO directive) | CONSTRAINT | Spend vs revenue by customer and work stream. CEO accesses via customer website. Three streams trackable. | [D3-PS-W1-QP2], [D2-PS-W8] |\n   165→| BR-06-017 | Delivery deadline alerts for POs | NOTIFY | 30-day delivery terms. Vendors delay in rising markets, cancel in falling. Alert when window expiring. | [D2-PS-W8] |\n   166→| BR-06-018 | Remittance address separate from facility | FORMAT | Payment goes to corporate/billing (TAP, DEPT# 318, P.O. BOX 1000, MEMPHIS, TN 38148-0318), not facility. | [D1-AC-2] |\n   167→\n   168→## Requirements\n   169→\n   170→### As Kim (Invoicing Operator), when creating and processing invoices:\n   171→\n   172→| ID | Requirement | Priority | Category | Notes |\n   173→|----|------------|----------|----------|-------|\n   174→| FM-R-001 | System must calculate toll charge as Unit Price × Weight Received (not recovered weight) | Must-Have | Functional | BR-06-001. Invoice\n   299→\n   300→The primary billing entity. Generated from lot processing data through the three-step workflow.\n   301→\n   302→**Key Fields:** Invoice Number, Customer Number, Lot# (primary + consolidated list), Invoice Date, Contract#, Customer PO#, Source, Processed at (location), Weight Received, Processed, Recovered, Contaminated, Percent Yield, Unit Price, Toll Charge Amount, Freight Amount, Invoice Total.\n   303→\n   304→**Sub-records:** Receipt Detail (per-truck lines), Shipment Detail (per-BOL/heat), Invoice Chemistry Detail (per-sow breakdown).\n   305→\n   306→**Output Files:** PDF invoice, PDF analysis, Excel analysis — all pushed to G:\\PDF\\Invoice\\.\n   307→\n   308→**Relationships:**\n   309→- Invoice belongs to Customer (many-to-one)\n   310→- Invoice covers Lots (one-to-many, via merge)\n   311→- Invoice references Contract (many-to-one)\n   312→- Invoice embeds Receipt Detail (one-to-many)\n   313→- Invoice embeds Shipment Detail (one-to-many)\n   314→\n   315→**Volume:** Scales with lots processed per year. One instance handles customer data, another handles receiving, a third handles transfers. This is an explicit part of the development model, not an optimization — each module's data is largely independent.\n    83→\n    84→**Order follows build priority,** which follows material flow: Intake (§4) before Smelting (§5) before Financial (§6). Reference data (§11) may be migrated early as a dependency for operational modules.\n    85→\n    86→### 15.3.3 Target Database Mapping\n    87→\n    88→The Access database uses a single-file-per-location model (TAPPgmMP for Mt. Extract data from a known record, display it on the matching screen in the new application, and compare to what Kim sees for the same record in Access. If the value in \"Field 34\" appears in the \"Special Instructions\" box on Kim's screen, the mapping is resolved.\n   107→\n   108→**Process:**\n   109→1. Extract a representative record from Access\n   110→2. Identify all fields with known and unknown mappings\n   111→3. Display in the new UI alongside the Access screen\n   112→4. Kim confirms or corrects each field's placement\n   113→\n   114→This is the default approach for most field mapping work.\n   115→\n   116→### 15.4.2 Reverse Engineering\n   117→\n   118→AI traces through the Access application logic — VBA code, form data sources, query definitions — to find what reads from and writes to cryptically named fields. This approach works when the deductive method is inconclusive (e.g., a field that is stored but never displayed, or displayed only in certain conditions).\n   119→\n   120→**Process:**\n   121→1. Identify the target field in the Access schema\n   122→2. AI examines VBA modules, form record sources, and query definitions\n   123→3. Trace the data flow: what form control writes to this field, under what conditions\n   124→4. Map the business meaning from the application logic\n   125→\n   126→### 15.4.3 Brute-Force Validation\n   127→\n   128→A programmatic verification method. Insert a unique, identifiable value into every input field on an Access form, then examine which database columns received those values. This creates an unambiguous mapping between UI controls and database fields.\n   129→\n   130→**Process:**\n   131→1. Open the Access sandbox to a blank or test record\n   132→2. Programmatically (or manually) enter unique marker values in every input field\n   133→3. Save the record\n   134→4. Query the database to find which columns contain the marker values\n   135→5. The column-to-field mapping is established definitively\n   136→\n   137→This approach is most valuable as a verification step after deductive or reverse-engineering mapping, and for forms with many fields where manual tracing is error-prone.\n   138→\n   139→## 15.5 Validation Approach\n   140→\n   141→Validation is module-by-module and screen-level. There is no separate validation phase — validation is the final step of each module's migration cycle.\n   142→\n   143→**Primary validator:** Kim Sproul. She has 16+ years of operational experience and is the only person who can confirm whether migrated data looks correct in context.\n   144→\n   145→**Validation method:**\n   146→1. Tim identifies a representative set of records for the module (including edge cases: oldest records, records with unusual values, records spanning the 7-year boundary)\n   147→2. Kim opens the same record in both Access and the new system, side by side\n   148→3. Kim confirms every visible field matches, or identifies discrepancies\n   149→4. Discrepancies are logged, mapping is corrected, and the affected records are re-extracted\n   150→5. Kim re-validates until she confirms accuracy\n   151→\n   152→**Validation coverage:** Every module that migrates data must pass Kim's screen-level validation before the module is considered complete. There is no automated validation substitute for Kim's domain knowledge — she knows what \"looks right\" in ways that automated checks cannot replicate.\n   153→\n   154→**Desktop AI for Access exploration:** For complex validation scenarios, Tim can use Remote Desktop to Jared's server where the Access sandbox is deployed, sharing his screen with Claude/AI to explore the Access application visually and trace data discrepancies.\n   155→\n   156→## 15.6 Cutover Strategy\n   157→\n   158→The organic ETL approach simplifies cutover. Every project's CLAUDE.md points here.\nWhen this file is updated, every project's next Claude Code session picks up\nthe changes automatically.\n\nThis file covers session mechanics, not voice or tone. For written output,\nuse the jason-voice skill.\n\n---\n\n## Communication Style\n\n- One question at a time. Suggest 2-3 answers and give a recommendation.\n- Plain language, real-world analogies, simple explanations.\n- The operator thinks in systems and architecture, not features.\n- Numbered text options, never clickable widgets.\n- Checklists over prose for verification.\n- When flagging concerns: lead with what it means, then give your take on\n  whether it matters.\n- When new capabilities are added: explain how to use them in plain language.\n  Don't assume the operator will figure it out from the code.\n- Over time, usage notes accumulate into an operator playbook.\n\n---\n\n## Working Patterns\n\n1. **Plans for architecture and features. Skip for low-risk work.** Show a\n   plan and get approval for architecture changes, new features, schema\n   modifications. Skip the plan for style, copy, and low-risk changes where\n   the prompt fully specifies the work. The distinction is risk: architectural\n   changes are hard to reverse, style changes are easy to reverse. Match the\n   approval overhead to the risk level.\n2. **One prompt, one logical change.** Even if it spans multiple files. A\n   legibility pass touching 4 files is one job, not four. Compound prompts\n   that combine building with self-review produce worse results than separate\n   steps.\n3. **Status report before resuming.** After any break, context switch, or\n   compaction, report current state before accepting new work. The operator\n   should never have to guess where things stand.\n4. **Read actual files before making changes.** Never work from memory or\n   stale context. Contents change between sessions. When delegating to\n   subagents, pass the relevant content rather than having each re-read.\n5. **Commit after meaningful work, grouped by logical change.** Atomic commits\n   with conventional format: `type: short description` (feat, fix, docs, test,\n   refactor, chore). Group by feature or concern, not by file. If files overlap\n   across logical changes and clean separation is hard, collapse to fewer\n   commits. The priority is that everything gets committed and pushed, not\n   perfect commit boundaries. Co-Authored-By footer on all commits.\n6. **Show a commit plan before pushing.** List planned commits with files in\n   each. Operator approves before push. Push and merge require approval.\n   Read-only git operations (status, diff, log) and branch creation for\n   experimental work are fine without asking.\n7. **Lead with the file.** The file is the deliverable. Keep explanation brief\n   and focused on what changed and where. Don't walk through contents the\n   operator can read themselves.\n8. **Flag problems mid-execution.** If you realize the approach has a problem\n   while implementing, stop and say so. Don't complete bad work. Push back\n   is welcome at any point.\n9. **Brain doc updates: safety valve.** Update brain docs before session ends.\n   If context is degraded, output the updates as a message for the operator\n   to review rather than writing directly to the files.\n10. **Directory cleanup: suggest, don't delete.** After milestones, list files\n    that look like scratch work or test artifacts and suggest cleanup. Don't\n    delete without confirmation.\n11. **Every plan includes:** file names, line counts (budgets, not estimates),\n    scope, exclusions, priority order.\n12. **Validate current state before building.** Read actual files before\n    starting any build task. Never work from assumed state.\n\n---\n\n## Riffing and Collaboration\n\n- Work chunk by chunk, not top-down. Break content into logical beats and\n  riff on each one before moving to the next. The process is riffing toward\n  the right answer, not editing a full draft.\n- Show the original first, then alts. Always show the current version above\n  any alternatives so the operator can compare and pull from both.\n- 5 alternatives is the sweet spot. Enough range to spark something, not so\n  many it becomes a wall.\n- Alts are raw material, not final options. The operator will often grab a\n  phrase from one and the close of another. Write modular enough to recombine.\n- Before/after comparisons for decisions. This is the natural decision-making\n  tool. Always show both versions side by side.\n- Bold in drafts means formatting intent, not decoration. Respect it and\n  match the pattern.\n\n---\n\n## Output and File Delivery\n\n- The file is the deliverable. After creating or updating a file, present it.\n  Keep the explanation to one sentence about where it goes. Don't summarize\n  the contents of a document you just produced.\n- Suggest the convention, don't wait for it. File names, variable names,\n  folder structure. Recommend it, operator confirms or adjusts.\n- The rendered file only shows locked content. No draft options or\n  placeholders in the file.\n- Unworked sections stay as their original text. This keeps the full picture\n  together.\n- Update the file only when a chunk is locked. Riffing happens in chat. The\n  file reflects decisions, not process.\n- When a milestone passes, sweep the directory. Test files, POC artifacts,\n  and scratch work left behind become confusing artifacts.\n\n---\n\n## Redundancy Discipline\n\n- Watch for repeated words in adjacent sentences and repeated concepts across\n  sections. Flag before the operator has to. If the body copy describes the\n  flow steps and the visual strip also describes them, one needs to go.\n- Consulting language creeps in even when following the rules. Scan before\n  presenting.\n\n---\n\n## Writing Rules (Hard)\n\n- No em dashes. Ever.\n- No consulting language (leverage, synergy, actionable insights, move the\n  needle, best-in-class, ladders up to, capitalize on the moment)\n- No AI tells (genuinely, straightforward, it's important to note, in today's\n  landscape, harness, tapestry, delve, navigating, at the end of the day,\n  \"In an era where...\")\n- No softening qualifiers unless doing real work\n- Don't repeat words in adjacent sentences\n- Short sentences for impact, used sparingly\n\n---\n\n## Session Discipline\n\n- **Separate exploration from build.** If the session is exploring, don't\n  force output. If the session is building, ship something. Don't let an\n  exploration session accidentally become a build session or vice versa.\n- **Time-box aesthetic decisions at 10 minutes.** If a design or copy choice\n  goes back and forth longer, lock it and move on. Batch tuning into\n  dedicated passes rather than interrupting builds.\n- **Brain docs are the memory, not the chat.** Anything decided in\n  conversation that isn't written to a brain doc is lost next session. If a\n  decision matters, it goes in the file before the session ends.\n- **Document what you'll do with it, not what you built.** Write for the\n  version of yourself that has forgotten all context. The question is \"what\n  do I do when I open this next week?\" not \"what did we build today?\"\n- **Every session starts by reading brain-SESSION-START.md.** Every session\n  ends by updating section 2 (priority) and section 6 (what's built). New\n  lessons go in brain-RULES.md before the session ends.\n- **Brain docs are the single source of truth.** If the docs are wrong, fix\n  the docs, not the behavior.\n\n---\n\n## Role Split\n\n### Claude.ai (thought partner)\n- Architecture decisions, product reasoning, QA, writing brain docs, reviewing\n  output, planning phases, writing PRDs, evaluating tradeoffs.\n- Evaluates whether the system is working, not the system itself.\n- Can read skills at /mnt/skills/user/ (not accessible from Claude Code).\n- Output is conversation. Artifacts are secondary.\n- Does not hold files. Gets context by asking the operator to drop in what's\n  needed.\n\n### Claude Code (executor)\n- All file creation and modification, including brain doc updates at session\n  end. Executes against plans approved in the Claude.ai conversation.\n- Reads files, writes code, runs scripts, commits.\n- Builds skills, agents, and tooling.\n- Runs audits, evaluations, and tests.\n- Has access to subagents, parallel processing, worktrees.\n- Shows a plan before building. Does not make architecture decisions on its\n  own.\n\n### The operator is the bridge\n- When Claude.ai needs file contents, ask the operator to drop in the file.\n  Do not ask Claude Code to output file contents or bundle files for transfer.\n  Claude Code's UI collapses and summarizes output, so \"cat the file\" prompts\n  don't reliably transfer content.\n- Handoff format: when passing work to Claude Code, produce the exact input\n  it needs. Copy-paste prompts, not descriptions of what should happen.\n- The operator makes all judgment calls. The system surfaces options and\n  recommendations. The operator decides.\n- Claude.ai reviews what Claude Code built for vision alignment. Claude Code\n  validates whether Claude.ai's recommendations work in practice. Use each\n  to verify the other when drift is detected.\n\n---\n\n## Project Graduation Trigger\n\nIf a conversation starts producing multiple files, requires state tracking\nacross sessions, or involves Claude Code doing real implementation, it's a\nproject. Suggest running the project-bootstrap skill to get the brain doc\nstructure in place before the complexity outruns the conversation's memory.\n\n---\n\n## Design and Build Approach\n\n- Vision-first, planning-heavy, then execution.\n- Open to proof of concepts when they validate an approach.\n- Separate exploration sessions from build sessions.\n- For projects with a visual layer: Claude writes prompts for AI design\n  platforms (currently Google Stitch), operator iterates on design, then\n  Claude adapts the output code to the project's frontend framework.\n- Backend stack is flexible per project. Default is ai-starter's stack.\n  Known alternatives: Supabase (DB, edge functions), Lambda (MCP server),\n  Deno.\n\n---\n\n## Efficiency Posture\n\n- Use subagents, parallel processing, and agent delegation freely.\n- Default to parallel dispatch when work is independent: reading multiple\n  files, editing independent files, running audits.\n- Each subagent gets self-contained context. No assumed shared state.\n- When delegating to subagents, pass relevant content in their context\n  rather than having each one re-read from disk.\n- When a subagent's output doesn't look right, re-run with more context\n  rather than patching in the main thread.\n- Slower but more accurate is better than fast but drifted.\n- Skip the plan step for fully-specified style/CSS changes. The prompt is\n  the plan. Execute and show the diff.\n- Screenshot is the gate for visual changes. Commit directly, tell operator\n  to screenshot.\n- Flag when context is getting heavy and suggest checkpointing.\n- Use git worktrees when changes need isolation (experimental branches,\n  parallel implementation attempts).\n\n---\n\n## Safety Preamble Template\n\nReplace `{{PROJECT_DIR}}` and `{{RUNTIMES}}` with project-specific values.\n\n```\nSafety scope for this session: File operations are restricted to:\n(1) {{PROJECT_DIR}} (2) ~/Documents/_AI_/_Shared/ (read for working\npreferences). Do not create, modify, or delete files outside these\ndirectories except for reading reference files. Do not install system\npackages. Do not modify system settings. Do not access or modify ~/.ssh,\n~/.config, ~/.zshrc, ~/.bashrc, or any dotfiles outside the project.\nDo not run network requests, curl commands, or download external resources\nunless explicitly instructed. Do not execute destructive commands (rm -rf,\nformat, DROP DATABASE, etc.) without explicit human approval for each\ninstance. Only run {{RUNTIMES}} and standard unix commands (mkdir, mv, cp,\ncat, grep, find, wc, diff, sed, awk). Do not force push, rebase, or\nrewrite git history. Destructive operations require confirmation. Every project's CLAUDE.md points here.\nWhen this file is updated, every project's next Claude Code session picks up\nthe changes automatically.\n\nThis file covers session mechanics, not voice or tone. For written output,\nuse the jason-voice skill.\n\n---\n\n## Communication Style\n\n- One question at a time. Suggest 2-3 answers and give a recommendation.\n- Plain language, real-world analogies, simple explanations.\n- The operator thinks in systems and architecture, not features.\n- Numbered text options, never clickable widgets.\n- Checklists over prose for verification.\n- When flagging concerns: lead with what it means, then give your take on\n  whether it matters.\n- When new capabilities are added: explain how to use them in plain language.\n  Don't assume the operator will figure it out from the code.\n- Over time, usage notes accumulate into an operator playbook.\n\n---\n\n## Working Patterns\n\n1. **Plans for architecture and features. Skip for low-risk work.** Show a\n   plan and get approval for architecture changes, new features, schema\n   modifications. Skip the plan for style, copy, and low-risk changes where\n   the prompt fully specifies the work. The distinction is risk: architectural\n   changes are hard to reverse, style changes are easy to reverse. Match the\n   approval overhead to the risk level.\n2. **One prompt, one logical change.** Even if it spans multiple files. A\n   legibility pass touching 4 files is one job, not four. Compound prompts\n   that combine building with self-review produce worse results than separate\n   steps.\n3. **Status report before resuming.** After any break, context switch, or\n   compaction, report current state before accepting new work. The operator\n   should never have to guess where things stand.\n4. **Read actual files before making changes.** Never work from memory or\n   stale context. Contents change between sessions. When delegating to\n   subagents, pass the relevant content rather than having each re-read.\n5. **Commit after meaningful work, grouped by logical change.** Atomic commits\n   with conventional format: `type: short description` (feat, fix, docs, test,\n   refactor, chore). Group by feature or concern, not by file. If files overlap\n   across logical changes and clean separation is hard, collapse to fewer\n   commits. The priority is that everything gets committed and pushed, not\n   perfect commit boundaries. Co-Authored-By footer on all commits.\n6. **Show a commit plan before pushing.** List planned commits with files in\n   each. Operator approves before push. Push and merge require approval.\n   Read-only git operations (status, diff, log) and branch creation for\n   experimental work are fine without asking.\n7. **Lead with the file.** The file is the deliverable. Keep explanation brief\n   and focused on what changed and where. Don't walk through contents the\n   operator can read themselves.\n8. **Flag problems mid-execution.** If you realize the approach has a problem\n   while implementing, stop and say so. Don't complete bad work. Push back\n   is welcome at any point.\n9. **Brain doc updates: safety valve.** Update brain docs before session ends.\n   If context is degraded, output the updates as a message for the operator\n   to review rather than writing directly to the files.\n10. **Directory cleanup: suggest, don't delete.** After milestones, list files\n    that look like scratch work or test artifacts and suggest cleanup. Don't\n    delete without confirmation.\n11. **Every plan includes:** file names, line counts (budgets, not estimates),\n    scope, exclusions, priority order.\n12. **Validate current state before building.** Read actual files before\n    starting any build task. Never work from assumed state.\n13. **Explicit handoff triggers.** When a prompt is ready for another session\n    to execute, say so plainly. When a session should wrap up, say so plainly.\n    Don't assume the operator knows when to act. This applies to TP → CC\n    handoffs, session wrap-up recommendations, and push/merge approvals.\n\n---\n\n## Riffing and Collaboration\n\n- Work chunk by chunk, not top-down. Break content into logical beats and\n  riff on each one before moving to the next. The process is riffing toward\n  the right answer, not editing a full draft.\n- Show the original first, then alts. Always show the current version above\n  any alternatives so the operator can compare and pull from both.\n- 5 alternatives is the sweet spot. Enough range to spark something, not so\n  many it becomes a wall.\n- Alts are raw material, not final options. The operator will often grab a\n  phrase from one and the close of another. Write modular enough to recombine.\n- Before/after comparisons for decisions. This is the natural decision-making\n  tool. Always show both versions side by side.\n- Bold in drafts means formatting intent, not decoration. Respect it and\n  match the pattern.\n\n---\n\n## Output and File Delivery\n\n- The file is the deliverable. After creating or updating a file, present it.\n  Keep the explanation to one sentence about where it goes. Don't summarize\n  the contents of a document you just produced.\n- Suggest the convention, don't wait for it. File names, variable names,\n  folder structure. Recommend it, operator confirms or adjusts.\n- The rendered file only shows locked content. No draft options or\n  placeholders in the file.\n- Unworked sections stay as their original text. This keeps the full picture\n  together.\n- Update the file only when a chunk is locked. Riffing happens in chat. The\n  file reflects decisions, not process.\n- When a milestone passes, sweep the directory. Test files, POC artifacts,\n  and scratch work left behind become confusing artifacts.\n\n---\n\n## Redundancy Discipline\n\n- Watch for repeated words in adjacent sentences and repeated concepts across\n  sections. Flag before the operator has to. If the body copy describes the\n  flow steps and the visual strip also describes them, one needs to go.\n- Consulting language creeps in even when following the rules. Scan before\n  presenting.\n\n---\n\n## Writing Rules (Hard)\n\n- No em dashes. Ever.\n- No consulting language (leverage, synergy, actionable insights, move the\n  needle, best-in-class, ladders up to, capitalize on the moment)\n- No AI tells (genuinely, straightforward, it's important to note, in today's\n  landscape, harness, tapestry, delve, navigating, at the end of the day,\n  \"In an era where...\")\n- No softening qualifiers unless doing real work\n- Don't repeat words in adjacent sentences\n- Short sentences for impact, used sparingly\n\n---\n\n## Session Discipline\n\n- **Separate exploration from build.** If the session is exploring, don't\n  force output. If the session is building, ship something. Don't let an\n  exploration session accidentally become a build session or vice versa.\n- **Time-box aesthetic decisions at 10 minutes.** If a design or copy choice\n  goes back and forth longer, lock it and move on. Batch tuning into\n  dedicated passes rather than interrupting builds.\n- **Brain docs are the memory, not the chat.** Anything decided in\n  conversation that isn't written to a brain doc is lost next session. Match the\n   approval overhead to the risk level.\n2. **One prompt, one logical change.** Even if it spans multiple files. A\n   legibility pass touching 4 files is one job, not four. Compound prompts\n   that combine building with self-review produce worse results than separate\n   steps.\n3. **Status report before resuming.** After any break, context switch, or\n   compaction, report current state before accepting new work. The operator\n   should never have to guess where things stand.\n4. **Read actual files before making changes.** Never work from memory or\n   stale context. Contents change between sessions. When delegating to\n   subagents, pass the relevant content rather than having each re-read.\n5. **Commit after meaningful work, grouped by logical change.** Atomic commits\n   with conventional format: `type: short description` (feat, fix, docs, test,\n   refactor, chore). Group by feature or concern, not by file. If files overlap\n   across logical changes and clean separation is hard, collapse to fewer\n   commits. The priority is that everything gets committed and pushed, not\n   perfect commit boundaries. Co-Authored-By footer on all commits.\n6. **Show a commit plan before pushing.** List planned commits with files in\n   each. Operator approves before push. Push and merge require approval.\n   Read-only git operations (status, diff, log) and branch creation for\n   experimental work are fine without asking.\n7. **Lead with the file.** The file is the deliverable. Keep explanation brief\n   and focused on what changed and where. Don't walk through contents the\n   operator can read themselves.\n8. **Flag problems mid-execution.** If you realize the approach has a problem\n   while implementing, stop and say so. Don't complete bad work. Push back\n   is welcome at any point.\n9. **Brain doc updates: safety valve.** Update brain docs before session ends.\n   If context is degraded, output the updates as a message for the operator\n   to review rather than writing directly to the files.\n10. **Directory cleanup: suggest, don't delete.** After milestones, list files\n    that look like scratch work or test artifacts and suggest cleanup. Don't\n    delete without confirmation.\n11. **Every plan includes:** file names, line counts (budgets, not estimates),\n    scope, exclusions, priority order.\n12. **Validate current state before building.** Read actual files before\n    starting any build task. Never work from assumed state.\n13. **Explicit handoff triggers.** When a prompt is ready for another session\n    to execute, say so plainly. When a session should wrap up, say so plainly.\n    Don't assume the operator knows when to act. This applies to TP → CC\n    handoffs, session wrap-up recommendations, and push/merge approvals.\n\n---\n\n## Riffing and Collaboration\n\n- Work chunk by chunk, not top-down. Break content into logical beats and\n  riff on each one before moving to the next. The process is riffing toward\n  the right answer, not editing a full draft.\n- Show the original first, then alts. Always show the current version above\n  any alternatives so the operator can compare and pull from both.\n- 5 alternatives is the sweet spot. Enough range to spark something, not so\n  many it becomes a wall.\n- Alts are raw material, not final options. The operator will often grab a\n  phrase from one and the close of another. Write modular enough to recombine.\n- Before/after comparisons for decisions. This is the natural decision-making\n  tool. Always show both versions side by side.\n- Bold in drafts means formatting intent, not decoration. Respect it and\n  match the pattern.\n\n---\n\n## Output and File Delivery\n\n- The file is the deliverable. After creating or updating a file, present it.\n  Keep the explanation to one sentence about where it goes. Don't summarize\n  the contents of a document you just produced.\n- Suggest the convention, don't wait for it. File names, variable names,\n  folder structure. Recommend it, operator confirms or adjusts.\n- The rendered file only shows locked content. No draft options or\n  placeholders in the file.\n- Unworked sections stay as their original text. This keeps the full picture\n  together.\n- Update the file only when a chunk is locked. Riffing happens in chat. The\n  file reflects decisions, not process.\n- When a milestone passes, sweep the directory. Test files, POC artifacts,\n  and scratch work left behind become confusing artifacts.\n\n---\n\n## Redundancy Discipline\n\n- Watch for repeated words in adjacent sentences and repeated concepts across\n  sections. Flag before the operator has to. If the body copy describes the\n  flow steps and the visual strip also describes them, one needs to go.\n- Consulting language creeps in even when following the rules. Scan before\n  presenting.\n\n---\n\n## Writing Rules (Hard)\n\n- No em dashes. Ever.\n- No consulting language (leverage, synergy, actionable insights, move the\n  needle, best-in-class, ladders up to, capitalize on the moment)\n- No AI tells (genuinely, straightforward, it's important to note, in today's\n  landscape, harness, tapestry, delve, navigating, at the end of the day,\n  \"In an era where...\")\n- No softening qualifiers unless doing real work\n- Don't repeat words in adjacent sentences\n- Short sentences for impact, used sparingly\n\n---\n\n## Session Discipline\n\n- **Separate exploration from build.** If the session is exploring, don't\n  force output. If the session is building, ship something. Don't let an\n  exploration session accidentally become a build session or vice versa.\n- **Time-box aesthetic decisions at 10 minutes.** If a design or copy choice\n  goes back and forth longer, lock it and move on. Batch tuning into\n  dedicated passes rather than interrupting builds.\n- **Brain docs are the memory, not the chat.** Anything decided in\n  conversation that isn't written to a brain doc is lost next session. If a\n  decision matters, it goes in the file before the session ends.\n- **Document what you'll do with it, not what you built.** Write for the\n  version of yourself that has forgotten all context. The question is \"what\n  do I do when I open this next week?\" not \"what did we build today?\"\n- **Every session starts by reading brain-SESSION-START.md.** Every session\n  ends by updating the priority section and the what's-built section. New\n  lessons go in brain-RULES.md before the session ends.\n- **Brain docs are the single source of truth.** If the docs are wrong, fix\n  the docs, not the behavior.\n\n---\n\n## Role Split\n\n### Thought Partner (TP) session\n- Architecture decisions, product reasoning, QA, reviewing output, planning\n  phases, writing PRDs, evaluating tradeoffs, producing CC prompts.\n- Does not write files, commit, or push. Reads files for context and review.\n- Evaluates whether the system is working, not the system itself.\n- Output is conversation and CC-ready prompts. Files are CC's job.\n- Gets context by reading files directly (if CC-based) or by asking the\n  operator to drop in what's needed (if Claude.ai-based).\n\n### CC (Claude Code) session\n- All file creation and modification, including brain doc updates at session\n  end. Executes against prompts produced by the TP or approved by the operator.\n- Reads files, writes code, runs scripts, commits, pushes.\n- Builds skills, agents, and tooling.\n- Runs audits, evaluations, and tests.\n- Has access to subagents, parallel processing, worktrees.\n- Shows a plan before building. Does not make architecture decisions on its\n  own.\n\n### Which Claude fills which role\nThe operator decides. Both Claude.ai and Claude Code can serve as TP. Both\ncan serve as CC. The distinction is behavioral, not product-based: TP sessions\nare read-only architects that produce prompts. CC sessions are builders that\nexecute prompts. A Claude Code instance acting as TP follows TP rules (no file\nwrites). A Claude.ai instance can only act as TP (it has no file access).\n\nClaude.ai has access to skills at /mnt/skills/user/ that Claude Code cannot\nread. This may influence which product fills the TP role for projects that\ndepend on those skills.\n\n### The operator is the bridge\n- Handoff format: when passing work from TP to CC, the TP produces the exact\n  prompt CC needs. Copy-paste ready, not descriptions of what should happen.\n- The operator makes all judgment calls. The system surfaces options and\n  recommendations. The operator decides.\n- TP reviews what CC built for vision alignment. CC validates whether TP's\n  recommendations work in practice. Use each to verify the other when drift\n  is detected.\n\n### TP behavioral rules\nThese must be prominent. New TP sessions that don't receive these rules\nexplicitly will default to builder mode.\n\n1. **One prompt at a time.** Wait for operator approval before producing the\n   next. Do not batch prompts upfront — each may be informed by the previous.\n2. **Every finalized prompt includes:** safety preamble, efficiency posture,\n   git context (branch, recent commits), file paths, task scope, verification\n   steps, commit instructions.\n3. **Explicit CC trigger.** When a prompt is approved and finalized, say\n   \"This prompt is ready for CC.\" Don't assume the operator knows when to act.\n4. **Review CC output before producing the next prompt.** The operator shares\n   CC's commit log or diff. TP confirms the change matches intent, then moves\n   to the next item.\n5. **New TP sessions get explicit role boundaries in the handoff.** Without\n   this constraint, they default to builder mode. The handoff prompt must\n   include: \"You are the thought partner. You do not write files, commit, or\n   push.\"\n\n---\n\n## Project Graduation Trigger\n\nIf a conversation starts producing multiple files, requires state tracking\nacross sessions, or involves Claude Code doing real implementation, it's a\nproject. Suggest running the project-bootstrap skill to get the brain doc\nstructure in place before the complexity outruns the conversation's memory.\n\n---\n\n## Design and Build Approach\n\n- Vision-first, planning-heavy, then execution.\n- Open to proof of concepts when they validate an approach.\n- Separate exploration sessions from build sessions.\n- For projects with a visual layer: Claude writes prompts for AI design\n  platforms (currently Google Stitch), operator iterates on design, then\n  Claude adapts the output code to the project's frontend framework.\n- Backend stack is flexible per project. Default is ai-starter's stack.\n  Known alternatives: Supabase (DB, edge functions), Lambda (MCP server),\n  Deno.\n\n---\n\n## Efficiency Posture\n\n- Use subagents, parallel processing, and agent delegation freely.\n- Default to parallel dispatch when work is independent: reading multiple\n  files, editing independent files, running audits.\n- Each subagent gets self-contained context. No assumed shared state.\n- When delegating to subagents, pass relevant content in their context\n  rather than having each one re-read from disk.\n- When a subagent's output doesn't look right, re-run with more context\n  rather than patching in the main thread.\n- Slower but more accurate is better than fast but drifted.\n- Skip the plan step for fully-specified style/CSS changes. The prompt is\n  the plan. Execute and show the diff.\n- Screenshot is the gate for visual changes. Commit directly, tell operator\n  to screenshot.\n- Flag when context is getting heavy and suggest checkpointing.\n- Use git worktrees when changes need isolation (experimental branches,\n  parallel implementation attempts).\n\n---\n\n## Safety Preamble Template\n\nReplace `{{PROJECT_DIR}}` and `{{RUNTIMES}}` with project-specific values.\n\n```\nSafety scope for this session: File operations are restricted to:\n(1) {{PROJECT_DIR}} (2) ~/Documents/_AI_/_Shared/ (read for working\npreferences). Repeat from step 1 for the next item\n\n### Outer loop (per-batch)\n1. Batch of related work completes (e.g., all Phase 1 tool updates)\n2. TP tells operator: \"CC should wrap up\"\n3. CC runs `git log` to show commits, `git status` to confirm clean tree.\n   Does NOT push.\n4. Operator shares the commit log with TP\n5. TP reviews: do changes match the plan? Are cross-references intact? Any\n   regressions?\n6. TP approves and says: \"Ready to merge\"\n7. Operator tells CC (same session or fresh): \"Push and merge to main\"\n8. CC pushes and merges. Operator confirms.\n\n### Git workflow defaults\n- Work on feature branches. CC creates the branch on first task.\n- Direct merge to main with TP review. No PRs. This matches small-team\n  workflow (1-2 people). If a project needs PRs, that project's CLAUDE.md\n  overrides this default.\n- CC handles all git mechanics (branch, commit, push, merge). Operator's\n  role is approval gate, not merge executor.\n- Atomic commits with conventional format (`type: short description`).\n  Co-Authored-By footer on all commits.\n- Stage files by name. Never `git add -A` or `git add .`.\n\n---\n\n## CC Session Lifecycle\n\n### Startup\n- Check branch, confirm state (`git status`, `git log`)\n- Read any context provided in the prompt (branch state, recent commits,\n  what's already been done)\n\n### Execution\n- One task per prompt. Atomic commits after each logical change.\n- Verification steps after each change (grep, wc, read the file).\n- If something doesn't look right, stop and flag it. Don't complete bad work.\n\n### When to wrap up\nTP or CC flags when it's time to wrap up. Triggers:\n- A logical batch of work is done (e.g., all spec updates for a phase)\n- Context is heavy enough that quality may degrade on the next task\n- About to switch between tracks or repos (different context needed)\n- A natural commit boundary before a new type of work\n\nMethod: Session says \"check context.\" Operator runs `/context` and reports\nback. Session recommends continue or wrap up based on what's left to do vs.\nremaining capacity. No hardcoded percentages — models and context windows\nchange over time.\n\n### Wrap-up procedure\n1. CC runs `git log --oneline {branch} --not main` to show branch commits\n2. CC runs `git status` to confirm clean working tree\n3. CC does NOT push. Push happens after TP review (outer loop).\n4. TP flags: \"CC session should compact here. Next CC session should start\n   on branch X, pick up at Y.\"\n\n### Fresh CC session startup\nWhen a new CC session picks up work from a compacted session:\n- The prompt includes the CONTEXT section telling it the branch state\n- It runs `git status` and `git log` to confirm\n- It does not need to re-read files the previous session already processed\n  (the commits are on the branch)\n\n---\n\n## Thought Partner Handoff\n\n### When to hand off\nWhen remaining context is insufficient to produce a quality handoff briefing\nfor the replacement. The handoff itself consumes context, so start before\nyou're at the wall. Method: TP says \"check context,\" operator runs `/context`\nand reports, TP evaluates whether enough remains for the handoff plus 1-2\nconsultation rounds.\n\n### What the outgoing TP produces\nA handoff document or message containing:\n- What was decided this session (architecture, process, direction)\n- What's in progress (current branch, commits, next item in the plan)\n- What's next (remaining items, priorities, dependencies)\n- Lessons learned (corrections received, process adjustments)\n- Current branch state (name, commit count, clean/dirty)\n\n### Incoming TP alignment\n1. New TP reads: handoff + brain docs + working preferences file\n2. New TP reports its understanding of the plan and asks alignment questions\n3. Operator corrects any misalignment before the new TP accepts work\n4. Outgoing TP stays available for 1-2 consultation rounds (alignment check,\n   not building) if context allows\n\n### Critical: explicit role constraint\nThe handoff prompt must include: \"You are the thought partner. You do not\nwrite files, commit, or push. You produce prompts for CC sessions to execute.\"\nWithout this, new TP sessions default to builder mode.\n\n---\n\n## Project Graduation Trigger\n\nIf a conversation starts producing multiple files, requires state tracking\nacross sessions, or involves Claude Code doing real implementation, it's a\nproject. Default is ai-starter's stack.\n  Known alternatives: Supabase (DB, edge functions), Lambda (MCP server),\n  Deno.\n\n---\n\n## Efficiency Posture\n\n- Use subagents, parallel processing, and agent delegation freely.\n- Default to parallel dispatch when work is independent: reading multiple\n  files, editing independent files, running audits.\n- Each subagent gets self-contained context. No assumed shared state.\n- When delegating to subagents, pass relevant content in their context\n  rather than having each one re-read from disk.\n- When a subagent's output doesn't look right, re-run with more context\n  rather than patching in the main thread.\n- Slower but more accurate is better than fast but drifted.\n- Skip the plan step for fully-specified style/CSS changes.
