Skip for low-risk work.** Show a\n   plan and get approval for architecture changes, new features, schema\n   modifications. Skip the plan for style, copy, and low-risk changes where\n   the prompt fully specifies the work. The distinction is risk: architectural\n   changes are hard to reverse, style changes are easy to reverse. Match the\n   approval overhead to the risk level.\n2. **One prompt, one logical change.** Even if it spans multiple files. A\n   legibility pass touching 4 files is one job, not four. Compound prompts\n   that combine building with self-review produce worse results than separate\n   steps.\n3. **Status report before resuming.** After any break, context switch, or\n   compaction, report current state before accepting new work. The operator\n   should never have to guess where things stand.\n4. **Read actual files before making changes.** Never work from memory or\n   stale context. Contents change between sessions. When delegating to\n   subagents, pass the relevant content rather than having each re-read.\n5. **Commit after meaningful work, grouped by logical change.** Atomic commits\n   with conventional format: `type: short description` (feat, fix, docs, test,\n   refactor, chore). Group by feature or concern, not by file. If files overlap\n   across logical changes and clean separation is hard, collapse to fewer\n   commits. The priority is that everything gets committed and pushed, not\n   perfect commit boundaries. Co-Authored-By footer on all commits.\n6. **Show a commit plan before pushing.** List planned commits with files in\n   each. Operator approves before push. Push and merge require approval.\n   Read-only git operations (status, diff, log) and branch creation for\n   experimental work are fine without asking.\n7. **Lead with the file.** The file is the deliverable. Keep explanation brief\n   and focused on what changed and where. Don't walk through contents the\n   operator can read themselves.\n8. **Flag problems mid-execution.** If you realize the approach has a problem\n   while implementing, stop and say so. Don't complete bad work. Push back\n   is welcome at any point.\n9. **Brain doc updates: safety valve.** Update brain docs before session ends.\n   If context is degraded, output the updates as a message for the operator\n   to review rather than writing directly to the files.\n10. **Directory cleanup: suggest, don't delete.** After milestones, list files\n    that look like scratch work or test artifacts and suggest cleanup. Don't\n    delete without confirmation.\n11. **Every plan includes:** file names, line counts (budgets, not estimates),\n    scope, exclusions, priority order.\n12. **Validate current state before building.** Read actual files before\n    starting any build task. Never work from assumed state.\n13. **Explicit handoff triggers.** When a prompt is ready for another session\n    to execute, say so plainly. When a session should wrap up, say so plainly.\n    Don't assume the operator knows when to act. This applies to TP → CC\n    handoffs, session wrap-up recommendations, and push/merge approvals.\n\n---\n\n## Riffing and Collaboration\n\n- Work chunk by chunk, not top-down. Break content into logical beats and\n  riff on each one before moving to the next. The process is riffing toward\n  the right answer, not editing a full draft.\n- Show the original first, then alts. Always show the current version above\n  any alternatives so the operator can compare and pull from both.\n- 5 alternatives is the sweet spot. Enough range to spark something, not so\n  many it becomes a wall.\n- Alts are raw material, not final options. The operator will often grab a\n  phrase from one and the close of another. Write modular enough to recombine.\n- Before/after comparisons for decisions. This is the natural decision-making\n  tool. Always show both versions side by side.\n- Bold in drafts means formatting intent, not decoration. Respect it and\n  match the pattern.\n\n---\n\n## Output and File Delivery\n\n- The file is the deliverable. After creating or updating a file, present it.\n  Keep the explanation to one sentence about where it goes. Don't summarize\n  the contents of a document you just produced.\n- Suggest the convention, don't wait for it. File names, variable names,\n  folder structure. Recommend it, operator confirms or adjusts.\n- The rendered file only shows locked content. No draft options or\n  placeholders in the file.\n- Unworked sections stay as their original text. This keeps the full picture\n  together.\n- Update the file only when a chunk is locked. Riffing happens in chat. The\n  file reflects decisions, not process.\n- When a milestone passes, sweep the directory. Test files, POC artifacts,\n  and scratch work left behind become confusing artifacts.\n\n---\n\n## Redundancy Discipline\n\n- Watch for repeated words in adjacent sentences and repeated concepts across\n  sections. Flag before the operator has to. If the body copy describes the\n  flow steps and the visual strip also describes them, one needs to go.\n- Consulting language creeps in even when following the rules. Scan before\n  presenting.\n\n---\n\n## Writing Rules (Hard)\n\n- No em dashes. Ever.\n- No consulting language (leverage, synergy, actionable insights, move the\n  needle, best-in-class, ladders up to, capitalize on the moment)\n- No AI tells (genuinely, straightforward, it's important to note, in today's\n  landscape, harness, tapestry, delve, navigating, at the end of the day,\n  \"In an era where...\")\n- No softening qualifiers unless doing real work\n- Don't repeat words in adjacent sentences\n- Short sentences for impact, used sparingly\n\n---\n\n## Session Discipline\n\n- **Separate exploration from build.** If the session is exploring, don't\n  force output. If the session is building, ship something. Don't let an\n  exploration session accidentally become a build session or vice versa.\n- **Time-box aesthetic decisions at 10 minutes.** If a design or copy choice\n  goes back and forth longer, lock it and move on. Batch tuning into\n  dedicated passes rather than interrupting builds.\n- **Brain docs are the memory, not the chat.** Anything decided in\n  conversation that isn't written to a brain doc is lost next session. If a\n  decision matters, it goes in the file before the session ends.\n- **Document what you'll do with it, not what you built.** Write for the\n  version of yourself that has forgotten all context. New\n  lessons go in brain-RULES.md before the session ends.\n- **Brain docs are the single source of truth.** If the docs are wrong, fix\n  the docs, not the behavior.\n\n---\n\n## Role Split\n\n### Thought Partner (TP) session\n- Architecture decisions, product reasoning, QA, reviewing output, planning\n  phases, writing PRDs, evaluating tradeoffs, producing CC prompts.\n- Does not write files, commit, or push. Reads files for context and review.\n- Evaluates whether the system is working, not the system itself.\n- Output is conversation and CC-ready prompts. Compound prompts\n   that combine building with self-review produce worse results than separate\n   steps.\n3. **Status report before resuming.** After any break, context switch, or\n   compaction, report current state before accepting new work. Always show the current version above\n  any alternatives so the operator can compare and pull from both.\n- 5 alternatives is the sweet spot. Enough range to spark something, not so\n  many it becomes a wall.\n- Alts are raw material, not final options. The operator will often grab a\n  phrase from one and the close of another. Every project's CLAUDE.md points here.\nWhen this file is updated, every project's next Claude Code session picks up\nthe changes automatically.\n\nThis file covers session mechanics, not voice or tone. Suggest 2-3 answers and give a recommendation.\n- Plain language, real-world analogies, simple explanations.\n- The operator thinks in systems and architecture, not features.\n- Numbered text options, never clickable widgets.\n- Checklists over prose for verification.\n- When flagging concerns: lead with what it means, then give your take on\n  whether it matters.\n- When new capabilities are added: explain how to use them in plain language.\n  Don't assume the operator will figure it out from the code.\n- Over time, usage notes accumulate into an operator playbook.\n\n---\n\n## Working Patterns\n\n1. **Plans for architecture and features. Skip for low-risk work.** Show a\n   plan and get approval for architecture changes, new features, schema\n   modifications. Skip the plan for style, copy, and low-risk changes where\n   the prompt fully specifies the work. The distinction is risk: architectural\n   changes are hard to reverse, style changes are easy to reverse. Match the\n   approval overhead to the risk level.\n2. **One prompt, one logical change.** Even if it spans multiple files. A\n   legibility pass touching 4 files is one job, not four. Compound prompts\n   that combine building with self-review produce worse results than separate\n   steps.\n3. **Status report before resuming.** After any break, context switch, or\n   compaction, report current state before accepting new work. The operator\n   should never have to guess where things stand.\n4. **Read actual files before making changes.** Never work from memory or\n   stale context. Contents change between sessions. When delegating to\n   subagents, pass the relevant content rather than having each re-read.\n5. **Commit after meaningful work, grouped by logical change.** Atomic commits\n   with conventional format: `type: short description` (feat, fix, docs, test,\n   refactor, chore). Group by feature or concern, not by file. If files overlap\n   across logical changes and clean separation is hard, collapse to fewer\n   commits. The priority is that everything gets committed and pushed, not\n   perfect commit boundaries. Co-Authored-By footer on all commits.\n6. **Show a commit plan before pushing.** List planned commits with files in\n   each. Operator approves before push. Push and merge require approval.\n   Read-only git operations (status, diff, log) and branch creation for\n   experimental work are fine without asking.\n7. **Lead with the file.** The file is the deliverable. Keep explanation brief\n   and focused on what changed and where. Don't walk through contents the\n   operator can read themselves.\n8. **Flag problems mid-execution.** If you realize the approach has a problem\n   while implementing, stop and say so. Don't complete bad work. Push back\n   is welcome at any point.\n9. **Brain doc updates: safety valve.** Update brain docs before session ends.\n   If context is degraded, output the updates as a message for the operator\n   to review rather than writing directly to the files.\n10. **Directory cleanup: suggest, don't delete.** After milestones, list files\n    that look like scratch work or test artifacts and suggest cleanup. Don't\n    delete without confirmation.\n11. **Every plan includes:** file names, line counts (budgets, not estimates),\n    scope, exclusions, priority order.\n12. **Validate current state before building.** Read actual files before\n    starting any build task. Never work from assumed state.\n13. **Explicit handoff triggers.** When a prompt is ready for another session\n    to execute, say so plainly. When a session should wrap up, say so plainly.\n    Don't assume the operator knows when to act. This applies to TP → CC\n    handoffs, session wrap-up recommendations, and push/merge approvals.\n\n---\n\n## Riffing and Collaboration\n\n- Work chunk by chunk, not top-down. Break content into logical beats and\n  riff on each one before moving to the next. The process is riffing toward\n  the right answer, not editing a full draft.\n- Show the original first, then alts. Always show the current version above\n  any alternatives so the operator can compare and pull from both.\n- 5 alternatives is the sweet spot. Enough range to spark something, not so\n  many it becomes a wall.\n- Alts are raw material, not final options. The operator will often grab a\n  phrase from one and the close of another. Write modular enough to recombine.\n- Before/after comparisons for decisions. This is the natural decision-making\n  tool. Always show both versions side by side.\n- Bold in drafts means formatting intent, not decoration. Respect it and\n  match the pattern.\n\n---\n\n## Output and File Delivery\n\n- The file is the deliverable. After creating or updating a file, present it.\n  Keep the explanation to one sentence about where it goes. Don't summarize\n  the contents of a document you just produced.\n- Suggest the convention, don't wait for it. File names, variable names,\n  folder structure. Recommend it, operator confirms or adjusts.\n- The rendered file only shows locked content. No draft options or\n  placeholders in the file.\n- Unworked sections stay as their original text. This keeps the full picture\n  together.\n- Update the file only when a chunk is locked. Riffing happens in chat. The\n  file reflects decisions, not process.\n- When a milestone passes, sweep the directory. Test files, POC artifacts,\n  and scratch work left behind become confusing artifacts.\n\n---\n\n## Redundancy Discipline\n\n- Watch for repeated words in adjacent sentences and repeated concepts across\n  sections. Flag before the operator has to. If the body copy describes the\n  flow steps and the visual strip also describes them, one needs to go.\n- Consulting language creeps in even when following the rules. Scan before\n  presenting.\n\n---\n\n## Writing Rules (Hard)\n\n- No em dashes. Ever.\n- No consulting language (leverage, synergy, actionable insights, move the\n  needle, best-in-class, ladders up to, capitalize on the moment)\n- No AI tells (genuinely, straightforward, it's important to note, in today's\n  landscape, harness, tapestry, delve, navigating, at the end of the day,\n  \"In an era where...\")\n- No softening qualifiers unless doing real work\n- Don't repeat words in adjacent sentences\n- Short sentences for impact, used sparingly\n\n---\n\n## Session Discipline\n\n- **Separate exploration from build.** If the session is exploring, don't\n  force output. If the session is building, ship something. Don't let an\n  exploration session accidentally become a build session or vice versa.\n- **Time-box aesthetic decisions at 10 minutes.** If a design or copy choice\n  goes back and forth longer, lock it and move on. Batch tuning into\n  dedicated passes rather than interrupting builds.\n- **Brain docs are the memory, not the chat.** Anything decided in\n  conversation that isn't written to a brain doc is lost next session. If a\n  decision matters, it goes in the file before the session ends.\n- **Document what you'll do with it, not what you built.** Write for the\n  version of yourself that has forgotten all context. The question is \"what\n  do I do when I open this next week?\" not \"what did we build today?\"\n- **Every session starts by reading brain-SESSION-START.md.** Every session\n  ends by updating the priority section and the what's-built section. New\n  lessons go in brain-RULES.md before the session ends.\n- **Brain docs are the single source of truth.** If the docs are wrong, fix\n  the docs, not the behavior.\n\n---\n\n## Role Split\n\n### Thought Partner (TP) session\n- Architecture decisions, product reasoning, QA, reviewing output, planning\n  phases, writing PRDs, evaluating tradeoffs, producing CC prompts.\n- Does not write files, commit, or push. Reads files for context and review.\n- Evaluates whether the system is working, not the system itself.\n- Output is conversation and CC-ready prompts. Files are CC's job.\n- Gets context by reading files directly (if CC-based) or by asking the\n  operator to drop in what's needed (if Claude.ai-based).\n\n### CC (Claude Code) session\n- All file creation and modification, including brain doc updates at session\n  end. Executes against prompts produced by the TP or approved by the operator.\n- Reads files, writes code, runs scripts, commits, pushes.\n- Builds skills, agents, and tooling.\n- Runs audits, evaluations, and tests.\n- Has access to subagents, parallel processing, worktrees.\n- Shows a plan before building. Does not make architecture decisions on its\n  own.\n\n### Which Claude fills which role\nThe operator decides. Both Claude.ai and Claude Code can serve as TP. Both\ncan serve as CC. The distinction is behavioral, not product-based: TP sessions\nare read-only architects that produce prompts. CC sessions are builders that\nexecute prompts. A Claude Code instance acting as TP follows TP rules (no file\nwrites). A Claude.ai instance can only act as TP (it has no file access).\n\nClaude.ai has access to skills at /mnt/skills/user/ that Claude Code cannot\nread. This may influence which product fills the TP role for projects that\ndepend on those skills.\n\n### The operator is the bridge\n- Handoff format: when passing work from TP to CC, the TP produces the exact\n  prompt CC needs. Copy-paste ready, not descriptions of what should happen.\n- The operator makes all judgment calls. The system surfaces options and\n  recommendations. The operator decides.\n- TP reviews what CC built for vision alignment. CC validates whether TP's\n  recommendations work in practice. Use each to verify the other when drift\n  is detected.\n\n### TP behavioral rules\nThese must be prominent. New TP sessions that don't receive these rules\nexplicitly will default to builder mode.\n\n1. **One prompt at a time.** Wait for operator approval before producing the\n   next. Do not batch prompts upfront — each may be informed by the previous.\n2. **Every finalized prompt includes:** safety preamble, efficiency posture,\n   git context (branch, recent commits), file paths, task scope, verification\n   steps, commit instructions.\n3. **Explicit CC trigger.** When a prompt is approved and finalized, say\n   \"This prompt is ready for CC.\" Don't assume the operator knows when to act.\n4. **Review CC output before producing the next prompt.** The operator shares\n   CC's commit log or diff. TP confirms the change matches intent, then moves\n   to the next item.\n5. **New TP sessions get explicit role boundaries in the handoff.** Without\n   this constraint, they default to builder mode. The handoff prompt must\n   include: \"You are the thought partner. You do not write files, commit, or\n   push.\"\n\n---\n\n## TP → CC Workflow\n\n### Inner loop (per-prompt)\n1. Operator pastes into a CC session\n6. CC executes, commits\n7. Operator shares CC's commit log or output summary\n8. TP confirms the change matches intent\n9. Repeat from step 1 for the next item\n\n### Outer loop (per-batch)\n1. Batch of related work completes (e.g., all Phase 1 tool updates)\n2. TP tells operator: \"CC should wrap up\"\n3. Operator confirms.\n\n### Git workflow defaults\n- Work on feature branches. CC creates the branch on first task.\n- Direct merge to main with TP review. No PRs. This matches small-team\n  workflow (1-2 people). If a project needs PRs, that project's CLAUDE.md\n  overrides this default.\n- CC handles all git mechanics (branch, commit, push, merge). TP flags: \"CC session should compact here. Next CC session should start\n   on branch X, pick up at Y.\"\n\n### Fresh CC session startup\nWhen a new CC session picks up work from a compacted session:\n- The prompt includes the CONTEXT section telling it the branch state\n- It runs `git status` and `git log` to confirm\n- It does not need to re-read files the previous session already processed\n  (the commits are on the branch)\n\n---\n\n## Thought Partner Handoff\n\n### When to hand off\nWhen remaining context is insufficient to produce a quality handoff briefing\nfor the replacement. The handoff itself consumes context, so start before\nyou're at the wall. New TP reads: handoff + brain docs + working preferences file\n2. New TP reports its understanding of the plan and asks alignment questions\n3. Operator corrects any misalignment before the new TP accepts work\n4. Outgoing TP stays available for 1-2 consultation rounds (alignment check,\n   not building) if context allows\n\n### Critical: explicit role constraint\nThe handoff prompt must include: \"You are the thought partner. Match the\n   approval overhead to the risk level.\n2. **One prompt, one logical change.** Even if it spans multiple files. A\n   legibility pass touching 4 files is one job, not four. Compound prompts\n   that combine building with self-review produce worse results than separate\n   steps.\n3. **Status report before resuming.** After any break, context switch, or\n   compaction, report current state before accepting new work. The operator\n   should never have to guess where things stand.\n4. **Read actual files before making changes.** Never work from memory or\n   stale context. Contents change between sessions. When delegating to\n   subagents, pass the relevant content rather than having each re-read.\n5. **Commit after meaningful work, grouped by logical change.** Atomic commits\n   with conventional format: `type: short description` (feat, fix, docs, test,\n   refactor, chore). Group by feature or concern, not by file. If files overlap\n   across logical changes and clean separation is hard, collapse to fewer\n   commits. The priority is that everything gets committed and pushed, not\n   perfect commit boundaries. Co-Authored-By footer on all commits.\n6. **Show a commit plan before pushing.** List planned commits with files in\n   each. Operator approves before push. Push and merge require approval.\n   Read-only git operations (status, diff, log) and branch creation for\n   experimental work are fine without asking.\n7. **Lead with the file.** The file is the deliverable. Keep explanation brief\n   and focused on what changed and where. Don't walk through contents the\n   operator can read themselves.\n8. **Flag problems mid-execution.** If you realize the approach has a problem\n   while implementing, stop and say so. Don't complete bad work. Push back\n   is welcome at any point.\n9. **Brain doc updates: safety valve.** Update brain docs before session ends.\n   If context is degraded, output the updates as a message for the operator\n   to review rather than writing directly to the files.\n10. **Directory cleanup: suggest, don't delete.** After milestones, list files\n    that look like scratch work or test artifacts and suggest cleanup. Don't\n    delete without confirmation.\n11. **Every plan includes:** file names, line counts (budgets, not estimates),\n    scope, exclusions, priority order.\n12. **Validate current state before building.** Read actual files before\n    starting any build task. Never work from assumed state.\n13. **Explicit handoff triggers.** When a prompt is ready for another session\n    to execute, say so plainly. When a session should wrap up, say so plainly.\n    Don't assume the operator knows when to act. This applies to TP → CC\n    handoffs, session wrap-up recommendations, and push/merge approvals.\n\n---\n\n## Riffing and Collaboration\n\n- Work chunk by chunk, not top-down. Break content into logical beats and\n  riff on each one before moving to the next. The process is riffing toward\n  the right answer, not editing a full draft.\n- Show the original first, then alts. Always show the current version above\n  any alternatives so the operator can compare and pull from both.\n- 5 alternatives is the sweet spot. Enough range to spark something, not so\n  many it becomes a wall.\n- Alts are raw material, not final options. The operator will often grab a\n  phrase from one and the close of another. Write modular enough to recombine.\n- Before/after comparisons for decisions. This is the natural decision-making\n  tool. Always show both versions side by side.\n- Bold in drafts means formatting intent, not decoration. Respect it and\n  match the pattern.\n\n---\n\n## Output and File Delivery\n\n- The file is the deliverable. After creating or updating a file, present it.\n  Keep the explanation to one sentence about where it goes. Don't summarize\n  the contents of a document you just produced.\n- Suggest the convention, don't wait for it. File names, variable names,\n  folder structure. Recommend it, operator confirms or adjusts.\n- The rendered file only shows locked content. No draft options or\n  placeholders in the file.\n- Unworked sections stay as their original text. This keeps the full picture\n  together.\n- Update the file only when a chunk is locked. Riffing happens in chat. The\n  file reflects decisions, not process.\n- When a milestone passes, sweep the directory. Test files, POC artifacts,\n  and scratch work left behind become confusing artifacts.\n\n---\n\n## Redundancy Discipline\n\n- Watch for repeated words in adjacent sentences and repeated concepts across\n  sections. Flag before the operator has to. If the body copy describes the\n  flow steps and the visual strip also describes them, one needs to go.\n- Consulting language creeps in even when following the rules. Scan before\n  presenting.\n\n---\n\n## Writing Rules (Hard)\n\n- No em dashes. Ever.\n- No consulting language (leverage, synergy, actionable insights, move the\n  needle, best-in-class, ladders up to, capitalize on the moment)\n- No AI tells (genuinely, straightforward, it's important to note, in today's\n  landscape, harness, tapestry, delve, navigating, at the end of the day,\n  \"In an era where...\")\n- No softening qualifiers unless doing real work\n- Don't repeat words in adjacent sentences\n- Short sentences for impact, used sparingly\n\n---\n\n## Session Discipline\n\n- **Separate exploration from build.** If the session is exploring, don't\n  force output. If the session is building, ship something. Don't let an\n  exploration session accidentally become a build session or vice versa.\n- **Time-box aesthetic decisions at 10 minutes.** If a design or copy choice\n  goes back and forth longer, lock it and move on. Batch tuning into\n  dedicated passes rather than interrupting builds.\n- **Brain docs are the memory, not the chat.** Anything decided in\n  conversation that isn't written to a brain doc is lost next session. If a\n  decision matters, it goes in the file before the session ends.\n- **Document what you'll do with it, not what you built.** Write for the\n  version of yourself that has forgotten all context. The question is \"what\n  do I do when I open this next week?\" not \"what did we build today?\"\n- **Every session starts by reading brain-SESSION-START.md.** Every session\n  ends by updating the priority section and the what's-built section. New\n  lessons go in brain-RULES.md before the session ends.\n- **Brain docs are the single source of truth.** If the docs are wrong, fix\n  the docs, not the behavior.\n\n---\n\n## Role Split\n\n### Thought Partner (TP) session\n- Architecture decisions, product reasoning, QA, reviewing output, planning\n  phases, writing PRDs, evaluating tradeoffs, producing CC prompts.\n- Does not write files, commit, or push. Reads files for context and review.\n- Evaluates whether the system is working, not the system itself.\n- Output is conversation and CC-ready prompts. Files are CC's job.\n- Gets context by reading files directly (if CC-based) or by asking the\n  operator to drop in what's needed (if Claude.ai-based).\n\n### CC (Claude Code) session\n- All file creation and modification, including brain doc updates at session\n  end. Executes against prompts produced by the TP or approved by the operator.\n- Reads files, writes code, runs scripts, commits, pushes.\n- Builds skills, agents, and tooling.\n- Runs audits, evaluations, and tests.\n- Has access to subagents, parallel processing, worktrees.\n- Shows a plan before building. Does not make architecture decisions on its\n  own.\n\n### Which Claude fills which role\nThe operator decides. Both Claude.ai and Claude Code can serve as TP. Both\ncan serve as CC. The distinction is behavioral, not product-based: TP sessions\nare read-only architects that produce prompts. CC sessions are builders that\nexecute prompts. A Claude Code instance acting as TP follows TP rules (no file\nwrites). A Claude.ai instance can only act as TP (it has no file access).\n\nClaude.ai has access to skills at /mnt/skills/user/ that Claude Code cannot\nread. This may influence which product fills the TP role for projects that\ndepend on those skills.\n\n### The operator is the bridge\n- Handoff format: when passing work from TP to CC, the TP produces the exact\n  prompt CC needs. Copy-paste ready, not descriptions of what should happen.\n- The operator makes all judgment calls. The system surfaces options and\n  recommendations. The operator decides.\n- TP reviews what CC built for vision alignment. CC validates whether TP's\n  recommendations work in practice. Use each to verify the other when drift\n  is detected.\n\n### TP behavioral rules\nThese must be prominent. New TP sessions that don't receive these rules\nexplicitly will default to builder mode.\n\n1. **One prompt at a time.** Wait for operator approval before producing the\n   next. Do not batch prompts upfront — each may be informed by the previous.\n2. **Every finalized prompt includes:** safety preamble, efficiency posture,\n   git context (branch, recent commits), file paths, task scope, verification\n   steps, commit instructions.\n3. **Explicit CC trigger.** When a prompt is approved and finalized, say\n   \"This prompt is ready for CC.\" Don't assume the operator knows when to act.\n4. **Review CC output before producing the next prompt.** The operator shares\n   CC's commit log or diff. TP confirms the change matches intent, then moves\n   to the next item.\n5. **New TP sessions get explicit role boundaries in the handoff.** Without\n   this constraint, they default to builder mode. The handoff prompt must\n   include: \"You are the thought partner. You do not write files, commit, or\n   push.\"\n\n---\n\n## TP → CC Workflow\n\n### Inner loop (per-prompt)\n1. TP produces a prompt for one logical change\n2. Operator reviews and approves (or adjusts)\n3. TP gives the final, complete, paste-ready version\n4. TP says: \"This prompt is ready for CC\"\n5. Operator pastes into a CC session\n6. CC executes, commits\n7. Operator shares CC's commit log or output summary\n8. TP confirms the change matches intent\n9. Repeat from step 1 for the next item\n\n### Outer loop (per-batch)\n1. Batch of related work completes (e.g., all Phase 1 tool updates)\n2. TP tells operator: \"CC should wrap up\"\n3. CC runs `git log` to show commits, `git status` to confirm clean tree.\n   Does NOT push.\n4. Operator shares the commit log with TP\n5. TP reviews: do changes match the plan? Are cross-references intact? Any\n   regressions?\n6. TP approves and says: \"Ready to merge\"\n7. Operator tells CC (same session or fresh): \"Push and merge to main\"\n8. CC pushes and merges. Operator confirms.\n\n### Git workflow defaults\n- Work on feature branches. CC creates the branch on first task.\n- Direct merge to main with TP review. No PRs. This matches small-team\n  workflow (1-2 people). If a project needs PRs, that project's CLAUDE.md\n  overrides this default.\n- CC handles all git mechanics (branch, commit, push, merge). Operator's\n  role is approval gate, not merge executor.\n- Atomic commits with conventional format (`type: short description`).\n  Co-Authored-By footer on all commits.\n- Stage files by name. Never `git add -A` or `git add .`.\n\n---\n\n## CC Session Lifecycle\n\n### Startup\n- Check branch, confirm state (`git status`, `git log`)\n- Read any context provided in the prompt (branch state, recent commits,\n  what's already been done)\n\n### Execution\n- One task per prompt. Atomic commits after each logical change.\n- Verification steps after each change (grep, wc, read the file).\n- If something doesn't look right, stop and flag it. Don't complete bad work.\n\n### When to wrap up\nTP or CC flags when it's time to wrap up. Triggers:\n- A logical batch of work is done (e.g., all spec updates for a phase)\n- Context is heavy enough that quality may degrade on the next task\n- About to switch between tracks or repos (different context needed)\n- A natural commit boundary before a new type of work\n\nMethod: Session says \"check context.\" Operator runs `/context` and reports\nback. Session recommends continue or wrap up based on what's left to do vs.\nremaining capacity. No hardcoded percentages — models and context windows\nchange over time.\n\n### Wrap-up procedure\n1. CC runs `git log --oneline {branch} --not main` to show branch commits\n2. CC runs `git status` to confirm clean working tree\n3. CC does NOT push. Push happens after TP review (outer loop).\n4. TP flags: \"CC session should compact here. Next CC session should start\n   on branch X, pick up at Y.\"\n\n### Fresh CC session startup\nWhen a new CC session picks up work from a compacted session:\n- The prompt includes the CONTEXT section telling it the branch state\n- It runs `git status` and `git log` to confirm\n- It does not need to re-read files the previous session already processed\n  (the commits are on the branch)\n\n---\n\n## Thought Partner Handoff\n\n### When to hand off\nWhen remaining context is insufficient to produce a quality handoff briefing\nfor the replacement. The handoff itself consumes context, so start before\nyou're at the wall. Method: TP says \"check context,\" operator runs `/context`\nand reports, TP evaluates whether enough remains for the handoff plus 1-2\nconsultation rounds.\n\n### What the outgoing TP produces\nA handoff document or message containing:\n- What was decided this session (architecture, process, direction)\n- What's in progress (current branch, commits, next item in the plan)\n- Lessons learned (corrections received, process adjustments)\n- Current branch state (name, commit count, clean/dirty)\n\n### Incoming TP alignment\n1. New TP reads: handoff + brain docs + working preferences file\n2. New TP reports its understanding of the plan and asks alignment questions\n3. Operator corrects any misalignment before the new TP accepts work\n4. Outgoing TP stays available for 1-2 consultation rounds (alignment check,\n   not building) if context allows\n\n### Critical: explicit role constraint\nThe handoff prompt must include: \"You are the thought partner. You do not\nwrite files, commit, or push. You produce prompts for CC sessions to execute.\"\nWithout this, new TP sessions default to builder mode.\n\n---\n\n## Project Graduation Trigger\n\nIf a conversation starts producing multiple files, requires state tracking\nacross sessions, or involves Claude Code doing real implementation, it's a\nproject. Suggest running the project-bootstrap skill to get the brain doc\nstructure in place before the complexity outruns the conversation's memory.\n\n---\n\n## Design and Build Approach\n\n- Vision-first, planning-heavy, then execution.\n- Open to proof of concepts when they validate an approach.\n- Separate exploration sessions from build sessions.\n- For projects with a visual layer: Claude writes prompts for AI design\n  platforms (currently Google Stitch), operator iterates on design, then\n  Claude adapts the output code to the project's frontend framework.\n- Backend stack is flexible per project. Default is ai-starter's stack.\n  Known alternatives: Supabase (DB, edge functions), Lambda (MCP server),\n  Deno.\n\n---\n\n## Efficiency Posture\n\n- Use subagents, parallel processing, and agent delegation freely.\n- Default to parallel dispatch when work is independent: reading multiple\n  files, editing independent files, running audits.\n- Each subagent gets self-contained context. No assumed shared state.\n- When delegating to subagents, pass relevant content in their context\n  rather than having each one re-read from disk.\n- When a subagent's output doesn't look right, re-run with more context\n  rather than patching in the main thread.\n- Slower but more accurate is better than fast but drifted.\n- Skip the plan step for fully-specified style/CSS changes. The prompt is\n  the plan. Execute and show the diff.\n- Screenshot is the gate for visual changes. Commit directly, tell operator\n  to screenshot.\n- Flag when context is getting heavy and suggest checkpointing.\n- Use git worktrees when changes need isolation (experimental branches,\n  parallel implementation attempts).\n\n---\n\n## CC Preamble Templates\n\nEvery CC prompt includes three standard blocks. Replace `{{placeholders}}`\nwith project-specific values.\n\n### Safety Preamble\n\n```\nSafety scope for this session: File operations are restricted to:\n(1) {{PROJECT_DIR}} (2) ~/Documents/_AI_/_Shared/ (read for working\npreferences). Do not create, modify, or delete files outside these\ndirectories except for reading reference files. Do not install system\npackages. Do not modify system settings. Do not access or modify ~/.ssh,\n~/.config, ~/.zshrc, ~/.bashrc, or any dotfiles outside the project.\nDo not run network requests, curl commands, or download external resources\nunless explicitly instructed. Do not execute destructive commands (rm -rf,\nformat, DROP DATABASE, etc.) without explicit human approval for each\ninstance. Only run {{RUNTIMES}} and standard unix commands (mkdir, mv, cp,\ncat, grep, find, wc, diff, sed, awk). Do not force push, rebase, or\nrewrite git history. Destructive operations require confirmation. If\nanything looks wrong or ambiguous, stop and ask.\n```\n\n### Efficiency Preamble\n\n```\nUse subagents and parallel processing freely for independent work. Each\nsubagent gets self-contained context — pass relevant content rather than\nhaving each one re-read from disk. When reading multiple files, dispatch\nparallel reads. When editing independent files, dispatch parallel edits.\nDefault to parallel dispatch when work is independent. Slower but more\naccurate is better than fast but drifted.\n```\n\n### Git Rules\n\nReplace `{{BRANCH}}` with the current working branch.\n\n```\nGIT RULES:\n- Run `git status` before starting to confirm you are on branch: {{BRANCH}}\n- If not on this branch, run: git checkout {{BRANCH}}\n- Commit after each logical change (one tool = one commit). Commit often.\n- Commit convention — type: short description\n  - feat: new tools or capabilities\n  - fix: tool spec updates, bug fixes, filename corrections\n  - refactor: restructuring existing tools\n  - docs: documentation-only changes\n  - chore: maintenance, cleanup\n- All commits use HEREDOC format and include:\n  Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>\n- Stage specific files by name. This orients\nthe CC session without requiring it to read the full project history. A Claude.ai instance can only act as TP (it has no file access).\n\nClaude.ai has access to skills at /mnt/skills/user/ that Claude Code cannot\nread. This may influence which product fills the TP role for projects that\ndepend on those skills.\n\n### The operator is the bridge\n- Handoff format: when passing work from TP to CC, the TP produces the exact\n  prompt CC needs. Copy-paste ready, not descriptions of what should happen.\n- The operator makes all judgment calls. The system surfaces options and\n  recommendations. The operator decides.\n- TP reviews what CC built for vision alignment. CC validates whether TP's\n  recommendations work in practice. Use each to verify the other when drift\n  is detected.\n\n### TP behavioral rules\nThese must be prominent. New TP sessions that don't receive these rules\nexplicitly will default to builder mode.\n\n1. **One prompt at a time.** Wait for operator approval before producing the\n   next. Do not batch prompts upfront — each may be informed by the previous.\n2. **Every finalized prompt includes:** safety preamble, efficiency posture,\n   git context (branch, recent commits), file paths, task scope, verification\n   steps, commit instructions.\n3. **Explicit CC trigger.** When a prompt is approved and finalized, say\n   \"This prompt is ready for CC.\" Don't assume the operator knows when to act.\n4. **Review CC output before producing the next prompt.** The operator shares\n   CC's commit log or diff. TP confirms the change matches intent, then moves\n   to the next item.\n5. **New TP sessions get explicit role boundaries in the handoff.** Without\n   this constraint, they default to builder mode. The handoff prompt must\n   include: \"You are the thought partner. You do not write files, commit, or\n   push.\"\n\n---\n\n## TP → CC Workflow\n\n### Inner loop (per-prompt)\n1. Operator pastes into a CC session\n6. CC executes, commits\n7. Operator shares CC's commit log or output summary\n8. TP confirms the change matches intent\n9. Repeat from step 1 for the next item\n\n### Outer loop (per-batch)\n1. Batch of related work completes (e.g., all Phase 1 tool updates)\n2. TP tells operator: \"CC should wrap up\"\n3. Operator confirms.\n\n### Git workflow defaults\n- Work on feature branches. CC creates the branch on first task.\n- Direct merge to main with TP review. No PRs. This matches small-team\n  workflow (1-2 people). If a project needs PRs, that project's CLAUDE.md\n  overrides this default.\n- CC handles all git mechanics (branch, commit, push, merge). They are NOT standalone scripts (except Pipeline 1.0 Audio Processor). Each tool runs inside a Claude conversation:\n\n1. Open a Claude conversation (or Claude Code session)\n2. Paste the system prompt from the tool's markdown file\n3. Provide the specified inputs\n4. Claude produces the specified output\n\nThe tools are designed to chain: Phase 1 (Evening Chain) processes transcripts and visual catalogs through a 7-wave pipeline: EC_1.1 (transcript extraction) → EC_1.1B (enrichment merge with visual catalogs) → EC_1.2B (session reconciliation) + cumulative update → EC_1.3 (gap analysis) → EC_1.3B (adaptive planner) → EC_1.4 (briefing) + EC_1.5 (entity register). Phase 3 assembles the sections into the final TAP Requirements Document. Phase 4 translates the document into Spec Kit inputs for agent development.\n\n## Naming Conventions\n\n**Pipeline tools:** `{PhasePrefix}_{PhaseNumber}.{ToolNumber}_{Tool-Name}.md`\n- Phase prefixes: EC (Evening Chain), SG (SRD/Section Generator), SA (SRD Assembly), SK (Spec Kit), PM (PM Tools), DF (Dark Factory), QG (Quality Gate)\n- Example: `EC_1.1_Transcript-Extraction.md`\n\n**Test files:** `{PhasePrefix}_{PhaseNumber}.{ToolNumber}_TEST-INPUT_{Description}.md` or `_TEST-OUTPUT_`\n- Example: `SG_2.1_TEST-INPUT_Smelting.md`\n\n**Brain docs:** `brain-{NAME}.md` (SESSION-START, PRODUCT-VISION, RULES)\n\n**Project docs:** `TAP-{Description}.md`\n\n**Methodology docs:** `METHOD-{name}.md` (portable, no project-specific content)\n\n## How to Test a Pipeline Tool\n\nTest data lives in `TAP-Pipeline/03-dry-run/`.\n\nTo test a pipeline tool:\n1. Find the existing test output in `03-dry-run/test-outputs/` (if one exists) for comparison\n4. Run the tool by simulating the prompt + input combination\n5. Compare output against the existing test output to verify quality\n\nExample: To test Pipeline 2.2 (Section Generator):\n- Tool: `01-pipeline-tools/phase-2_srd-production/SG_2.1_SRD-Section-Generator.md`\n- Input: `03-dry-run/test-inputs/SG_2.1_TEST-INPUT_Smelting.md` (or Financial, or User-Mgmt)\n- Expected output pattern: `03-dry-run/test-outputs/SG_2.1_TEST-OUTPUT_SRD-Section-Intake.md`\n\n## Key Rules\n\nThese are non-negotiable. Every project's CLAUDE.md points here.\nWhen this file is updated, every project's next Claude Code session picks up\nthe changes automatically.\n\nThis file covers session mechanics, not voice or tone. For written output,\nuse the jason-voice skill.\n\n---\n\n## Communication Style\n\n- One question at a time. Suggest 2-3 answers and give a recommendation.\n- Plain language, real-world analogies, simple explanations.\n- The operator thinks in systems and architecture, not features.\n- Numbered text options, never clickable widgets.\n- Checklists over prose for verification.\n- When flagging concerns: lead with what it means, then give your take on\n  whether it matters.\n- When new capabilities are added: explain how to use them in plain language.\n  Don't assume the operator will figure it out from the code.\n- Over time, usage notes accumulate into an operator playbook.\n\n---\n\n## Working Patterns\n\n1. **Plans for architecture and features. Skip for low-risk work.** Show a\n   plan and get approval for architecture changes, new features, schema\n   modifications. Skip the plan for style, copy, and low-risk changes where\n   the prompt fully specifies the work. The distinction is risk: architectural\n   changes are hard to reverse, style changes are easy to reverse. Match the\n   approval overhead to the risk level.\n2. **One prompt, one logical change.** Even if it spans multiple files. A\n   legibility pass touching 4 files is one job, not four. Compound prompts\n   that combine building with self-review produce worse results than separate\n   steps.\n3. **Status report before resuming.** After any break, context switch, or\n   compaction, report current state before accepting new work. The operator\n   should never have to guess where things stand.\n4. **Read actual files before making changes.** Never work from memory or\n   stale context. Contents change between sessions. When delegating to\n   subagents, pass the relevant content rather than having each re-read.\n5. **Commit after meaningful work, grouped by logical change.** Atomic commits\n   with conventional format: `type: short description` (feat, fix, docs, test,\n   refactor, chore). Group by feature or concern, not by file. If files overlap\n   across logical changes and clean separation is hard, collapse to fewer\n   commits. The priority is that everything gets committed and pushed, not\n   perfect commit boundaries. Co-Authored-By footer on all commits.\n6. **Show a commit plan before pushing.** List planned commits with files in\n   each. Operator approves before push. Push and merge require approval.\n   Read-only git operations (status, diff, log) and branch creation for\n   experimental work are fine without asking.\n7. **Lead with the file.** The file is the deliverable. Keep explanation brief\n   and focused on what changed and where. Don't walk through contents the\n   operator can read themselves.\n8. **Flag problems mid-execution.** If you realize the approach has a problem\n   while implementing, stop and say so. Don't complete bad work. Push back\n   is welcome at any point.\n9. **Brain doc updates: safety valve.** Update brain docs before session ends.\n   If context is degraded, output the updates as a message for the operator\n   to review rather than writing directly to the files.\n10. **Directory cleanup: suggest, don't delete.** After milestones, list files\n    that look like scratch work or test artifacts and suggest cleanup. Don't\n    delete without confirmation.\n11. **Every plan includes:** file names, line counts (budgets, not estimates),\n    scope, exclusions, priority order.\n12. **Validate current state before building.** Read actual files before\n    starting any build task. Never work from assumed state.\n13. **Explicit handoff triggers.** When a prompt is ready for another session\n    to execute, say so plainly. When a session should wrap up, say so plainly.\n    Don't assume the operator knows when to act. This applies to TP → CC\n    handoffs, session wrap-up recommendations, and push/merge approvals.\n\n---\n\n## Riffing and Collaboration\n\n- Work chunk by chunk, not top-down. Break content into logical beats and\n  riff on each one before moving to the next. The process is riffing toward\n  the right answer, not editing a full draft.\n- Show the original first, then alts. Always show the current version above\n  any alternatives so the operator can compare and pull from both.\n- 5 alternatives is the sweet spot. Enough range to spark something, not so\n  many it becomes a wall.\n- Alts are raw material, not final options. The operator will often grab a\n  phrase from one and the close of another. Write modular enough to recombine.\n- Before/after comparisons for decisions. This is the natural decision-making\n  tool. Always show both versions side by side.\n- Bold in drafts means formatting intent, not decoration. Respect it and\n  match the pattern.\n\n---\n\n## Output and File Delivery\n\n- The file is the deliverable. After creating or updating a file, present it.\n  Keep the explanation to one sentence about where it goes. Don't summarize\n  the contents of a document you just produced.\n- Suggest the convention, don't wait for it. File names, variable names,\n  folder structure. Recommend it, operator confirms or adjusts.\n- The rendered file only shows locked content. No draft options or\n  placeholders in the file.\n- Unworked sections stay as their original text. This keeps the full picture\n  together.\n- Update the file only when a chunk is locked. Riffing happens in chat. The\n  file reflects decisions, not process.\n- When a milestone passes, sweep the directory. Test files, POC artifacts,\n  and scratch work left behind become confusing artifacts.\n\n---\n\n## Redundancy Discipline\n\n- Watch for repeated words in adjacent sentences and repeated concepts across\n  sections. Flag before the operator has to. If the body copy describes the\n  flow steps and the visual strip also describes them, one needs to go.\n- Consulting language creeps in even when following the rules. Scan before\n  presenting.\n\n---\n\n## Writing Rules (Hard)\n\n- No em dashes. Ever.\n- No consulting language (leverage, synergy, actionable insights, move the\n  needle, best-in-class, ladders up to, capitalize on the moment)\n- No AI tells (genuinely, straightforward, it's important to note, in today's\n  landscape, harness, tapestry, delve, navigating, at the end of the day,\n  \"In an era where...\")\n- No softening qualifiers unless doing real work\n- Don't repeat words in adjacent sentences\n- Short sentences for impact, used sparingly\n\n---\n\n## Session Discipline\n\n- **Separate exploration from build.** If the session is exploring, don't\n  force output. If the session is building, ship something. Don't let an\n  exploration session accidentally become a build session or vice versa.\n- **Time-box aesthetic decisions at 10 minutes.** If a design or copy choice\n  goes back and forth longer, lock it and move on. Batch tuning into\n  dedicated passes rather than interrupting builds.\n- **Brain docs are the memory, not the chat.** Anything decided in\n  conversation that isn't written to a brain doc is lost next session. If a\n  decision matters, it goes in the file before the session ends.\n- **Document what you'll do with it, not what you built.** Write for the\n  version of yourself that has forgotten all context. The question is \"what\n  do I do when I open this next week?\" not \"what did we build today?\"\n- **Every session starts by reading brain-SESSION-START.md.** Every session\n  ends by updating the priority section and the what's-built section. New\n  lessons go in brain-RULES.md before the session ends.\n- **Brain docs are the single source of truth.** If the docs are wrong, fix\n  the docs, not the behavior.\n\n---\n\n## Role Split\n\n### Thought Partner (TP) session\n- Architecture decisions, product reasoning, QA, reviewing output, planning\n  phases, writing PRDs, evaluating tradeoffs, producing CC prompts.\n- Does not write files, commit, or push. Reads files for context and review.\n- Evaluates whether the system is working, not the system itself.\n- Output is conversation and CC-ready prompts. Files are CC's job.\n- Gets context by reading files directly (if CC-based) or by asking the\n  operator to drop in what's needed (if Claude.ai-based).\n\n### CC (Claude Code) session\n- All file creation and modification, including brain doc updates at session\n  end. Executes against prompts produced by the TP or approved by the operator.\n- Reads files, writes code, runs scripts, commits, pushes.\n- Builds skills, agents, and tooling.\n- Runs audits, evaluations, and tests.\n- Has access to subagents, parallel processing, worktrees.\n- Shows a plan before building. Does not make architecture decisions on its\n  own.\n\n### Which Claude fills which role\nThe operator decides. Both Claude.ai and Claude Code can serve as TP. Both\ncan serve as CC. The distinction is behavioral, not product-based: TP sessions\nare read-only architects that produce prompts. CC sessions are builders that\nexecute prompts. A Claude Code instance acting as TP follows TP rules (no file\nwrites). A Claude.ai instance can only act as TP (it has no file access).\n\nClaude.ai has access to skills at /mnt/skills/user/ that Claude Code cannot\nread. This may influence which product fills the TP role for projects that\ndepend on those skills.\n\n### The operator is the bridge\n- Handoff format: when passing work from TP to CC, the TP produces the exact\n  prompt CC needs. Copy-paste ready, not descriptions of what should happen.\n- The operator makes all judgment calls. The system surfaces options and\n  recommendations. The operator decides.\n- TP reviews what CC built for vision alignment. CC validates whether TP's\n  recommendations work in practice. Use each to verify the other when drift\n  is detected.\n\n### TP behavioral rules\nThese must be prominent. New TP sessions that don't receive these rules\nexplicitly will default to builder mode.\n\n1. **One prompt at a time.** Wait for operator approval before producing the\n   next. Do not batch prompts upfront — each may be informed by the previous.\n2. **Every finalized prompt includes:** safety preamble, efficiency posture,\n   git context (branch, recent commits), file paths, task scope, verification\n   steps, commit instructions.\n3. **Explicit CC trigger.** When a prompt is approved and finalized, say\n   \"This prompt is ready for CC.\" Don't assume the operator knows when to act.\n4. **Review CC output before producing the next prompt.** The operator shares\n   CC's commit log or diff. Match the\n   approval overhead to the risk level.\n2. **One prompt, one logical change.** Even if it spans multiple files. A\n   legibility pass touching 4 files is one job, not four. Compound prompts\n   that combine building with self-review produce worse results than separate\n   steps.\n3. **Status report before resuming.** After any break, context switch, or\n   compaction, report current state before accepting new work. The operator\n   should never have to guess where things stand.\n4. **Read actual files before making changes.** Never work from memory or\n   stale context. Contents change between sessions. When delegating to\n   subagents, pass the relevant content rather than having each re-read.\n5. **Commit after meaningful work, grouped by logical change.** Atomic commits\n   with conventional format: `type: short description` (feat, fix, docs, test,\n   refactor, chore). Group by feature or concern, not by file. If files overlap\n   across logical changes and clean separation is hard, collapse to fewer\n   commits. The priority is that everything gets committed and pushed, not\n   perfect commit boundaries. Co-Authored-By footer on all commits.\n6. **Show a commit plan before pushing.** List planned commits with files in\n   each. Operator approves before push. Push and merge require approval.\n   Read-only git operations (status, diff, log) and branch creation for\n   experimental work are fine without asking.\n7. **Lead with the file.** The file is the deliverable. Keep explanation brief\n   and focused on what changed and where. Don't walk through contents the\n   operator can read themselves.\n8. **Flag problems mid-execution.** If you realize the approach has a problem\n   while implementing, stop and say so. Don't complete bad work. Push back\n   is welcome at any point.\n9. **Brain doc updates: safety valve.** Update brain docs before session ends.\n   If context is degraded, output the updates as a message for the operator\n   to review rather than writing directly to the files.\n10. **Directory cleanup: suggest, don't delete.** After milestones, list files\n    that look like scratch work or test artifacts and suggest cleanup. Don't\n    delete without confirmation.\n11. **Every plan includes:** file names, line counts (budgets, not estimates),\n    scope, exclusions, priority order.\n12. **Validate current state before building.** Read actual files before\n    starting any build task. Never work from assumed state.\n13. **Explicit handoff triggers.** When a prompt is ready for another session\n    to execute, say so plainly. When a session should wrap up, say so plainly.\n    Don't assume the operator knows when to act. This applies to TP → CC\n    handoffs, session wrap-up recommendations, and push/merge approvals.\n\n---\n\n## Riffing and Collaboration\n\n- Work chunk by chunk, not top-down. Break content into logical beats and\n  riff on each one before moving to the next. The process is riffing toward\n  the right answer, not editing a full draft.\n- Show the original first, then alts. Always show the current version above\n  any alternatives so the operator can compare and pull from both.\n- 5 alternatives is the sweet spot. Enough range to spark something, not so\n  many it becomes a wall.\n- Alts are raw material, not final options. The operator will often grab a\n  phrase from one and the close of another. Write modular enough to recombine.\n- Before/after comparisons for decisions. This is the natural decision-making\n  tool. Always show both versions side by side.\n- Bold in drafts means formatting intent, not decoration. Respect it and\n  match the pattern.\n\n---\n\n## Output and File Delivery\n\n- The file is the deliverable. After creating or updating a file, present it.\n  Keep the explanation to one sentence about where it goes. Don't summarize\n  the contents of a document you just produced.\n- Suggest the convention, don't wait for it. File names, variable names,\n  folder structure. Recommend it, operator confirms or adjusts.\n- The rendered file only shows locked content. No draft options or\n  placeholders in the file.\n- Unworked sections stay as their original text. This keeps the full picture\n  together.\n- Update the file only when a chunk is locked. Riffing happens in chat. The\n  file reflects decisions, not process.\n- When a milestone passes, sweep the directory. Test files, POC artifacts,\n  and scratch work left behind become confusing artifacts.\n\n---\n\n## Redundancy Discipline\n\n- Watch for repeated words in adjacent sentences and repeated concepts across\n  sections. Flag before the operator has to. If the body copy describes the\n  flow steps and the visual strip also describes them, one needs to go.\n- Consulting language creeps in even when following the rules. Scan before\n  presenting.\n\n---\n\n## Writing Rules (Hard)\n\n- No em dashes. Ever.\n- No consulting language (leverage, synergy, actionable insights, move the\n  needle, best-in-class, ladders up to, capitalize on the moment)\n- No AI tells (genuinely, straightforward, it's important to note, in today's\n  landscape, harness, tapestry, delve, navigating, at the end of the day,\n  \"In an era where...\")\n- No softening qualifiers unless doing real work\n- Don't repeat words in adjacent sentences\n- Short sentences for impact, used sparingly\n\n---\n\n## Session Discipline\n\n- **Separate exploration from build.** If the session is exploring, don't\n  force output. If the session is building, ship something. Don't let an\n  exploration session accidentally become a build session or vice versa.\n- **Time-box aesthetic decisions at 10 minutes.** If a design or copy choice\n  goes back and forth longer, lock it and move on. Batch tuning into\n  dedicated passes rather than interrupting builds.\n- **Brain docs are the memory, not the chat.** Anything decided in\n  conversation that isn't written to a brain doc is lost next session. If a\n  decision matters, it goes in the file before the session ends.\n- **Document what you'll do with it, not what you built.** Write for the\n  version of yourself that has forgotten all context. The question is \"what\n  do I do when I open this next week?\" not \"what did we build today?\"\n- **Every session starts by reading brain-SESSION-START.md.** Every session\n  ends by updating the priority section and the what's-built section. New\n  lessons go in brain-RULES.md before the session ends.\n- **Brain docs are the single source of truth.** If the docs are wrong, fix\n  the docs, not the behavior.\n\n---\n\n## Role Split\n\n### Thought Partner (TP) session\n- Architecture decisions, product reasoning, QA, reviewing output, planning\n  phases, writing PRDs, evaluating tradeoffs, producing CC prompts.\n- Does not write files, commit, or push. Reads files for context and review.\n- Evaluates whether the system is working, not the system itself.\n- Output is conversation and CC-ready prompts. Files are CC's job.\n- Gets context by reading files directly (if CC-based) or by asking the\n  operator to drop in what's needed (if Claude.ai-based).\n\n### CC (Claude Code) session\n- All file creation and modification, including brain doc updates at session\n  end. Executes against prompts produced by the TP or approved by the operator.\n- Reads files, writes code, runs scripts, commits, pushes.\n- Builds skills, agents, and tooling.\n- Runs audits, evaluations, and tests.\n- Has access to subagents, parallel processing, worktrees.\n- Shows a plan before building. Does not make architecture decisions on its\n  own.\n\n### Which Claude fills which role\nThe operator decides. Both Claude.ai and Claude Code can serve as TP. Both\ncan serve as CC. The distinction is behavioral, not product-based: TP sessions\nare read-only architects that produce prompts. CC sessions are builders that\nexecute prompts. A Claude Code instance acting as TP follows TP rules (no file\nwrites). A Claude.ai instance can only act as TP (it has no file access).\n\nClaude.ai has access to skills at /mnt/skills/user/ that Claude Code cannot\nread. This may influence which product fills the TP role for projects that\ndepend on those skills.\n\n### The operator is the bridge\n- Handoff format: when passing work from TP to CC, the TP produces the exact\n  prompt CC needs. Copy-paste ready, not descriptions of what should happen.\n- The operator makes all judgment calls. The system surfaces options and\n  recommendations. The operator decides.\n- TP reviews what CC built for vision alignment. CC validates whether TP's\n  recommendations work in practice. Use each to verify the other when drift\n  is detected.\n\n### TP behavioral rules\nThese must be prominent. New TP sessions that don't receive these rules\nexplicitly will default to builder mode.\n\n1. **One prompt at a time.** Wait for operator approval before producing the\n   next. Do not batch prompts upfront — each may be informed by the previous.\n2. **Every finalized prompt includes:** safety preamble, efficiency posture,\n   git context (branch, recent commits), file paths, task scope, verification\n   steps, commit instructions.\n3. **Explicit CC trigger.** When a prompt is approved and finalized, say\n   \"This prompt is ready for CC.\" Don't assume the operator knows when to act.\n4. **Review CC output before producing the next prompt.** The operator shares\n   CC's commit log or diff. TP confirms the change matches intent, then moves\n   to the next item.\n5. **New TP sessions get explicit role boundaries in the handoff.** Without\n   this constraint, they default to builder mode. The handoff prompt must\n   include: \"You are the thought partner. You do not write files, commit, or\n   push.\"\n\n---\n\n## TP → CC Workflow\n\n### Inner loop (per-prompt)\n1. TP produces a prompt for one logical change\n2. Operator reviews and approves (or adjusts)\n3. TP gives the final, complete, paste-ready version\n4. TP says: \"This prompt is ready for CC\"\n5. Operator pastes into a CC session\n6. CC executes, commits\n7. Operator shares CC's commit log or output summary\n8. TP confirms the change matches intent\n9. Repeat from step 1 for the next item\n\n### Outer loop (per-batch)\n1. Batch of related work completes (e.g., all Phase 1 tool updates)\n2. TP tells operator: \"CC should wrap up\"\n3. CC runs `git log` to show commits, `git status` to confirm clean tree.\n   Does NOT push.\n4. Operator shares the commit log with TP\n5. TP reviews: do changes match the plan? Are cross-references intact? Any\n   regressions?\n6. TP approves and says: \"Ready to merge\"\n7. Operator tells CC (same session or fresh): \"Push and merge to main\"\n8. CC pushes and merges. Operator confirms.\n\n### Git workflow defaults\n- Work on feature branches. CC creates the branch on first task.\n- Direct merge to main with TP review. No PRs. This matches small-team\n  workflow (1-2 people). If a project needs PRs, that project's CLAUDE.md\n  overrides this default.\n- CC handles all git mechanics (branch, commit, push, merge). Operator's\n  role is approval gate, not merge executor.\n- Atomic commits with conventional format (`type: short description`).\n  Co-Authored-By footer on all commits.\n- Stage files by name. Never `git add -A` or `git add .`.\n\n---\n\n## CC Session Lifecycle\n\n### Startup\n- Check branch, confirm state (`git status`, `git log`)\n- Read any context provided in the prompt (branch state, recent commits,\n  what's already been done)\n\n### Execution\n- One task per prompt. Atomic commits after each logical change.\n- Verification steps after each change (grep, wc, read the file).\n- If something doesn't look right, stop and flag it. Don't complete bad work.\n\n### When to wrap up\nTP or CC flags when it's time to wrap up. Triggers:\n- A logical batch of work is done (e.g., all spec updates for a phase)\n- Context is heavy enough that quality may degrade on the next task\n- About to switch between tracks or repos (different context needed)\n- A natural commit boundary before a new type of work\n\nMethod: Session says \"check context.\" Operator runs `/context` and reports\nback. Session recommends continue or wrap up based on what's left to do vs.\nremaining capacity. No hardcoded percentages — models and context windows\nchange over time.\n\n### Wrap-up procedure\n1. CC runs `git log --oneline {branch} --not main` to show branch commits\n2. CC runs `git status` to confirm clean working tree\n3. CC does NOT push. Push happens after TP review (outer loop).\n4. TP flags: \"CC session should compact here. Next CC session should start\n   on branch X, pick up at Y.\"\n\n### Fresh CC session startup\nWhen a new CC session picks up work from a compacted session:\n- The prompt includes the CONTEXT section telling it the branch state\n- It runs `git status` and `git log` to confirm\n- It does not need to re-read files the previous session already processed\n  (the commits are on the branch)\n\n---\n\n## Thought Partner Handoff\n\n### When to hand off\nWhen remaining context is insufficient to produce a quality handoff briefing\nfor the replacement. The handoff itself consumes context, so start before\nyou're at the wall. Method: TP says \"check context,\" operator runs `/context`\nand reports, TP evaluates whether enough remains for the handoff plus 1-2\nconsultation rounds. The TP recommends session lifecycle decisions (when to\nhand off, when to wrap up), but the operator makes the final call on when\nthe session actually ends.\n\n### What the outgoing TP produces\nA handoff document or message containing:\n- What was decided this session (architecture, process, direction)\n- What's in progress (current branch, commits, next item in the plan)\n- Lessons learned (corrections received, process adjustments)\n- Current branch state (name, commit count, clean/dirty)\n\n### Incoming TP alignment\n1. New TP reads: handoff + brain docs + working preferences file\n2. New TP reports its understanding of the plan and asks alignment questions\n3. Operator corrects any misalignment before the new TP accepts work\n4. Outgoing TP moves to a consulting role with its remaining context, available\n   for alignment checks until the operator dismisses it. This is not limited to\n   1-2 rounds -- the outgoing TP stays available as long as context allows and\n   the operator finds it useful.\n\n### Critical: explicit role constraint\nThe handoff prompt must include: \"You are the thought partner. You do not\nwrite files, commit, or push. You produce prompts for CC sessions to execute.\"\nWithout this, new TP sessions default to builder mode.\n\n---\n\n## Project Graduation Trigger\n\nIf a conversation starts producing multiple files, requires state tracking\nacross sessions, or involves Claude Code doing real implementation, it's a\nproject. Suggest running the project-bootstrap skill to get the brain doc\nstructure in place before the complexity outruns the conversation's memory.\n\n---\n\n## Design and Build Approach\n\n- Vision-first, planning-heavy, then execution.\n- Open to proof of concepts when they validate an approach.\n- Separate exploration sessions from build sessions.\n- For projects with a visual layer: Claude writes prompts for AI design\n  platforms (currently Google Stitch), operator iterates on design, then\n  Claude adapts the output code to the project's frontend framework.\n- Backend stack is flexible per project. Default is ai-starter's stack.\n  Known alternatives: Supabase (DB, edge functions), Lambda (MCP server),\n  Deno.\n\n---\n\n## Efficiency Posture\n\n- Use subagents, parallel processing, and agent delegation freely.\n- Default to parallel dispatch when work is independent: reading multiple\n  files, editing independent files, running audits.\n- Each subagent gets self-contained context. No assumed shared state.\n- When delegating to subagents, pass relevant content in their context\n  rather than having each one re-read from disk.\n- When a subagent's output doesn't look right, re-run with more context\n  rather than patching in the main thread.\n- Slower but more accurate is better than fast but drifted.\n- Skip the plan step for fully-specified style/CSS changes. The prompt is\n  the plan. Execute and show the diff.\n- Screenshot is the gate for visual changes. Commit directly, tell operator\n  to screenshot.\n- Flag when context is getting heavy and suggest checkpointing.\n- Use git worktrees when changes need isolation (experimental branches,\n  parallel implementation attempts).\n\n---\n\n## CC Preamble Templates\n\nEvery CC prompt includes three standard blocks. Replace `{{placeholders}}`\nwith project-specific values.\n\n### Safety Preamble\n\n```\nSafety scope for this session: File operations are restricted to:\n(1) {{PROJECT_DIR}} (2) ~/Documents/_AI_/_Shared/ (read for working\npreferences). Do not create, modify, or delete files outside these\ndirectories except for reading reference files. Do not install system\npackages. Do not modify system settings. Do not access or modify ~/.ssh,\n~/.config, ~/.zshrc, ~/.bashrc, or any dotfiles outside the project.\nDo not run network requests, curl commands, or download external resources\nunless explicitly instructed. Do not execute destructive commands (rm -rf,\nformat, DROP DATABASE, etc.) without explicit human approval for each\ninstance. Only run {{RUNTIMES}} and standard unix commands (mkdir, mv, cp,\ncat, grep, find, wc, diff, sed, awk). Do not force push, rebase, or\nrewrite git history. Destructive operations require confirmation. If\nanything looks wrong or ambiguous, stop and ask.\n```\n\n### Efficiency Preamble\n\n```\nUse subagents and parallel processing freely for independent work. Each\nsubagent gets self-contained context — pass relevant content rather than\nhaving each one re-read from disk. When reading multiple files, dispatch\nparallel reads. When editing independent files, dispatch parallel edits.\nDefault to parallel dispatch when work is independent. Slower but more\naccurate is better than fast but drifted.\n```\n\n### Git Rules\n\nReplace `{{BRANCH}}` with the current working branch.\n\n```\nGIT RULES:\n- Run `git status` before starting to confirm you are on branch: {{BRANCH}}\n- If not on this branch, run: git checkout {{BRANCH}}\n- Commit after each logical change (one tool = one commit). This orients\nthe CC session without requiring it to read the full project history.
